verseByVerse.quote: Meshobab, Jamlech, Joshah the son of Amaziah, Joel, Jehu the son of Joshibiah, son of Seraiah, son of Asiel, Elioenai, Jaakobah, Jeshohaiah, Asaiah, Adiel, Jesimiel, Benaiah, Ziza the son of Shiphi, son of Allon, son of Jedaiah, son of Shimri, son of Shemaiah— these mentioned by name were princes in their clans, and their fathers' houses increased greatly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thirteen princes are named, and the reason for naming them is at the end: these mentioned by name were princes in their clans, and their fathers' houses increased greatly.

Increase, in a tribe the text has just said did not increase. The general trend was decline and inside it these households grew. The Chronicler will not let a summary sentence flatten the individual cases, which is a small mercy of the same kind he showed the men who died childless in chapter 2.

verseByVerse.quote: They journeyed to the entrance of Gedor, to the east side of the valley, to seek pasture for their flocks, where they found rich, good pasture, and the land was very broad, quiet, and peaceful, for the former inhabitants there belonged to Ham. These, registered by name, came in the days of Hezekiah, king of Judah, and destroyed their tents and the Meunites who were found there, and marked them for destruction to this day, and settled in their place, because there was pasture there for their flocks. And some of them, five hundred men of the Simeonites, went to Mount Seir, having as their leaders Pelatiah, Neariah, Rephaiah, and Uzziel, the sons of Ishi. And they defeated the remnant of the Amalekites who had escaped, and they have lived there to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two expeditions close the chapter, and both are about land: men from a tribe with too little of it going out to find some.

The first party went east to Gedor and found what the text calls rich, good pasture, and the land was very broad, quiet, and peaceful, and took it in Hezekiah's day. The second went south to Mount Seir — five hundred men, four leaders named — and defeated the remnant of the Amalekites who had escaped.

That last clause finishes something. Amalek entered this book as a name in a genealogy: Timna bore Amalek to Eliphaz (1:36), and the nation that came from him ambushed Israel on the way out of Egypt, and Saul was ordered to end them and kept the king and the best of the sheep. Generations later, five hundred men of the smallest tribe walk into the hills and finish the job, and there is no song about it and no prophet present.

God's purposes do not lapse when the man commissioned to carry them out refuses. They are handed on, quietly, to people whose names nobody remembers, and they are completed.

5.title: Reuben, Gad, and Manasseh: Faithfulness and Failure East of the Jordan
5.text: <sup>1</sup>The sons of Reuben the firstborn of Israel (for he was the firstborn, but because he defiled his father's couch, his birthright was given to the sons of Joseph the son of Israel, so that he could not be enrolled as the oldest son;<sup>2</sup>though Judah became strong among his brothers and a chief came from him, yet the birthright belonged to Joseph),<sup>3</sup>the sons of Reuben, the firstborn of Israel: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi.<sup>4</sup>The sons of Joel: Shemaiah his son, Gog his son, Shimei his son,<sup>5</sup>Micah his son, Reaiah his son, Baal his son,<sup>6</sup>Beerah his son, whom Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria carried away into exile; he was a chief of the Reubenites.<sup>7</sup>And his kinsmen by their clans, when the genealogy of their generations was recorded: the chief, Jeiel, and Zechariah,<sup>8</sup>and Bela the son of Azaz, son of Shema, son of Joel, who lived in Aroer, as far as Nebo and Baal-meon.<sup>9</sup>He also lived to the east as far as the entrance of the desert this side of the Euphrates, because their livestock had multiplied in the land of Gilead.<sup>10</sup>And in the days of Saul they waged war against the Hagrites, who fell into their hand. And they lived in their tents throughout all the region east of Gilead.<sup>11</sup>The sons of Gad lived over against them in the land of Bashan as far as Salecah:<sup>12</sup>Joel the chief, Shapham the second, Janai, and Shaphat in Bashan.<sup>13</sup>And their kinsmen according to their fathers' houses: Michael, Meshullam, Sheba, Jorai, Jacan, Zia and Eber, seven.<sup>14</sup>These were the sons of Abihail the son of Huri, son of Jaroah, son of Gilead, son of Michael, son of Jeshishai, son of Jahdo, son of Buz.<sup>15</sup>Ahi the son of Abdiel, son of Guni, was chief in their fathers' houses,<sup>16</sup>and they lived in Gilead, in Bashan and in its towns, and in all the pasturelands of Sharon to their limits.<sup>17</sup>All of these were recorded in genealogies in the days of Jotham king of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam king of Israel.<sup>18</sup>The Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh had valiant men who carried shield and sword, and drew the bow, expert in war, 44,760, able to go to war.<sup>19</sup>They waged war against the Hagrites, Jetur, Naphish, and Nodab.<sup>20</sup>And when they prevailed over them, the Hagrites and all who were with them were given into their hands, for they cried out to God in the battle, and he granted their urgent plea because they trusted in him.<sup>21</sup>They carried off their livestock: 50,000 of their camels, 250,000 sheep, 2,000 donkeys, and 100,000 men alive.<sup>22</sup>For many fell, because the war was of God. And they lived in their place until the exile.<sup>23</sup>The members of the half-tribe of Manasseh lived in the land. They were very numerous from Bashan to Baal-hermon, Senir, and Mount Hermon.<sup>24</sup>These were the heads of their fathers' houses: Epher, Ishi, Eliel, Azriel, Jeremiah, Hodaviah, and Jahdiel, mighty warriors, famous men, heads of their fathers' houses.<sup>25</sup>But they broke faith with the God of their fathers, and whored after the gods of the peoples of the land, whom God had destroyed before them.<sup>26</sup>So the God of Israel stirred up the spirit of Pul king of Assyria, the spirit of Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria, and he took them into exile, namely, the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, and brought them to Halah, Habor, Hara, and the river Gozan, to this day.
5.overview:
The two and a half tribes east of the Jordan are recorded together: Reuben, with the explanation of why the firstborn's birthright went elsewhere (vv. 1-10); Gad beside him, with a note that the survey was taken in the eighth century (vv. 11-17); the combined fighting strength and their victory over the Hagrites (vv. 18-22); and half-Manasseh, numerous and famous, ending in idolatry and deportation (vv. 23-26).

The chapter is arranged around a reversal that is easy to read past. Verse 20 records a prayer answered in the middle of a battle. Verse 25 records the same people breaking faith with the God who answered it. Between them lies everything the book has to say about why a nation with such a history ended up in Babylon.
5.theology:
Verse 20 is one of the clearest statements in the Old Testament of how prayer and means work together: 44,760 expert soldiers, and a victory attributed to a cry and a trust. The Chronicler does not resolve the tension because he does not feel one. Human competence is not a rival to divine action; it is one of the ways divine action arrives.

Verse 26 says the same thing about judgment. God stirred up the spirit of a pagan king, and a pagan king did what pagan kings do, and the exile was both an Assyrian policy and a divine act. This is the doctrine the whole book will need when it comes to explain why Jerusalem fell: not that God lost, but that God was doing something.
5.examples:
The hardest verse here for a Christian reader is not verse 25 but verse 20 read alongside it. A man can look back on a time when he cried out and was heard, and treat that memory as evidence about himself. These tribes had exactly such a memory, and it did not hold them for a generation.

What holds is not the memory of an answered prayer but the God who answered it, and he was as present in the deportation as in the victory. The tribes who crossed back over Jordan into Assyrian hands did not stop being his. Their names are in this chapter, written down by a man in Jerusalem centuries after their nation had ceased to exist.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter opens by explaining itself. Reuben was the firstborn, and because he defiled his father's couch, his birthright was given to the sons of Joseph — and yet the ruler came from Judah (vv. 1-2). Reuben's clans are then traced east of the Jordan, ending on a chief named Beerah whom Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria carried away into exile (v. 6), and on the pasture their multiplying livestock pushed them into (vv. 9-10).
verseByVerse.theology: Three things are separated here that are usually confused: the birthright, the double portion, and the throne. Reuben lost all of it by one act. Joseph received the inheritance and Judah the crown, and neither of them was the eldest. Primogeniture is the world's way of ordering a family, and God has overruled it in nearly every generation of this book.
verseByVerse.examples: A single night's sin cost Reuben's descendants a status they never recovered, and the register still names him first out of respect for a birth order that no longer meant anything.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Reuben the firstborn of Israel (for he was the firstborn, but because he defiled his father's couch, his birthright was given to the sons of Joseph the son of Israel, so that he could not be enrolled as the oldest son; though Judah became strong among his brothers and a chief came from him, yet the birthright belonged to Joseph),
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two verses of explanation, and they answer a question the book raised three chapters ago without acknowledging it.

Why does a genealogy of Israel start with Judah, who was fourth? Because Reuben, who was first, defiled his father's couch — he slept with his father's concubine — and his birthright went to the sons of Joseph. And yet, the Chronicler adds, the birthright and the crown did not travel together: though Judah became strong among his brothers and a chief came from him, yet the birthright belonged to Joseph.

So the double portion went to one brother and the throne to another, and the eldest got neither. Nothing in this family has ever been decided by the order of birth. Isaac over Ishmael, Jacob over Esau, Judah and Joseph over Reuben, David over seven brothers — the pattern is so consistent that by the time God passes over an obvious man for an unlikely one, it has stopped being a surprise and become a signature.

verseByVerse.quote: the sons of Reuben, the firstborn of Israel: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi. The sons of Joel: Shemaiah his son, Gog his son, Shimei his son, Micah his son, Reaiah his son, Baal his son, Beerah his son, whom Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria carried away into exile; he was a chief of the Reubenites. And his kinsmen by their clans, when the genealogy of their generations was recorded: the chief, Jeiel, and Zechariah, and Bela the son of Azaz, son of Shema, son of Joel, who lived in Aroer, as far as Nebo and Baal-meon. He also lived to the east as far as the entrance of the desert this side of the Euphrates, because their livestock had multiplied in the land of Gilead. And in the days of Saul they waged war against the Hagrites, who fell into their hand. And they lived in their tents throughout all the region east of Gilead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Reuben's clans, spreading east into Gilead because their livestock had multiplied. That is how the tribe ended up where it did: good grazing on the wrong side of the river, chosen back in Numbers when Reuben and Gad looked at Jazer and Gilead and asked not to cross over.

It was a reasonable request and it put them outside the Jordan, first in the path of anything coming from the north. Verse 6 records the result in a subordinate clause: Beerah, a chief of the Reubenites, whom Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria carried away into exile. The name of the empire that ended the northern tribes appears in this book for the first time inside a list of fathers and sons.

A decision about pasture, taken for sound agricultural reasons by men who meant no harm by it, set the geography that four centuries later decided who went into captivity first.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–22 — The War That Was of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Gad's clans are set down beside Reuben's in Bashan and Gilead, recorded in the days of Jotham and Jeroboam (vv. 11-17). Then the fighting strength of all two and a half tribes — 44,760 men, expert in war (v. 18) — and a campaign against the Hagrites in which they cried out to God in the battle, and he granted their urgent plea because they trusted in him (v. 20). The plunder is counted in six figures, and the reason for the victory is given flatly: the war was of God (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: The verse gives the whole doctrine of prayer in war in one line, and gives it in the right order: they cried out, he granted, because they trusted. The trust is named as the ground and the crying out as the act. Neither the number of men nor the expertise in verse 18 is offered as an explanation.
verseByVerse.examples: Men who are genuinely good at something cried out to God in the middle of doing it. Competence and dependence are not rivals here, and the register mentions both in the same paragraph without embarrassment.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Gad lived over against them in the land of Bashan as far as Salecah: Joel the chief, Shapham the second, Janai, and Shaphat in Bashan. And their kinsmen according to their fathers' houses: Michael, Meshullam, Sheba, Jorai, Jacan, Zia and Eber, seven. These were the sons of Abihail the son of Huri, son of Jaroah, son of Gilead, son of Michael, son of Jeshishai, son of Jahdo, son of Buz. Ahi the son of Abdiel, son of Guni, was chief in their fathers' houses, and they lived in Gilead, in Bashan and in its towns, and in all the pasturelands of Sharon to their limits. All of these were recorded in genealogies in the days of Jotham king of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam king of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gad settled alongside Reuben, from Bashan to Salecah, and their record was compiled in the days of Jotham king of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam king of Israel (v. 17).

That is an administrative note and it is quietly remarkable. Somebody conducted a genealogical survey of the trans-Jordan tribes in the eighth century, and the document survived the destruction of those very tribes, and a scribe in Jerusalem still had it three hundred years later after his own city had burned.

Records outlive the people they record. That is the assumption the entire book rests on, and the reason a returning exile could be handed nine chapters of names at all.

verseByVerse.quote: The Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh had valiant men who carried shield and sword, and drew the bow, expert in war, 44,760, able to go to war. They waged war against the Hagrites, Jetur, Naphish, and Nodab. And when they prevailed over them, the Hagrites and all who were with them were given into their hands, for they cried out to God in the battle, and he granted their urgent plea because they trusted in him. They carried off their livestock: 50,000 of their camels, 250,000 sheep, 2,000 donkeys, and 100,000 men alive. For many fell, because the war was of God. And they lived in their place until the exile.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now a battle, and it is described twice — once in terms of the army and once in terms of God, and the two accounts do not compete.

The army first: 44,760 men who carried shield and sword, and drew the bow, expert in war. Then the battle: they prevailed, and the Hagrites were given into their hands, for they cried out to God in the battle, and he granted their urgent plea because they trusted in him.

Notice where the crying out happens. Not the night before, not at a shrine, not through a priest — in the battle, mid-fight, by men who were themselves expert. The Chronicler puts the professional competence and the desperate prayer in adjacent verses and treats neither as a substitute for the other.

And then the plunder, counted like an inventory: fifty thousand camels, a quarter of a million sheep, a hundred thousand captives. Followed by the explanation, which is four words long: the war was of God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–26 — And Then They Broke Faith
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Half-Manasseh is described as very numerous, its heads of houses mighty warriors, famous men (v. 24). And then the sentence the chapter has been walking towards: But they broke faith with the God of their fathers, and whored after the gods of the peoples of the land, whom God had destroyed before them (v. 25). So God stirred up the spirit of Pul king of Assyria, and the tribes east of the Jordan went into exile first (v. 26).
verseByVerse.theology: The Chronicler's verb returns. Achan broke faith and Israel lost a battle; these tribes broke faith and lost a territory; Judah will break faith and lose the temple (9:1); Saul broke faith and lost a kingdom (10:13). One word carries the book's entire account of why things went wrong.
verseByVerse.examples: Assyria is not the subject of verse 26. God is. The empire that deported them is described as a spirit stirred up by the God they had left, which is a far more frightening reading of the news than the political one.

verseByVerse.quote: The members of the half-tribe of Manasseh lived in the land. They were very numerous from Bashan to Baal-hermon, Senir, and Mount Hermon. These were the heads of their fathers' houses: Epher, Ishi, Eliel, Azriel, Jeremiah, Hodaviah, and Jahdiel, mighty warriors, famous men, heads of their fathers' houses. But they broke faith with the God of their fathers, and whored after the gods of the peoples of the land, whom God had destroyed before them. So the God of Israel stirred up the spirit of Pul king of Assyria, the spirit of Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria, and he took them into exile, namely, the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, and brought them to Halah, Habor, Hara, and the river Gozan, to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Half-Manasseh is numerous, its chiefs are mighty warriors, famous men, and the chapter has been going well for eleven verses. Then one word turns it over.

But they broke faith with the God of their fathers, and whored after the gods of the peoples of the land, whom God had destroyed before them. The last clause is the sting: they took up the worship of nations that were no longer there, and the reason those nations were no longer there was that God had removed them for that worship.

Set verse 25 against verse 20 and the chapter's real subject appears. The men who cried out to God in the battle and were heard are the same men, or their sons, who are here worshipping the gods of the people they defeated. An answered prayer is not a character reference. It settles nothing about the next generation, or about the next decade of the same generation.

So the God of Israel stirred up the spirit of Pul king of Assyria, and the tribes who had asked for the land east of the river were the first to lose it. The sentence is written from the wrong side of the empire on purpose: the superpower is not the actor, it is the instrument, and the God who granted their urgent plea in verse 20 is the God who moved Assyria in verse 26. He was not less faithful in the judgment than he had been in the victory.

pasturelands,<sup>81</sup>Heshbon with its pasturelands, and Jazer with its pasturelands.
6.overview:
The longest chapter in the book, and it does three things. It runs the high-priestly line from Aaron to the man who went to Babylon (vv. 1-15). It traces the three Levite clans and then, from within them, the singers David appointed over the service of song — Heman, Asaph and Ethan, with their pedigrees (vv. 16-48). And it maps the forty-eight towns given to a tribe that had no land of its own (vv. 49-81), with one verse in the middle stating what the whole tribe existed to do: make atonement for Israel (v. 49).

Two things are buried in it that repay the reading. Samuel's family line runs back to Korah, and Samuel's grandson is the chief musician (vv. 22-33). And the landless tribe turns out to hold all six cities of refuge (vv. 57, 67).
6.theology:
Two offices are given equal footing here, and one of them is usually treated as decoration. Priests offered blood; singers offered song; both were appointed, both had to prove descent, both are recorded in the same chapter with the same care. Israel's worship was never a service with music added to it.

And underneath the whole tribe lies verse 49. Atonement is the reason Levi exists, and the arrangement was permanent, daily and unfinished — every morning and every evening for a thousand years, because no offering ever settled the matter. The chapter is a monument to a system that worked and could not conclude, kept going by twenty-two generations of men who died in office.
6.examples:
Korah's descendants are the pastoral centre of this chapter. A man rebelled so catastrophically that the ground opened, and his children were spared, and their family produced a prophet, a chief musician and eleven psalms. Nobody in that family chose their ancestor. What they did with him was to spend the next four centuries singing in the building he had tried to storm.

Asaph, standing at Heman's right hand, wrote the psalm that begins by admitting he had almost stumbled from envying the prosperity of the wicked. The man appointed over Israel's praise put his worst doubt in the hymn book, and Israel sang it for centuries. There has never been a requirement to be resolved before leading worship.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — The High Priests, Down to the Exile
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The line runs from Levi through Kohath and Amram to Aaron, Moses, and Miriam (v. 3), and then follows Aaron's third son Eleazar — because the first two died before the LORD — through Phinehas and Zadok (v. 8) and on for twenty-two generations. It ends in one clause: Jehozadak went into exile when the LORD sent Judah and Jerusalem into exile by the hand of Nebuchadnezzar (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: The priesthood is presented as a succession, not as a career, and the succession is unbroken from Sinai to Babylon. The Chronicler stops the list at the deportation without comment, though every reader of his knew that Jehozadak's son came home with Zerubbabel and stood in the rebuilt courts. A line that goes into exile is not a line that has ended.
verseByVerse.examples: Nadab and Abihu are named in verse 3 alongside Eleazar and Ithamar with nothing said about the strange fire. The register records that they were born; the reason the line runs through their younger brother it leaves for another book to explain.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Levi: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. The sons of Kohath: Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel. The children of Amram: Aaron, Moses, and Miriam. The sons of Aaron: Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three sons of Levi, and the chapter follows the middle one. Kohath's grandson Amram fathered Aaron, Moses, and Miriam — and the Chronicler, who is building towards a temple, follows Aaron and lets Moses go.

That is a startling piece of editing. The man who brought Israel out of Egypt is named once, in a list, between his brother and his sister, and does not appear in the genealogy again. The line this book needs runs through the priest, not the prophet.

Aaron's four sons are given in order, and nothing is said about the first two. Nadab and Abihu offered unauthorised fire before the LORD and died in front of the altar on the day it was consecrated. The register lists them, because they were born, and passes on to Eleazar, because the priesthood did.

verseByVerse.quote: Eleazar fathered Phinehas, Phinehas fathered Abishua, Abishua fathered Bukki, Bukki fathered Uzzi, Uzzi fathered Zerahiah, Zerahiah fathered Meraioth, Meraioth fathered Amariah, Amariah fathered Ahitub, Ahitub fathered Zadok, Zadok fathered Ahimaaz,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Five verses, ten generations, and two names in them carry weight far beyond their clause.

Phinehas is the grandson of Aaron who drove a spear through an Israelite and a Midianite woman in the middle of a plague, and was given a covenant of perpetual priesthood for it. Zadok is the priest who stayed with David when Absalom took the city and would not carry the ark out of Jerusalem with the fugitives, and whose house held the high priesthood until the Maccabees.

Neither story is told. The Chronicler is running a line of custody: who held the office, and from whom, and in what order. What a man did in the office belongs to the narrative books; that he held it, and handed it on, belongs here.

verseByVerse.quote: Ahimaaz fathered Azariah, Azariah fathered Johanan, and Johanan fathered Azariah (it was he who served as priest in the house that Solomon built in Jerusalem). Azariah fathered Amariah, Amariah fathered Ahitub, Ahitub fathered Zadok, Zadok fathered Shallum, Shallum fathered Hilkiah, Hilkiah fathered Azariah, Azariah fathered Seraiah, Seraiah fathered Jehozadak; and Jehozadak went into exile when the LORD sent Judah and Jerusalem into exile by the hand of Nebuchadnezzar.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Twenty-two generations of high priests, one name a clause, and then the sentence the whole list has been travelling towards.

And Jehozadak went into exile when the LORD sent Judah and Jerusalem into exile by the hand of Nebuchadnezzar.

Read the grammar of it. Nebuchadnezzar is the hand; the LORD is the subject. The most powerful man in the world, at the head of the army that broke the city, is described in Israel's own priestly records as an instrument. The Chronicler will not let his readers think of Babylon as something that happened to God.

And then the list simply stops. No return, no restoration, no comment — which is odd, because the men reading it knew perfectly well that Jehozadak's son Jeshua had come home with the first company and stood in the new courts. The line is left ending in captivity, and the reader is expected to supply the sequel out of his own memory, because the reader is the sequel.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The three Levite clans are traced (vv. 16-30), and inside Kohath's branch sit Korah (v. 22), Elkanah, and the sons of Samuel (v. 28). Then the chapter turns: David put men in charge of the service of song in the house of the LORD after the ark rested there (v. 31), and their pedigrees are given as carefully as any priest's — Heman in the centre, son of Joel, son of Samuel (v. 33); Asaph on his right (v. 39); Ethan and the Merarites on his left (v. 44); and the rest of the Levites appointed for all the service of the tabernacle (v. 48).
verseByVerse.theology: Music in Israel's worship is not an atmosphere or a preference. It is an office, with a charter from the king, a place in the building, and a genealogy behind it. The men who sang had to prove their descent exactly as the men who sacrificed did.
verseByVerse.examples: Trace Heman's line back far enough and it reaches Korah, whom the earth swallowed for rebelling against Aaron. Numbers adds, almost in passing, that the sons of Korah did not die. Eleven psalms carry their name. The family that led the revolt against the priesthood ended up leading the singing.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Levi: Gershom, Kohath, and Merari. And these are the names of the sons of Gershom: Libni and Shimei. The sons of Kohath: Amram, Izhar, Hebron and Uzziel. The sons of Merari: Mahli and Mushi. These are the clans of the Levites according to their fathers. Of Gershom: Libni his son, Jahath his son, Zimmah his son, Joah his son, Iddo his son, Zerah his son, Jeatherai his son.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The three clans again, from the top and in more detail, because the priests were one family inside Levi and the rest of the tribe was the other twenty-three twenty-fourths of it.

Gershom's descendants and Merari's are set out with no office attached and no story told — Libni, Jahath, Zimmah, Joah, Iddo, Zerah, Jeatherai. These are the men who carried the frames and the curtains and the bases across a desert, and then kept the doors and the stores of a temple for four hundred years.

The register gives them the same treatment it gives the high priests: name, father, generation. In the tribe whose whole existence was proximity to God, there was no second class.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Kohath: Amminadab his son, Korah his son, Assir his son, Elkanah his son, Ebiasaph his son, Assir his son, Tahath his son, Uriel his son, Uzziah his son, and Shaul his son. The sons of Elkanah: Amasai and Ahimoth, Elkanah his son, Zophai his son, Nahath his son, Eliab his son, Jeroham his son, Elkanah his son. The sons of Samuel: Joel his firstborn, the second Abijah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Kohath's branch, and in the middle of it a name that ought to stop the reader dead. Korah his son (v. 22).

Korah led the rebellion. He stood up with two hundred and fifty men and told Moses and Aaron that the whole congregation was holy and the priesthood was a presumption, and the ground opened under him. Numbers records the earth closing over his household — and then adds, ten chapters later and almost as an aside, But the sons of Korah did not die (Num. 26:11).

They did not die, and this is what became of them. The line runs on through Elkanah and Jeroham and Elkanah again until it reaches a man whose two boys are named in verse 28: The sons of Samuel: Joel his firstborn, the second Abijah.

Samuel. The child at Shiloh who slept near the ark and heard his name called in the dark; the man who anointed Israel's first two kings. He is a descendant of the man who tried to seize the priesthood by force. The book that tells his story calls his father an Ephrathite of the hill country of Ephraim, which is where the family lived. This is where the family came from.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Merari: Mahli, Libni his son, Shimei his son, Uzzah his son, Shimea his son, Haggiah his son, and Asaiah his son.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Merari's line closes the section: Mahli, Libni, Shimei, Uzzah, Shimea, Haggiah, Asaiah. Seven names, no comment.

One of them is a warning the reader will meet in seven chapters. A man named Uzzah put out his hand to steady the ark on a new cart and died beside it, and David left the ark in a stranger's house for three months because he was afraid. The Uzzah of chapter 13 is not this man, but he is of this family, and the family is Merari — the clan whose ancestral task was to carry the sanctuary and who therefore, of all people, knew how it was to be carried.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the men whom David put in charge of the service of song in the house of the LORD after the ark rested there. They ministered with song before the tabernacle of the tent of meeting until Solomon built the house of the LORD in Jerusalem, and they performed their service according to their order.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the chapter changes register, and a new office appears. These are the men whom David put in charge of the service of song in the house of the LORD after the ark rested there.

Three things sit in that sentence. Song is a service, in the same word used of the sacrifices. It has an appointment, made by the king. And it begins after the ark rested there — the music is a response to God's arrival, not a device for summoning him.

Verse 32 adds that they sang before the tent until Solomon built the house, and then performed their service according to their order. Israel's praise was rostered. It had a rota, a place to stand, and a change of premises to manage, and none of that was thought to be in tension with its being worship.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the men who served and their sons. Of the sons of the Kohathites: Heman the singer the son of Joel, son of Samuel, son of Elkanah, son of Jeroham, son of Eliel, son of Toah, son of Zuph, son of Elkanah, son of Mahath, son of Amasai, son of Elkanah, son of Joel, son of Azariah, son of Zephaniah, son of Tahath, son of Assir, son of Ebiasaph, son of Korah, son of Izhar, son of Kohath, son of Levi, son of Israel;
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chief singer is named and his pedigree given for eighteen generations, which is longer than most of the priests are given. He is Heman the singer the son of Joel, son of Samuel — Samuel's grandson, and therefore Korah's descendant.

The family that was swallowed for wanting a place at the altar was given, four centuries later, a place in front of it, with a harp. Eleven of the psalms Israel sang carry the heading of the sons of Korah, and the first of them opens with a soul panting after God the way a deer pants for water. The great-grandchildren of the man who wanted the altar by force ended up writing the songs sung in front of it.

Nothing in the register explains it or draws attention to it. The names are simply laid end to end, and a reader who knows Numbers finds the mercy for himself.

verseByVerse.quote: and his brother Asaph, who stood on his right hand, namely, Asaph the son of Berechiah, son of Shimea, son of Michael, son of Baaseiah, son of Malchijah, son of Ethni, son of Zerah, son of Adaiah, son of Ethan, son of Zimmah, son of Shimei, son of Jahath, son of Gershom, son of Levi.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Asaph stood on his right hand, with his own line back through Gershom to Levi. The three chief singers were drawn one from each clan, so that the whole tribe was represented in the choir and no branch of it owned the music.

Asaph's name stands over twelve psalms, and several of them are the bleakest in the book. One begins by admitting that its writer had almost stumbled from envying the prosperity of the wicked and could not resolve it until he went into the sanctuary. Another asks how long God will be angry with his people's prayers.

The man appointed over Israel's praise put his worst doubt into the hymn book, and Israel sang it for centuries, and nobody struck him off the roster for it. There has never been a requirement to be resolved before leading worship.

verseByVerse.quote: On the left hand were their brothers, the sons of Merari: Ethan the son of Kishi, son of Abdi, son of Malluch, son of Hashabiah, son of Amaziah, son of Hilkiah, son of Amzi, son of Bani, son of Shemer, son of Mahli, son of Mushi, son of Merari, son of Levi. And their brothers the Levites were appointed for all the service of the tabernacle of the house of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ethan and the Merarites stood on the left hand, and the arrangement is complete: Kohath in the centre, Gershom right, Merari left.

Then verse 48, and the vast majority of the tribe. Their brothers the Levites were appointed for all the service of the tabernacle of the house of God. No names, no pedigrees, no instrument. One sentence covers thousands of men whose whole working lives were spent inside that building.

Three men are remembered by name and the rest are covered by a clause, and the clause is not a lesser thing to have been given. The service was the honour. Being recorded was never the point of doing it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 49–81 — Aaron's Altar, and Forty-Eight Towns
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: One verse states what the priests were actually for: Aaron and his sons made offerings on the two altars and to make atonement for Israel (v. 49). Aaron's line is repeated to Ahimaaz (vv. 50-53), and then the chapter becomes a map. Thirteen towns for the priests out of Judah, Simeon and Benjamin (vv. 54-60) — Hebron, Libnah, Anathoth — and the rest of Levi scattered across every other tribe, forty-eight towns in all, each one with its pasturelands (vv. 61-81).
verseByVerse.theology: Levi is the one tribe with no territory, and it was given custody of every place in the country where the guilty could not be touched. Twice the chapter stops to say it — to the sons of Aaron they gave the cities of refuge (v. 57), and again for the Kohathites (v. 67) — and all six are here: Hebron, Shechem, Golan, Kedesh, Bezer, Ramoth. The men whose office was atonement kept the towns where blood was not required, and the manslayer walked out free on the day the high priest died.
verseByVerse.examples: Anathoth is in verse 60, a priestly town like any other. Four centuries later a priest's son from Anathoth was told to buy a field there while the Babylonian army was outside the walls, as a sign that houses and fields would be bought in this land again.

verseByVerse.quote: But Aaron and his sons made offerings on the altar of burnt offering and on the altar of incense for all the work of the Most Holy Place, and to make atonement for Israel, according to all that Moses the servant of God had commanded. These are the sons of Aaron: Eleazar his son, Phinehas his son, Abishua his son, Bukki his son, Uzzi his son, Zerahiah his son, Meraioth his son, Amariah his son, Ahitub his son, Zadok his son, Ahimaaz his son.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After forty-eight verses of who was descended from whom, one verse says what any of it was for.

Aaron and his sons made offerings on the altar of burnt offering and on the altar of incense, and to make atonement for Israel, according to all that Moses the servant of God had commanded.

Atonement is the point of the tribe. Everything else in the chapter — the towns, the singers, the twenty-two generations — exists around that one function: blood carried to an altar so that a guilty people could go on living beside a holy God. The Chronicler states it once, plainly, and goes back to the lists.

It took a whole tribe, a portable sanctuary, forty-eight towns and eleven centuries to keep that sentence running. And it never finished, because the same offerings were made every morning and every evening for a thousand years, and every priest in this list died with the work still outstanding. The Son who ended it made one offering and sat down.

verseByVerse.quote: These are their dwelling places according to their settlements within their borders: to the sons of Aaron of the clans of Kohathites, for theirs was the first lot, to them they gave Hebron in the land of Judah and its surrounding pasturelands, but the fields of the city and its villages they gave to Caleb the son of Jephunneh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter becomes a map, and it opens on Hebron — the oldest town in the story, where Abraham buried Sarah and David reigned for seven years before Jerusalem.

Then a division that says a great deal in one verse. The priests were given the town and its pasturelands; but the fields of the city and its villages they gave to Caleb the son of Jephunneh. Caleb had asked Moses for that hill country forty-five years earlier, when he was eighty-five, on the ground that he had followed the LORD wholly. He got the farmland. The priests got the town and enough grass for their animals.

Nobody was cheated. The tribe that lived on the offerings did not need arable land, and the old soldier who had waited half a century for a promise was not asked to hand over his fields to make room for them.

verseByVerse.quote: To the sons of Aaron they gave the cities of refuge: Hebron, Libnah with its pasturelands, Jattir, Eshtemoa with its pasturelands, Hilen with its pasturelands, Debir with its pasturelands, Ashan with its pasturelands, and Beth-shemesh with its pasturelands; and from the tribe of Benjamin, Gibeon, Geba with its pasturelands, Alemeth with its pasturelands, and Anathoth with its pasturelands. All their cities throughout their clans were thirteen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And then the phrase that changes what this list is. To the sons of Aaron they gave the cities of refuge.

A city of refuge was where a man who had killed somebody without meaning to could run and live. He fled to the gate, stated his case to the elders, and stayed inside the walls until the high priest died — safe from the avenger of blood, who had every legal right to him outside. Six such towns were appointed in Israel, and this chapter records that the priests and the Levites held all six of them.

So the tribe with no land of its own was given custody of every place in the country where the guilty could not be touched. The men whose office was atonement kept the towns where blood was not required. And the day the fugitive walked out free was the day the high priest died.

Anathoth is in verse 60, a priestly town like the rest. Four centuries later a priest's son from Anathoth was told to buy a field there while the Babylonian army was outside the walls, and to put the deed in a jar, as a sign that houses and fields and vineyards would be bought in that land again.

verseByVerse.quote: To the rest of the Kohathites were given by lot out of the clan of the tribe, out of the half-tribe, the half of Manasseh, ten cities. To the Gershomites according to their clans were allotted thirteen cities out of the tribes of Issachar, Asher, Naphtali and Manasseh in Bashan. To the Merarites according to their clans were allotted twelve cities out of the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and Zebulun. So the people of Israel gave the Levites the cities with their pasturelands. They gave by lot out of the tribes of Judah, Simeon, and Benjamin these cities that are mentioned by name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rest of the Kohathites, the Gershomites and the Merarites are allotted towns out of the northern tribes, and verse 65 says how it was done: They gave by lot out of the tribes of Judah, Simeon, and Benjamin these cities that are mentioned by name.

By lot. No tribe chose which Levites it would house and no Levite chose his neighbours. The distribution that put a teaching family in every district of Israel was settled by a method that took the decision out of everybody's hands, which is exactly what a lot was for.

verseByVerse.quote: And some of the clans of the sons of Kohath had cities of their territory out of the tribe of Ephraim. They were given the cities of refuge: Shechem with its pasturelands in the hill country of Ephraim, Gezer with its pasturelands, Jokmeam with its pasturelands, Beth-horon with its pasturelands, Aijalon with its pasturelands, Gath-rimmon with its pasturelands, and out of the half-tribe of Manasseh, Aner with its pasturelands, and Bileam with its pasturelands, for the rest of the clans of the Kohathites. To the Gershomites were given out of the clan of the half-tribe of Manasseh: Golan in Bashan with its pasturelands and Ashtaroth with its pasturelands;
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second half of the map, and the refuge formula returns: They were given the cities of refuge: Shechem with its pasturelands in the hill country of Ephraim (v. 67). Shechem is where Joshua gathered Israel to choose whom they would serve, and where Joseph's bones were buried. Golan follows in Bashan (v. 71).

Every town in these verses belonged to somebody else. Ephraim, Dan, half-Manasseh each gave up settlements out of an inheritance they had fought for, so that the tribe with no inheritance could live among them.

verseByVerse.quote: and out of the tribe of Issachar: Kedesh with its pasturelands, Daberath with its pasturelands, Ramoth with its pasturelands, and Anem with its pasturelands; out of the tribe of Asher: Mashal with its pasturelands, Abdon with its pasturelands, Hukok with its pasturelands, and Rehob with its pasturelands; and out of the tribe of Naphtali: Kedesh in Galilee with its pasturelands, Hammon with its pasturelands, and Kiriathaim with its pasturelands. To the rest of the Merarites were allotted out of the tribe of Zebulun: Rimmono with its pasturelands, Tabor with its pasturelands, and beyond the Jordan at Jericho, on the east side of the Jordan, out of the tribe of Reuben: Bezer in the wilderness with its pasturelands, Jahzah with its pasturelands, Kedemoth with its pasturelands, and Mephaath with its pasturelands; and out of the tribe of Gad: Ramoth in Gilead with its pasturelands, Mahanaim with its pasturelands, Heshbon with its pasturelands, and Jazer with its pasturelands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ten more verses of towns — Issachar, Asher, Naphtali, Zebulun, Reuben, Gad — and the last two cities of refuge in them: Kedesh in Galilee (v. 76), Bezer in the wilderness (v. 78) and Ramoth in Gilead (v. 80). Forty-eight towns altogether, and not one of them in Levi's own country, because Levi had no country.

Every other tribe walked away from the division of the land holding a map — this valley, that ridge, the olive terraces, the well. Levi was handed nothing at all: no acres, no boundary stones, no deed. What he was given instead was a house in each of his brothers' territories, enough grass for the animals, and a promise that the LORD himself was his portion.

The arrangement was practical as well as theological. Scatter the teaching tribe across every border and no family in Israel lives more than a morning's walk from a man whose whole life is the law of God. The tribe with no inheritance was distributed so that everyone else could keep theirs.

The other tribes were given things God had made. Levi was given God.

7.title: The Northern Tribes: Every Name Counted
7.text: <sup>1</sup>The sons of Issachar: Tola, Puah, Jashub, and Shimron, four.<sup>2</sup>The sons of Tola: Uzzi, Rephaiah, Jeriel, Jahmai, Ibsam, and Shemuel, heads of their fathers' houses, namely of Tola, mighty warriors of their generations, their number in the days of David being 22,600.<sup>3</sup>The son of Uzzi: Izrahiah. And the sons of Izrahiah: Michael, Obadiah, Joel, and Isshiah, all five of them were chief men.<sup>4</sup>And along with them, by their generations, according to their fathers' houses, were units of the army for war, 36,000, for they had many wives and sons.<sup>5</sup>Their kinsmen belonging to all the clans of Issachar were in all 87,000 mighty warriors, enrolled by genealogy.<sup>6</sup>The sons of Benjamin: Bela, Becher, and Jediael, three.<sup>7</sup>The sons of Bela: Ezbon, Uzzi, Uzziel, Jerimoth, and Iri, five, heads of fathers' houses, mighty warriors. And their enrollment by genealogies was 22,034.<sup>8</sup>The sons of Becher: Zemirah, Joash, Eliezer, Elioenai, Omri, Jeremoth, Abijah, Anathoth, and Alemeth. All these were the sons of Becher.<sup>9</sup>And their enrollment by genealogies, according to their generations, as heads of their fathers' houses, mighty warriors, was 20,200.<sup>10</sup>The son of Jediael: Bilhan. And the sons of Bilhan: Jeush, Benjamin, Ehud, Chenaanah, Zethan, Tarshish, and Ahishahar.<sup>11</sup>All these were the sons of Jediael according to the heads of their fathers' houses, mighty warriors, 17,200, able to go to war.<sup>12</sup>And Shuppim and Huppim were the sons of Ir, Hushim the son of Aher.<sup>13</sup>The sons of Naphtali: Jahziel, Guni, Jezer and Shallum, the descendants of Bilhah.<sup>14</sup>The sons of Manasseh: Asriel, whom his Aramean concubine bore; she bore Machir the father of Gilead.<sup>15</sup>And Machir took a wife for Huppim and for Shuppim. The name of his sister was Maacah. And the name of the second was Zelophehad, and Zelophehad had daughters.<sup>16</sup>And Maacah the wife of Machir bore a son, and she called his name Peresh; and the name of his brother was Sheresh; and his sons were Ulam and Rakem.<sup>17</sup>The son of Ulam: Bedan. These were the sons of Gilead the son of Machir, son of Manasseh.<sup>18</sup>And his sister Hammolecheth bore Ishhod, Abiezer, and Mahlah.<sup>19</sup>The sons of Shemida were Ahian, Shechem, Likhi, and Aniam.<sup>20</sup>The sons of Ephraim: Shuthelah, and Bered his son, Tahath his son, Eleadah his son, Tahath his son,<sup>21</sup>Zabad his son, Shuthelah his son, and Ezer and Elead, whom the men of Gath who were born in the land killed, because they came down to raid their livestock.<sup>22</sup>And Ephraim their father mourned many days, and his brothers came to comfort him.<sup>23</sup>And Ephraim went in to his wife, and she conceived and bore a son. And he called his name Beriah, because disaster had befallen his house.<sup>24</sup>His daughter was Sheerah, who built both Lower and Upper Beth-horon, and Uzzen-sheerah.<sup>25</sup>Rephah was his son, Resheph his son, Telah his son, Tahan his son,<sup>26</sup>Ladan his son, Ammihud his son, Elishama his son,<sup>27</sup>Nun his son, Joshua his son.<sup>28</sup>Their possessions and settlements were Bethel and its towns, and to the east Naaran, and to the west Gezer and its towns, Shechem and its towns, and Ayyah and its towns;<sup>29</sup>also in possession of the Manassites, Beth-shean and its towns, Taanach and its towns, Megiddo and its towns, Dor and its towns. In these lived the sons of Joseph the son of Israel.<sup>30</sup>The sons of Asher: Imnah, Ishvah, Ishvi, Beriah, and their sister Serah.<sup>31</sup>The sons of Beriah: Heber, and Malchiel, who fathered Birzaith.<sup>32</sup>Heber fathered Japhlet, Shomer, Hotham, and their sister Shua.<sup>33</sup>The sons of Japhlet: Pasach, Bimhal, and Ashvath. These are the sons of Japhlet.<sup>34</sup>The sons of Shemer his brother: Rohgah, Jehubbah, and Aram.<sup>35</sup>The sons of Helem his brother: Zophah, Imna, Shelesh, and Amal.<sup>36</sup>The sons of Zophah: Suah, Harnepher, Shual, Beri, Imrah.<sup>37</sup>Bezer, Hod, Shamma, Shilshah, Ithran, and Beera.<sup>38</sup>The sons of Jether: Jephunneh, Pispa, and Ara.<sup>39</sup>The sons of Ulla: Arah, Hanniel, and Rizia.<sup>40</sup>All of these were men of Asher, heads of fathers' houses, approved, mighty warriors, chiefs of the princes. Their number enrolled by genealogies, for service in war, was 26,000 men.
7.overview:
Six tribes in forty verses, most of them handled as muster rolls: Issachar (vv. 1-5), Benjamin in brief (vv. 6-12), Naphtali in a single line (v. 13), Manasseh (vv. 14-19), Ephraim (vv. 20-29) and Asher (vv. 30-40). It is the last chapter to cover several tribes at once, and Dan and Zebulun never receive a genealogy at all.

In the middle of it the list breaks open. Ephraim loses two sons to a cattle raid, mourns for many days, and names the next child after the disaster (vv. 21-23); and his daughter Sheerah builds three towns, including the fortress at the top of the pass (v. 24). Those five verses are the only narrative in the genealogies apart from Jabez.
7.theology:
The chapter's numbers are memory, not muscle. A community that could not field an army wrote down the armies its tribes had once mustered, and the theological point is not national greatness but continuity: these people are those people. The identity survived the catastrophe because it never rested on the census in the first place.

Against that stands the honest gap. Two tribes are missing, and the Chronicler offers no reason. A book insisting that God keeps account of everyone contains holes it cannot fill, and it does not pretend otherwise. The completeness belongs to God's memory rather than to Israel's paperwork.
7.examples:
Ephraim is the pastoral centre of the chapter. A father buried two young men who died doing something reckless, grieved for a long time, was sat with by his brothers, and carried the loss into the name of the child who came next. Nobody in the text corrects him, hurries him, or suggests that a believer should be further along by now.

And the household that grief nearly ended went on to produce a woman who built the fortress at the pass and a man who led Israel into the land. What God does after a disaster in a family is very rarely visible to the generation that suffered it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Four tribes handled briskly and mostly by muster roll: Issachar's houses numbering 87,000 mighty warriors (vv. 1-5); Benjamin's three sons and their 59,434 fighting men (vv. 6-12); Naphtali in a single verse, the descendants of Bilhah (v. 13); and Manasseh, whose line begins with a son borne by his Aramean concubine and runs through Machir to a man with no sons at all — Zelophehad had daughters (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: These are fighting figures kept by a community that had no army. The Chronicler is not boasting about a militia the returned exiles could raise; he is recording what the tribes once were, which is a different and harder thing to write down.
verseByVerse.examples: Zelophehad's daughters went to Moses and said their father's name should not disappear because he had no son, and the law was changed for them. Verse 15 is why anyone knows their names.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Issachar: Tola, Puah, Jashub, and Shimron, four. The sons of Tola: Uzzi, Rephaiah, Jeriel, Jahmai, Ibsam, and Shemuel, heads of their fathers' houses, namely of Tola, mighty warriors of their generations, their number in the days of David being 22,600. The son of Uzzi: Izrahiah. And the sons of Izrahiah: Michael, Obadiah, Joel, and Isshiah, all five of them were chief men. And along with them, by their generations, according to their fathers' houses, were units of the army for war, 36,000, for they had many wives and sons. Their kinsmen belonging to all the clans of Issachar were in all 87,000 mighty warriors, enrolled by genealogy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Issachar first, and the entry is essentially a defence budget: houses, chiefs, and a total of 87,000 mighty warriors enrolled by genealogy.

The Chronicler keeps giving these numbers and it is easy to read them as pride. They are not. The men holding this book could not have raised a thousand soldiers. Jerusalem was a small town in a Persian province with a wall it had needed help to rebuild. These figures are a record of what the tribes had been, written by people who were now something much smaller.

There is a way of remembering a great past that poisons the present, and another way that steadies it. The difference is whether the memory is of what we were or of what God did, and the Chronicler is careful, all through these lists, to keep the subject of the sentence God.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Benjamin: Bela, Becher, and Jediael, three. The sons of Bela: Ezbon, Uzzi, Uzziel, Jerimoth, and Iri, five, heads of fathers' houses, mighty warriors. And their enrollment by genealogies was 22,034. The sons of Becher: Zemirah, Joash, Eliezer, Elioenai, Omri, Jeremoth, Abijah, Anathoth, and Alemeth. All these were the sons of Becher. And their enrollment by genealogies, according to their generations, as heads of their fathers' houses, mighty warriors, was 20,200. The son of Jediael: Bilhan. And the sons of Bilhan: Jeush, Benjamin, Ehud, Chenaanah, Zethan, Tarshish, and Ahishahar. All these were the sons of Jediael according to the heads of their fathers' houses, mighty warriors, 17,200, able to go to war. And Shuppim and Huppim were the sons of Ir, Hushim the son of Aher.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Benjamin, briefly — three sons, their houses, and 59,434 fighting men. The tribe gets a whole chapter to itself next, so this notice is a placeholder.

It is a placeholder with a shadow on it, though. Benjamin was nearly wiped out in the civil war at the end of Judges, reduced to six hundred men hiding at a rock. The numbers here are the recovery from that, and the tribe that came back from six hundred men produced Israel's first king, and later a Pharisee from Tarsus who described himself as of the tribe of Benjamin when he was listing everything he had counted as loss.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Naphtali: Jahziel, Guni, Jezer and Shallum, the descendants of Bilhah. The sons of Manasseh: Asriel, whom his Aramean concubine bore; she bore Machir the father of Gilead. And Machir took a wife for Huppim and for Shuppim. The name of his sister was Maacah. And the name of the second was Zelophehad, and Zelophehad had daughters. And Maacah the wife of Machir bore a son, and she called his name Peresh; and the name of his brother was Sheresh; and his sons were Ulam and Rakem. The son of Ulam: Bedan. These were the sons of Gilead the son of Machir, son of Manasseh. And his sister Hammolecheth bore Ishhod, Abiezer, and Mahlah. The sons of Shemida were Ahian, Shechem, Likhi, and Aniam.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Naphtali gets one verse and is named as the descendants of Bilhah — a servant's children, and the register says so without apology, exactly as it named the Aramean concubine in the next verse.

Then Manasseh, and inside his line a clause that stops the eye: Zelophehad had daughters. That is all it says. But those five women stood in front of Moses and the whole assembly at the tent of meeting and argued that their father's name should not vanish out of his clan because he had left no son — and God told Moses they were right, and the law of inheritance in Israel was changed on the spot.

Their names are in Numbers and their case is why anyone remembers a man who did nothing else. Here the whole affair is four words in a genealogy, which is the fate of most things that changed the world.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–29 — Ephraim: A Father Who Mourned, and a Daughter Who Built
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The list stops and becomes a story. Ephraim's sons Ezer and Elead went down to raid livestock and the men of Gath who were born in the land killed them; Ephraim their father mourned many days, and his brothers came to comfort him; and the son born afterwards was called Beriah, because disaster had befallen his house (vv. 21-23). Then his daughter Sheerah, who built both Lower and Upper Beth-horon, and Uzzen-sheerah (v. 24). The section closes with Joshua at the end of Ephraim's line (v. 27) and the towns of Joseph's sons (vv. 28-29).
verseByVerse.theology: The chronology of verses 21-23 is difficult — Ephraim is in Egypt and Gath is in Canaan — and the likeliest reading is that a later generation of the clan is meant, with the tribal father standing for the tribe. Name the difficulty and leave it there; solving it at the cost of these verses would trade a bereavement for a chronology.
verseByVerse.examples: Sheerah built three towns. She is one of only two people in nine chapters of genealogy credited with building anything — the other is Shemed, a chapter on (8:12) — one of the towns carries her name, and Beth-horon guarded the pass that armies used for the next eight hundred years.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Ephraim: Shuthelah, and Bered his son, Tahath his son, Eleadah his son, Tahath his son, Zabad his son, Shuthelah his son, and Ezer and Elead, whom the men of Gath who were born in the land killed, because they came down to raid their livestock. And Ephraim their father mourned many days, and his brothers came to comfort him. And Ephraim went in to his wife, and she conceived and bore a son. And he called his name Beriah, because disaster had befallen his house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And then, without warning, the list becomes a story.

Two of Ephraim's sons went down after cattle and the men of Gath who were born in the land killed them. And the next sentence is one of the few in these nine chapters with a heart in it: And Ephraim their father mourned many days, and his brothers came to comfort him.

Nothing is explained. We are not told whether the raid was justified or whether the boys were fools. We are told how long the grief lasted, which is many days, and that other men came and sat with him.

Then he had another son, and named him Beriah, because disaster had befallen his house. A father who buries two children and gives the next one a name that means the calamity. Every time he called that boy in from the field he said the word out loud. Scripture does not tell him to stop, and does not treat it as a failure of faith. The register simply carries the name down the generations, so that the loss is still legible a thousand years later in a list that had no obligation to mention it at all.

verseByVerse.quote: His daughter was Sheerah, who built both Lower and Upper Beth-horon, and Uzzen-sheerah. Rephah was his son, Resheph his son, Telah his son, Tahan his son, Ladan his son, Ammihud his son, Elishama his son, Nun his son, Joshua his son. Their possessions and settlements were Bethel and its towns, and to the east Naaran, and to the west Gezer and its towns, Shechem and its towns, and Ayyah and its towns; also in possession of the Manassites, Beth-shean and its towns, Taanach and its towns, Megiddo and its towns, Dor and its towns. In these lived the sons of Joseph the son of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His daughter was Sheerah, who built both Lower and Upper Beth-horon, and Uzzen-sheerah.

In nine chapters of genealogy, hundreds of men are recorded as having fathered somebody. Exactly one person is recorded as having built something, and it is a woman, and she built three towns, and one of them carries her name.

Beth-horon is not a village on a hill. It is the pass — the road up from the coastal plain into the highlands, the route every invading army took. Joshua chased the five kings down it in the day the sun stood still. Armies fought over it for the next eight hundred years. A woman fortified the ascent, and Israel kept the highlands.

Three verses later the line reaches Joshua the son of Nun, who is her descendant. The family that lost two sons to a cattle raid produced the woman who secured the pass and the man who took the land.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 30–40 — Asher, and the Two Tribes That Are Missing
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Asher's line is given with unusual care, down to their sister Serah (v. 30) and on through Heber and Malchiel to a closing muster: heads of fathers' houses, approved, mighty warriors, chiefs of the princes, 26,000 enrolled for war (v. 40). It is the last chapter to run through several tribes at once — Benjamin gets one to itself next — and two of the twelve never receive a genealogy at all.
verseByVerse.theology: Dan and Zebulun have no genealogy anywhere in 1 Chronicles. Neither does the Chronicler explain the gap. The register that has taken nine chapters to insist that God keeps track of everyone contains, at its edges, two silences it does not fill.
verseByVerse.examples: A returning exile from Dan would have opened this book and found his tribe not there. Whatever the reason, the honest thing is to say that the record has holes in it, and that the God whose record it is does not.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Asher: Imnah, Ishvah, Ishvi, Beriah, and their sister Serah. The sons of Beriah: Heber, and Malchiel, who fathered Birzaith. Heber fathered Japhlet, Shomer, Hotham, and their sister Shua. The sons of Japhlet: Pasach, Bimhal, and Ashvath. These are the sons of Japhlet. The sons of Shemer his brother: Rohgah, Jehubbah, and Aram. The sons of Helem his brother: Zophah, Imna, Shelesh, and Amal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Asher, and the register does something it has done only a handful of times: it names a sister. Imnah, Ishvah, Ishvi, Beriah, and their sister Serah.

Serah is named in Genesis too, among the seventy who went down into Egypt with Jacob, and again in the wilderness census, and nothing whatever is recorded about her. Three separate documents, kept centuries apart, all bothered to write her name and none of them explains why.

That is the strongest argument these chapters make. A person can be in the book of God for no reason that anyone can reconstruct, and stay there.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Zophah: Suah, Harnepher, Shual, Beri, Imrah. Bezer, Hod, Shamma, Shilshah, Ithran, and Beera. The sons of Jether: Jephunneh, Pispa, and Ara. The sons of Ulla: Arah, Hanniel, and Rizia. All of these were men of Asher, heads of fathers' houses, approved, mighty warriors, chiefs of the princes. Their number enrolled by genealogies, for service in war, was 26,000 men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The last of the multi-tribe registers closes on a muster: heads of fathers' houses, approved, mighty warriors, chiefs of the princes, twenty-six thousand men enrolled for war.

And then the genealogies of the tribes are finished, and two of the twelve have not appeared. There is no line of Dan in this book and no line of Zebulun. The Chronicler, who gave eighty-one verses to Levi and three chapters to Judah, does not account for the omission and does not seem troubled by it.

Whatever the reason — records lost, a scroll damaged, tribes that had ceased to be traceable — the effect on a returning exile from either tribe is not softened by the explanation. He opened the book and his family was not in it.

Set that beside what Scripture does at the other end. When the roll of Israel is read out for the last time, in the last book of the Bible, twelve thousand are sealed out of every tribe — and Zebulun, who has no genealogy in this book, is named there. Dan is still absent, and so is Ephraim under his own name, Joseph and Manasseh standing in his place.

So the two rolls do not match each other, and neither of them was ever the one that settles the matter. The names that finally count are written in a book the Lamb keeps, and no scroll in Jerusalem was ever the master copy.

8.title: Benjamin: The Tribe of Saul and the Background of David's Kingdom
8.text: <sup>1</sup>Benjamin fathered Bela his firstborn, Ashbel the second, Aharah the third,<sup>2</sup>Nohah the fourth, and Rapha the fifth.<sup>3</sup>And Bela had sons: Addar, Gera, Abihud,<sup>4</sup>Abishua, Naaman, Ahoah,<sup>5</sup>Gera, Shephuphan, and Huram.<sup>6</sup>These are the sons of Ehud (they were heads of fathers' houses of the inhabitants of Geba, and they were carried into exile to Manahath):<sup>7</sup>Naaman, Ahijah, and Gera, that is, Heglam, who fathered Uzza and Ahihud.<sup>8</sup>And Shaharaim fathered sons in the country of Moab after he had sent away Hushim and Baara his wives.<sup>9</sup>He fathered sons by Hodesh his wife: Jobab, Zibia, Mesha, Malcam,<sup>10</sup>Jeuz, Sachia, and Mirmah. These were his sons, heads of fathers' houses.<sup>11</sup>He also fathered sons by Hushim: Abitub and Elpaal.<sup>12</sup>The sons of Elpaal: Eber, Misham, and Shemed, who built Ono and Lod with its towns,<sup>13</sup>and Beriah and Shema (they were heads of fathers' houses of the inhabitants of Aijalon, who caused the inhabitants of Gath to flee);<sup>14</sup>and Ahio, Shashak, and Jeremoth.<sup>15</sup>Zebadiah, Arad, Eder,<sup>16</sup>Michael, Ishpah, and Joha were sons of Beriah.<sup>17</sup>Zebadiah, Meshullam, Hizki, Heber,<sup>18</sup>Ishmerai, Izliah, and Jobab were the sons of Elpaal.<sup>19</sup>Jakim, Zichri, Zabdi,<sup>20</sup>Elienai, Zillethai, Eliel,<sup>21</sup>Adaiah, Beraiah, and Shimrath were the sons of Shimei.<sup>22</sup>Ishpan, Eber, Eliel,<sup>23</sup>Abdon, Zichri, Hanan,<sup>24</sup>Hananiah, Elam, Anthothijah,<sup>25</sup>Iphdeiah, and Penuel were the sons of Shashak.<sup>26</sup>Shamsherai, Shehariah, Athaliah,<sup>27</sup>Jaareshiah, Elijah, and Zichri were the sons of Jeroham.<sup>28</sup>These were the heads of fathers' houses, according to their generations, chief men. These lived in Jerusalem.<sup>29</sup>Jeiel the father of Gibeon lived in Gibeon, and the name of his wife was Maacah.<sup>30</sup>His firstborn son: Abdon, then Zur, Kish, Baal, Nadab,<sup>31</sup>Gedor, Ahio, Zecher,<sup>32</sup>and Mikloth (he fathered Shimeah). Now these also lived opposite their kinsmen in Jerusalem, with their kinsmen.<sup>33</sup>Ner was the father of Kish, Kish of Saul, Saul of Jonathan, Malchi-shua, Abinadab and Eshbaal;<sup>34</sup>and the son of Jonathan was Merib-baal; and Merib-baal was the father of Micah.<sup>35</sup>The sons of Micah: Pithon, Melech, Tarea, and Ahaz.<sup>36</sup>Ahaz fathered Jehoaddah, and Jehoaddah fathered Alemeth, Azmaveth, and Zimri. Zimri fathered Moza.<sup>37</sup>Moza fathered Binea; Raphah was his son, Eleasah his son, Azel his son.<sup>38</sup>Azel had six sons, and these are their names: Azrikam, Bocheru, Ishmael, Sheariah, Obadiah, and Hanan. All these were the sons of Azel.<sup>39</sup>The sons of Eshek his brother: Ulam his firstborn, Jeush the second, and Eliphelet the third.<sup>40</sup>The sons of Ulam were men who were mighty warriors, bowmen, having many sons and grandsons, 150. All these were Benjaminites.
8.overview:
Benjamin is given a chapter of his own: the early houses, an exile to Manahath and a divorce in Moab (vv. 1-14); long lists of chiefs, ending with the note that they lived in Jerusalem (vv. 15-28); and then the family of Saul, from Jeiel of Gibeon down through Kish to Saul, Jonathan and Eshbaal, and on for six generations of bowmen (vv. 29-40).

The placement is the point. Nine chapters of genealogy end on the house that lost the kingdom, and the next verse in the book is the battle in which it lost it.
8.theology:
The chapter is evidence of how the Chronicler works. He prints Eshbaal and Merib-baal where Samuel prints Ish-bosheth and Mephibosheth, because his sources have them that way, and he is not in the business of tidying a document he did not write. A historian who will write Baal into a king's family can be trusted with the rest.

And the theological weight is in the arrangement. Saul is not written out. His genealogy is the last of the nine chapters, kept in full, six generations past the disaster, in the archive of the dynasty that replaced him. Rejection from an office is not erasure from the record.
8.examples:
Fourteen verses of this chapter distinguish men by nothing except an address: they lived in Jerusalem. Whole households are remembered for being in a particular place while it mattered, and that is closer to most Christian lives than anything heroic.

And the last family in the genealogies is the one that failed publicly, and it is written down carefully, with its children and its grandchildren and its skill with a bow. God's record of a house is not a verdict on it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Benjamin, already noticed briefly in the previous chapter, is now given a chapter of his own — five sons, then the houses of Ehud at Geba who were carried into exile to Manahath (v. 6), then Shaharaim, who fathered sons in Moab after he had sent away Hushim and Baara his wives (v. 8), and the heads of houses at Aijalon who put the inhabitants of Gath to flight (vv. 12-13).
verseByVerse.theology: Benjamin gets this attention because Benjamin produced the first king, and because Benjamin stayed with Judah when the ten tribes went north. In the Chronicler's day the returned community was essentially Judah, Benjamin and Levi, and these are their papers.
verseByVerse.examples: A man deported to Manahath, another divorcing two wives and starting again in Moab: the register carries small domestic catastrophes without a syllable of judgment, and carries the children of them into the tribe of the first king.

verseByVerse.quote: Benjamin fathered Bela his firstborn, Ashbel the second, Aharah the third, Nohah the fourth, and Rapha the fifth. And Bela had sons: Addar, Gera, Abihud, Abishua, Naaman, Ahoah, Gera, Shephuphan, and Huram. These are the sons of Ehud (they were heads of fathers' houses of the inhabitants of Geba, and they were carried into exile to Manahath): Naaman, Ahijah, and Gera, that is, Heglam, who fathered Uzza and Ahihud.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Benjamin gets a chapter to himself, which no tribe but Judah and Levi receives. There are two reasons and both are political. Benjamin gave Israel its first king, and Benjamin stayed with Judah when the north walked out.

By the Chronicler's day the people who had come home were essentially those two tribes and the Levites. These are not antiquarian notes about a vanished world; they are the family papers of the men reading the book.

And already in verse 6 there is an exile — heads of houses at Geba carried into exile to Manahath, centuries before Babylon and for reasons nobody records. Deportation was not a single catastrophe that fell out of a clear sky in 586. It had been happening in smaller ways for a very long time.

verseByVerse.quote: And Shaharaim fathered sons in the country of Moab after he had sent away Hushim and Baara his wives. He fathered sons by Hodesh his wife: Jobab, Zibia, Mesha, Malcam, Jeuz, Sachia, and Mirmah. These were his sons, heads of fathers' houses. He also fathered sons by Hushim: Abitub and Elpaal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One verse in this stretch has a marriage in it, and the marriage has ended. Shaharaim fathered sons in the country of Moab after he had sent away Hushim and Baara his wives.

A man divorced two women, left the country, and started a family somewhere else, and his children are in the official genealogy of the tribe of Israel's first king. The register neither approves nor condemns. It records that these particular people exist and how they came to.

There is a kind of piety that would have left him out, and Scripture is consistently less careful of its own reputation than that. The line of the Messiah already has a Canaanite wife, a deceived father-in-law, an Egyptian slave and a stoning in it. Benjamin's line has a divorce.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Elpaal: Eber, Misham, and Shemed, who built Ono and Lod with its towns, and Beriah and Shema (they were heads of fathers' houses of the inhabitants of Aijalon, who caused the inhabitants of Gath to flee); and Ahio, Shashak, and Jeremoth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three verses, and two of them do something no other verse in Benjamin's list does.

First, a builder. Shemed built Ono and Lod with its towns. Only one other person in these nine chapters is credited with building anything, and she was a woman in the previous chapter. Both towns outlive him by a very long way. Ono is where Sanballat tried to lure Nehemiah down from the wall to a meeting in the plain, and Nehemiah sent back the line about doing a great work and not being able to come down. Lod is Lydda, where Peter found a man who had been bedridden eight years and told him to get up and make his bed.

Second, a reversal. Beriah and Shema of Aijalon caused the inhabitants of Gath to flee. Four columns earlier, in the previous chapter, the men of Gath came down and killed two of Ephraim's sons over a cattle raid and left their father mourning for many days. Nobody connects the two verses and the text draws no moral. But the same city that took two sons from one tribe was put to flight by another, and both facts are kept in the same archive.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–28 — The Heads of Houses Who Lived in Jerusalem
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Long lists of Benjaminite chiefs — the sons of Beriah and Elpaal, of Shimei, Shashak and Jeroham — closing with the note that gives the section its point: These were the heads of fathers' houses, according to their generations, chief men. These lived in Jerusalem (v. 28).
verseByVerse.theology: Jerusalem sat on the border between Judah and Benjamin, and Benjaminites lived in it from the beginning. The city David took was not exclusively his own tribe's, and the record of who lived there mattered enormously to a generation trying to repopulate it.
verseByVerse.examples: Fourteen verses of names whose only distinction is an address. Living in the right place, and being written down as having lived there, is the whole of what these men are remembered for.

verseByVerse.quote: Zebadiah, Arad, Eder, Michael, Ishpah, and Joha were sons of Beriah. Zebadiah, Meshullam, Hizki, Heber, Ishmerai, Izliah, and Jobab were the sons of Elpaal. Jakim, Zichri, Zabdi, Elienai, Zillethai, Eliel, Adaiah, Beraiah, and Shimrath were the sons of Shimei.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Six or seven names to a house, three houses in seven verses, and not one word about any of them. Beriah's sons, Elpaal's sons, Shimei's sons.

This is the texture of the genealogies at their barest. Ask what a man was doing when he copied a list like this: preserving the claim of a family to belong. Every name here is somebody's grandfather, and somebody in the fifth century needed it written down.

verseByVerse.quote: Ishpan, Eber, Eliel, Abdon, Zichri, Hanan, Hananiah, Elam, Anthothijah, Iphdeiah, and Penuel were the sons of Shashak. Shamsherai, Shehariah, Athaliah, Jaareshiah, Elijah, and Zichri were the sons of Jeroham. These were the heads of fathers' houses, according to their generations, chief men. These lived in Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two more houses, and then the clause the whole section exists for: These were the heads of fathers' houses, according to their generations, chief men. These lived in Jerusalem.

The city stood on the seam between Judah and Benjamin, and Benjaminites had houses in it from the start. That mattered a great deal to the people holding this book, because Jerusalem after the return was half empty. Nehemiah eventually had to cast lots to force one family in ten to move into the city, and the rest of the people blessed the men who volunteered to go.

These verses are the precedent for that: a written record that Benjamin had always lived there. Somebody arguing about a ruined street in the fifth century could put his finger on verse 28 and say his family had held it before the fire.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter turns to Gibeon, to Jeiel and Maacah, and works down to the sentence the whole book has been approaching: Ner was the father of Kish, Kish of Saul, Saul of Jonathan, Malchi-shua, Abinadab and Eshbaal (v. 33), with Jonathan's son Merib-baal after him (v. 34). The line runs on for six more generations of Benjaminite bowmen, ending with a hundred and fifty of Ulam's descendants (v. 40).
verseByVerse.theology: The genealogies close on the family that failed. It is the last thing recorded before the narrative begins, and the first thing the narrative reports is Saul's death on Gilboa. The Chronicler has arranged nine chapters so that the story opens at a funeral.
verseByVerse.examples: Saul's line does not stop at Gilboa. Six generations of mighty bowmen come out of it, recorded with care in the official register of a kingdom his rival founded.

verseByVerse.quote: Jeiel the father of Gibeon lived in Gibeon, and the name of his wife was Maacah. His firstborn son: Abdon, then Zur, Kish, Baal, Nadab, Gedor, Ahio, Zecher, and Mikloth (he fathered Shimeah). Now these also lived opposite their kinsmen in Jerusalem, with their kinsmen. Ner was the father of Kish, Kish of Saul, Saul of Jonathan, Malchi-shua, Abinadab and Eshbaal; and the son of Jonathan was Merib-baal; and Merib-baal was the father of Micah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the line that the whole book has been walking towards, and it arrives quietly, through a man in Gibeon and his wife Maacah, down to a sentence of six names: Ner was the father of Kish, Kish of Saul, Saul of Jonathan, Malchi-shua, Abinadab and Eshbaal.

Two of those names need explaining, because a reader with Samuel open will not recognise them. Eshbaal is the son 2 Samuel calls Ish-bosheth, and Merib-baal in the next verse is Mephibosheth, Jonathan's crippled son. The names have been altered in Samuel: baal, which simply meant lord or master and was once used innocently, has been replaced with bosheth, the word for shame.

That substitution tells its own story about what happened to a word. In Saul's generation a man could name his son Eshbaal and mean nothing by it. By the time Samuel was copied, Baal was the god on Carmel and the name had become unusable, and the scribes would not put it in a child's mouth.
