The Chronicler restores the originals. He is working from older documents and he prints what they say, which is one small reason to trust him elsewhere: a man willing to write Eshbaal is not smoothing his sources.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Micah: Pithon, Melech, Tarea, and Ahaz. Ahaz fathered Jehoaddah, and Jehoaddah fathered Alemeth, Azmaveth, and Zimri. Zimri fathered Moza. Moza fathered Binea; Raphah was his son, Eleasah his son, Azel his son. Azel had six sons, and these are their names: Azrikam, Bocheru, Ishmael, Sheariah, Obadiah, and Hanan. All these were the sons of Azel. The sons of Eshek his brother: Ulam his firstborn, Jeush the second, and Eliphelet the third. The sons of Ulam were men who were mighty warriors, bowmen, having many sons and grandsons, 150. All these were Benjaminites.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Saul's family does not stop at Gilboa. Micah, Pithon, Melech, Tarea, Ahaz, and on for six more generations, ending with the sons of Ulam — mighty warriors, bowmen, having many sons and grandsons, 150.

Bowmen. The archers of Gilboa found Saul and wounded him, and he fell on his own sword rather than be taken; and his descendants are remembered for the bow. Nothing is made of it here. The register just records the trade.

And there the genealogies end. Nine chapters, from Adam to a hundred and fifty Benjaminite archers, and the last family named is the house that God rejected. Turn the page and the first sentence of the book's narrative is the Philistines on Mount Gilboa.

That arrangement is deliberate and it is merciful. Saul's line is written into the official record of the kingdom that replaced it, generations after it lost the throne, by a chronicler serving the house of David. God did not erase the family that failed. He kept their names in the book, and then told the truth about what happened.

9.title: The Returned Remnant and the Gatekeepers of the Holy
9.text: <sup>1</sup>So all Israel was recorded in genealogies, and these are written in the Book of the Kings of Israel. And Judah was taken into exile in Babylon because of their breach of faith.<sup>2</sup>Now the first to dwell again in their possessions in their cities were Israel, the priests, the Levites, and the temple servants.<sup>3</sup>And some of the people of Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim, and Manasseh lived in Jerusalem:<sup>4</sup>Uthai the son of Ammihud, son of Omri, son of Imri, son of Bani, from the sons of Perez the son of Judah.<sup>5</sup>And of the Shilonites: Asaiah the firstborn, and his sons.<sup>6</sup>Of the sons of Zerah: Jeuel and their kinsmen, 690.<sup>7</sup>Of the Benjaminites: Sallu the son of Meshullam, son of Hodaviah, son of Hassenuah,<sup>8</sup>Ibneiah the son of Jeroham, Elah the son of Uzzi, son of Michri, and Meshullam the son of Shephatiah, son of Reuel, son of Ibnijah;<sup>9</sup>and their kinsmen according to their generations, 956. All these were heads of fathers' houses according to their fathers' houses.<sup>10</sup>Of the priests: Jedaiah, Jehoiarib, Jachin,<sup>11</sup>and Azariah the son of Hilkiah, son of Meshullam, son of Zadok, son of Meraioth, son of Ahitub, the chief officer of the house of God;<sup>12</sup>and Adaiah the son of Jeroham, son of Pashhur, son of Malchijah, and Maasai the son of Adiel, son of Jahzerah, son of Meshullam, son of Meshillemith, son of Immer;<sup>13</sup>besides their kinsmen, heads of their fathers' houses, 1,760, mighty men for the work of the service of the house of God.<sup>14</sup>Of the Levites: Shemaiah the son of Hasshub, son of Azrikam, son of Hashabiah, of the sons of Merari;<sup>15</sup>and Bakbakkar, Heresh, Galal and Mattaniah the son of Mica, son of Zichri, son of Asaph;<sup>16</sup>and Obadiah the son of Shemaiah, son of Galal, son of Jeduthun, and Berechiah the son of Asa, son of Elkanah, who lived in the villages of the Netophathites.<sup>17</sup>The gatekeepers were Shallum, Akkub, Talmon, Ahiman, and their kinsmen (Shallum was the chief);<sup>18</sup>until then they were in the king's gate on the east side as the gatekeepers of the camps of the Levites.<sup>19</sup>Shallum the son of Kore, son of Ebiasaph, son of Korah, and his kinsmen of his fathers' house, the Korahites, were in charge of the work of the service, keepers of the thresholds of the tent, as their fathers had been in charge of the camp of the LORD, keepers of the entrance.<sup>20</sup>And Phinehas the son of Eleazar was the chief officer over them in time past; the LORD was with him.<sup>21</sup>Zechariah the son of Meshelemiah was gatekeeper at the entrance of the tent of meeting.<sup>22</sup>All these, who were chosen as gatekeepers at the thresholds, were 212. They were enrolled by genealogies in their villages. David and Samuel the seer established them in their office of trust.<sup>23</sup>So they and their sons were in charge of the gates of the house of the LORD, that is, the house of the tent, as guards.<sup>24</sup>The gatekeepers were on the four sides, east, west, north, and south.<sup>25</sup>And their kinsmen who were in their villages were obligated to come in every seven days, in turn, to be with these,<sup>26</sup>for the four chief gatekeepers, who were Levites, were entrusted to be over the chambers and the treasures of the house of God.<sup>27</sup>And they lodged around the house of God, for on them lay the duty of watching, and they had charge of opening it every morning.<sup>28</sup>Some of them had charge of the utensils of service, for they were required to count them when they were brought in and taken out.<sup>29</sup>Others of them were appointed over the furniture and over all the holy utensils, also over the fine flour, the wine, the oil, the incense, and the spices.<sup>30</sup>Others, of the sons of the priests, prepared the mixing of the spices,<sup>31</sup>and Mattithiah, one of the Levites, the firstborn of Shallum the Korahite, was entrusted with making the flat cakes.<sup>32</sup>Also some of their kinsmen of the Kohathites had charge of the showbread, to prepare it every Sabbath.<sup>33</sup>Now these, the singers, the heads of fathers' houses of the Levites, were in the chambers of the temple free from other service, for they were on duty day and night.<sup>34</sup>These were heads of fathers' houses of the Levites, according to their generations, leaders. These lived in Jerusalem.<sup>35</sup>In Gibeon lived the father of Gibeon, Jeiel, and the name of his wife was Maacah,<sup>36</sup>and his firstborn son Abdon, then Zur, Kish, Baal, Ner, Nadab,<sup>37</sup>Gedor, Ahio, Zechariah, and Mikloth;<sup>38</sup>and Mikloth was the father of Shimeam; and these also lived opposite their kinsmen in Jerusalem, with their kinsmen.<sup>39</sup>Ner fathered Kish, Kish fathered Saul, Saul fathered Jonathan, Malchi-shua, Abinadab, and Eshbaal.<sup>40</sup>And the son of Jonathan was Merib-baal, and Merib-baal fathered Micah.<sup>41</sup>The sons of Micah: Pithon, Melech, Tahrea, and Ahaz.<sup>42</sup>And Ahaz fathered Jarah, and Jarah fathered Alemeth, Azmaveth, and Zimri. And Zimri fathered Moza.<sup>43</sup>Moza fathered Binea, and Rephaiah was his son, Eleasah his son, Azel his son.<sup>44</sup>Azel had six sons and these are their names: Azrikam, Bocheru, Ishmael, Sheariah, Obadiah, and Hanan; these were the sons of Azel.
9.overview:
The genealogies close with the sentence they were written to explain — Judah went to Babylon because of their breach of faith (v. 1) — and then turn to the return: who came back, and to which streets (vv. 2-9). The bulk of the chapter is the temple staff: priests, Levites, and above all the gatekeepers, with their charter from David and Samuel, their rota, their inventories, their spices and their baking (vv. 10-34). The chapter ends by repeating Saul's genealogy (vv. 35-44), and the next verse of the book is his death.

It is the most ordinary chapter in the nine, and the most telling. A community that had lost everything is described in terms of who unlocked the doors.
9.theology:
Verse 1 completes the Chronicler's account of the exile, and it is entirely theological. No political cause is offered for the fall of Jerusalem. The nation broke faith, in the same words used of one man at Jericho, and the consequence followed. A history written this way is not naive about empires; it simply refuses to let them be the explanation.

And against the breach of faith stands the doorkeeping. The chapter's answer to covenant treachery is not a programme of reform but a rota: men enrolled by name, opening a building every morning, counting the vessels in and out, baking the bread every Sabbath. Faithfulness in Scripture is far more often a duty performed at dawn than a decision made at a crisis.
9.examples:
The men in this chapter are remembered for opening a door, counting spoons, mixing spices and making flat cakes. Nobody in it does anything a biographer would use. It is the closest the Bible comes to describing a normal working life inside the people of God, and it is written down with the same care as the covenant with David.

And the family at the centre of it is Korah's. They did not get the altar back. They got the threshold, and they wrote the psalm that says a day at that threshold is worth more than a thousand anywhere else. God's mercy to a disgraced family was not to restore its ambition but to give it something better to want.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Exile, and the First to Come Home
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: One verse closes the genealogies and states the reason for everything: all Israel was recorded, and Judah was taken into exile in Babylon because of their breach of faith (v. 1). Then the resettlement — the first to dwell again in their possessions in their cities were Israel, the priests, the Levites and the temple servants (v. 2) — and the households of Judah and Benjamin who took up residence in Jerusalem, counted to the man: 690 of Zerah's line, 956 Benjaminites (vv. 4-9).
verseByVerse.theology: The Chronicler's verb arrives at its largest subject. A thief broke faith and Israel lost a battle; two and a half tribes broke faith and lost a territory; now a nation breaks faith and loses the city and the house. The exile is not explained by Babylonian power. It is explained by covenant treachery, and the explanation is given in a single subordinate clause.
verseByVerse.examples: The people who came back are counted by name and household, which is what you do when a community is small enough to count. A returning family could find itself in verse 8 and know it had a place.

verseByVerse.quote: So all Israel was recorded in genealogies, and these are written in the Book of the Kings of Israel. And Judah was taken into exile in Babylon because of their breach of faith. Now the first to dwell again in their possessions in their cities were Israel, the priests, the Levites, and the temple servants. And some of the people of Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim, and Manasseh lived in Jerusalem:
verseByVerse.commentary:
The genealogies end, and the Chronicler tells us in one clause what all nine chapters were leading to. And Judah was taken into exile in Babylon because of their breach of faith.

The verb has been running through this book since chapter 2. Achan broke faith in the matter of the devoted thing and Israel lost a battle. The tribes east of the Jordan broke faith with the God of their fathers and lost their land. Now the whole nation, and the city, and the house of God.

Notice what is not given as the reason. Not Babylonian siege engineering, not the size of Nebuchadnezzar's army, not the failure of an alliance with Egypt, not the incompetence of Zedekiah. Every one of those was true and none of them is mentioned. The catastrophe is given a covenantal explanation in six words, and the six words are the same ones used of a single thief three hundred years earlier.

Then verse 2, and the sentence turns. Now the first to dwell again in their possessions in their cities — the exile has a full stop after it, and the people are back in the same towns. Priests, Levites, temple servants and ordinary Israelites, in that order, because the order tells you what the community was organised around.

verseByVerse.quote: Uthai the son of Ammihud, son of Omri, son of Imri, son of Bani, from the sons of Perez the son of Judah. And of the Shilonites: Asaiah the firstborn, and his sons. Of the sons of Zerah: Jeuel and their kinsmen, 690. Of the Benjaminites: Sallu the son of Meshullam, son of Hodaviah, son of Hassenuah, Ibneiah the son of Jeroham, Elah the son of Uzzi, son of Michri, and Meshullam the son of Shephatiah, son of Reuel, son of Ibnijah; and their kinsmen according to their generations, 956. All these were heads of fathers' houses according to their fathers' houses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The householders of Judah and Benjamin who settled in Jerusalem, named to the grandfather and totalled to the man: six hundred and ninety of Zerah's line, nine hundred and fifty-six Benjaminites.

These are small numbers, and they are recorded with the same precision the earlier chapters gave to armies of eighty-seven thousand. The Chronicler does not adjust his bookkeeping to match the size of the community. Two thousand people in a half-ruined city are counted as carefully as the tribes at their height, because the counting was never a measure of strength.

A man reading verse 8 could find his own family in it. That is the point of writing the number down.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–34 — The Men Who Kept the Doors
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The priests who returned are listed with their descent and their number — 1,760, mighty men for the work of the service of the house of God (v. 13) — and then the Levites, and then the gatekeepers. Two hundred and twelve of them, enrolled in their villages, whom David and Samuel the seer established ... in their office of trust (v. 22). Their duties are set out in detail: the four quarters, the chambers and the treasures, lodging around the house, the duty of watching, opening it every morning (vv. 23-27), the utensils counted in and out, the spices, the flat cakes, the showbread prepared every Sabbath (vv. 28-32), and the singers on duty day and night (v. 33).
verseByVerse.theology: The chief gatekeeper is Shallum the son of Kore, son of Ebiasaph, son of Korah, and his kinsmen the Korahites are keepers of the thresholds. The family that was swallowed by the earth for demanding a place at the altar spent the next thousand years holding the doors, and eleven psalms in Israel's hymn book carry their name. The post their ancestor thought beneath him became the family trade, and they wrote songs saying they were glad of it.
verseByVerse.examples: Mattithiah is named for making the flat cakes and his kinsmen for the showbread every Sabbath. Scripture records the baking rota of the temple with the same care it gives the high-priestly succession.

verseByVerse.quote: Of the priests: Jedaiah, Jehoiarib, Jachin, and Azariah the son of Hilkiah, son of Meshullam, son of Zadok, son of Meraioth, son of Ahitub, the chief officer of the house of God; and Adaiah the son of Jeroham, son of Pashhur, son of Malchijah, and Maasai the son of Adiel, son of Jahzerah, son of Meshullam, son of Meshillemith, son of Immer; besides their kinsmen, heads of their fathers' houses, 1,760, mighty men for the work of the service of the house of God. Of the Levites: Shemaiah the son of Hasshub, son of Azrikam, son of Hashabiah, of the sons of Merari; and Bakbakkar, Heresh, Galal and Mattaniah the son of Mica, son of Zichri, son of Asaph; and Obadiah the son of Shemaiah, son of Galal, son of Jeduthun, and Berechiah the son of Asa, son of Elkanah, who lived in the villages of the Netophathites.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The priests who came back, with their descent traced through Zadok and Ahitub, and a chief officer of the house of God named in verse 11. Then the total: 1,760, mighty men for the work of the service of the house of God.

Mighty men is a soldier's phrase, and the Chronicler uses it here of men whose work was sacrifice and instruction. Nothing in the vocabulary suggests that the priesthood was the gentler calling.

Then the Levites, including one described as living in the villages of the Netophathites — the ordinary settlements around Bethlehem. The staff of the temple commuted in from the villages, which is how it had always worked.

verseByVerse.quote: The gatekeepers were Shallum, Akkub, Talmon, Ahiman, and their kinsmen (Shallum was the chief); until then they were in the king's gate on the east side as the gatekeepers of the camps of the Levites. Shallum the son of Kore, son of Ebiasaph, son of Korah, and his kinsmen of his fathers' house, the Korahites, were in charge of the work of the service, keepers of the thresholds of the tent, as their fathers had been in charge of the camp of the LORD, keepers of the entrance. And Phinehas the son of Eleazar was the chief officer over them in time past; the LORD was with him. Zechariah the son of Meshelemiah was gatekeeper at the entrance of the tent of meeting.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The gatekeepers, and the first name in the list carries the whole weight of the chapter: Shallum the son of Kore, son of Ebiasaph, son of Korah.

Korah. The man who stood up against Moses and Aaron with two hundred and fifty princes of the congregation and said that the priesthood was a presumption, and went down alive into the earth for it. Numbers adds, almost in passing, that his sons did not die.

And here is what the family was doing eleven centuries later. His descendants are keepers of the thresholds of the tent — the doorkeepers. The house their ancestor tried to storm, they now open in the morning and shut at night, and they have done it, the verse says, as their fathers had been in charge of the camp of the LORD.

Eleven psalms in Israel's hymn book are headed with their name. One of them says that a single day in God's courts is better than a thousand anywhere else, and that its writer would rather stand at the door of the house of his God than live inside the tents of wickedness. That is not a poetic figure for the men who wrote it. It is a job description.

God did not restore Korah's family to the altar. He gave them the doorway, and they made a song out of it that Israel sang for a thousand years.

verseByVerse.quote: All these, who were chosen as gatekeepers at the thresholds, were 212. They were enrolled by genealogies in their villages. David and Samuel the seer established them in their office of trust. So they and their sons were in charge of the gates of the house of the LORD, that is, the house of the tent, as guards. The gatekeepers were on the four sides, east, west, north, and south. And their kinsmen who were in their villages were obligated to come in every seven days, in turn, to be with these, for the four chief gatekeepers, who were Levites, were entrusted to be over the chambers and the treasures of the house of God. And they lodged around the house of God, for on them lay the duty of watching, and they had charge of opening it every morning.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two hundred and twelve gatekeepers, enrolled by genealogies in their villages, and their charter is given: David and Samuel the seer established them in their office of trust.

David and Samuel — a king and a prophet, jointly, over a rota of doormen. The office is not improvised and it is not menial. It is a trust, established by the two men who between them founded the monarchy and the prophetic office.

Then the duties, and they are wonderfully ordinary. Four quarters, east, west, north and south. A week on and then back to the village. Charge of the chambers and the treasures. Lodging around the house, because on them lay the duty of watching, and they had charge of opening it every morning.

Somebody had to get up early and unlock the temple. Every morning for four hundred years, in the rain and in the cold and on the mornings when he did not feel like it, a man walked to a door and opened it so that Israel could come in and meet God. The Chronicler thought that worth recording by name, in the same book as the covenant with David.

verseByVerse.quote: Some of them had charge of the utensils of service, for they were required to count them when they were brought in and taken out. Others of them were appointed over the furniture and over all the holy utensils, also over the fine flour, the wine, the oil, the incense, and the spices. Others, of the sons of the priests, prepared the mixing of the spices, and Mattithiah, one of the Levites, the firstborn of Shallum the Korahite, was entrusted with making the flat cakes. Also some of their kinsmen of the Kohathites had charge of the showbread, to prepare it every Sabbath. Now these, the singers, the heads of fathers' houses of the Levites, were in the chambers of the temple free from other service, for they were on duty day and night. These were heads of fathers' houses of the Levites, according to their generations, leaders. These lived in Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The inventory. Some had charge of the utensils and had to count them when they were brought in and taken out. Others were over the flour, the wine, the oil, the incense and the spices. Some of the priests' sons mixed the spices. Mattithiah the Korahite was entrusted with making the flat cakes. Others had charge of the showbread, to prepare it every Sabbath.

A stock-take, a spice recipe and a baking rota, written into the same scroll as the genealogy of the Messiah. There is no line anywhere in this chapter between the sacred work and the domestic work, because in the house of God there was not one.

And the singers, in verse 33, are free from other service, for they were on duty day and night. A choir excused from carrying and counting because it was needed around the clock. Israel's worship never stopped, and somebody had to staff the night.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter closes by repeating, almost word for word, the genealogy of Saul already given at the end of chapter 8: Jeiel of Gibeon and Maacah, Ner, Kish, Saul, and his four sons including Eshbaal (v. 39), Jonathan's son Merib-baal, and the line on to Azel's six sons (vv. 41-44).
verseByVerse.theology: The repetition is structural, not accidental. The genealogies have taken nine chapters to establish who Israel is, and they end — twice — on the house that lost the kingdom. The next sentence in the book is the Philistines fighting against Israel on Mount Gilboa.
verseByVerse.examples: A reader who has just come through the return in verse 2 is handed Saul's family again in verse 35, and then a funeral. The Chronicler will not let the restored community read its own history without first reading how a king was lost.

verseByVerse.quote: In Gibeon lived the father of Gibeon, Jeiel, and the name of his wife was Maacah, and his firstborn son Abdon, then Zur, Kish, Baal, Ner, Nadab, Gedor, Ahio, Zechariah, and Mikloth; and Mikloth was the father of Shimeam; and these also lived opposite their kinsmen in Jerusalem, with their kinsmen. Ner fathered Kish, Kish fathered Saul, Saul fathered Jonathan, Malchi-shua, Abinadab, and Eshbaal. And the son of Jonathan was Merib-baal, and Merib-baal fathered Micah. The sons of Micah: Pithon, Melech, Tahrea, and Ahaz. And Ahaz fathered Jarah, and Jarah fathered Alemeth, Azmaveth, and Zimri. And Zimri fathered Moza. Moza fathered Binea, and Rephaiah was his son, Eleasah his son, Azel his son. Azel had six sons and these are their names: Azrikam, Bocheru, Ishmael, Sheariah, Obadiah, and Hanan; these were the sons of Azel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And then, with no transition, Saul's family again — the same names as the end of the previous chapter, repeated almost word for word.

The repetition is not an accident of copying. It is a door being opened. Nine chapters of genealogy have established who Israel is, and they close on the household of the king who lost the kingdom; and the moment the list ends, the narrative begins, and its first sentence is the Philistines fighting against Israel and the men of Israel falling on Mount Gilboa.

The Chronicler has arranged his whole book so that the reader passes out of the genealogies straight into a funeral. Before he is told anything about David, he is shown what happens to a king who does not seek the LORD.

So the genealogies end where they began — with a register, and a God who keeps it. From Adam through a Canaanite wife and an Egyptian slave and a thief and a rebel's children and two tribes that vanished, down to two thousand people rebuilding a wall and a man unlocking a door at dawn. Every name held. And at the end of the line, still four centuries off, the Son who would open a door himself and say that he was the door.

10.title: The Death of Saul: Unfaithfulness and Its Wages
10.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the Philistines fought against Israel, and the men of Israel fled before the Philistines and fell slain on Mount Gilboa.<sup>2</sup>And the Philistines overtook Saul and his sons, and the Philistines struck down Jonathan and Abinadab and Malchi-shua, the sons of Saul.<sup>3</sup>The battle pressed hard against Saul, and the archers found him, and he was wounded by the archers.<sup>4</sup>Then Saul said to his armor-bearer, "Draw your sword and thrust me through with it, lest these uncircumcised come and mistreat me." But his armor-bearer would not, for he feared greatly. Therefore Saul took his own sword and fell upon it.<sup>5</sup>And when his armor-bearer saw that Saul was dead, he also fell upon his sword and died.<sup>6</sup>Thus Saul died; he and his three sons and all his house died together.<sup>7</sup>And when all the men of Israel who were in the valley saw that the army had fled and that Saul and his sons were dead, they abandoned their cities and fled, and the Philistines came and lived in them.<sup>8</sup>The next day, when the Philistines came to strip the slain, they found Saul and his sons fallen on Mount Gilboa.<sup>9</sup>And they stripped him and took his head and his armor, and sent messengers throughout the land of the Philistines to carry the good news to their idols and to the people.<sup>10</sup>And they put his armor in the temple of their gods and fastened his head in the temple of Dagon.<sup>11</sup>But when all Jabesh-gilead heard all that the Philistines had done to Saul,<sup>12</sup>all the valiant men arose and took away the body of Saul and the bodies of his sons, and brought them to Jabesh. And they buried their bones under the oak in Jabesh and fasted seven days.<sup>13</sup>So Saul died for his breach of faith. He broke faith with the LORD in that he did not keep the command of the LORD, and also consulted a medium, seeking guidance.<sup>14</sup>He did not seek guidance from the LORD. Therefore the LORD put him to death and turned the kingdom over to David the son of Jesse.
10.overview:
The narrative of 1 Chronicles begins with a funeral. Israel is routed on Gilboa, Saul's three sons are killed, and Saul, wounded by archers and refused by his armour-bearer, falls on his own sword (vv. 1-7). The Philistines take his head and his armour into the temple of Dagon and send the good news to their idols (vv. 8-10). The men of Jabesh-gilead, whom Saul had rescued in the first week of his reign, come by night for the bodies (vv. 11-12). And then two verses of verdict: he broke faith, he did not seek the LORD, and the LORD put him to death and gave the kingdom to David (vv. 13-14).

Everything the Chronicler wants his readers to understand about their own history is in those last two verses, and he puts them where nobody can miss them: at the head of the story, before David has appeared.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: No introduction, no reign, no summary of the man: the narrative of this book opens in the middle of a defeat. Israel flees, Saul's three sons are struck down, the archers find Saul, and he asks his armour-bearer for a sword and is refused, and falls on his own (vv. 1-4). The armour-bearer follows him. Thus Saul died; he and his three sons and all his house died together (v. 6), and the men in the valley abandon their towns to the Philistines (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: Nine chapters of genealogy end on the house of Saul, and the first sentence after them is this. The Chronicler assumes his reader knows everything about the reign and tells him only how it ended. A king who is introduced by his death is being introduced as a warning.
verseByVerse.examples: The armour-bearer refused the order because he feared greatly, and then killed himself anyway. Fear of doing the wrong thing is not the same as trust, and it did not save him.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the Philistines fought against Israel, and the men of Israel fled before the Philistines and fell slain on Mount Gilboa. And the Philistines overtook Saul and his sons, and the Philistines struck down Jonathan and Abinadab and Malchi-shua, the sons of Saul. The battle pressed hard against Saul, and the archers found him, and he was wounded by the archers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nine chapters of names, and then this: Now the Philistines fought against Israel, and the men of Israel fled before the Philistines and fell slain on Mount Gilboa.

There is no introduction. Saul is not presented, his reign is not summarised, his anointing and his height and his early victories are all assumed. The first thing this book's narrative does is put the reader on a hillside in the middle of a rout that is already lost.

The order of the sentence matters. Israel flees first; Saul is overtaken second; the sons die third. Then the archers find him. A king whose calling was to go out before his people and fight their battles is the last man standing on a hill his army has already abandoned, and the arrows arrive while he is alone.

Two chapters ago the register recorded that Saul's descendants were mighty warriors, bowmen. It was archers who finished him.

And one of the three sons named in verse 2 is Jonathan. He had known for years that the throne was not coming to him, and had said so to the man it was coming to, in a wood at Horesh, while his father was hunting him: You shall be king over Israel, and I shall be next to you. Saul my father also knows this. He never got to be next to him. He stood with his father on a hill his father had lost, and died there.

The Chronicler gives him half a clause. It is the only mention of Jonathan in the book outside the genealogies, and it is his death. A man can do everything right, love the right person, tell the truth about God's choice against his own interest, and still go down with the house he was born into.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Saul said to his armor-bearer, "Draw your sword and thrust me through with it, lest these uncircumcised come and mistreat me." But his armor-bearer would not, for he feared greatly. Therefore Saul took his own sword and fell upon it. And when his armor-bearer saw that Saul was dead, he also fell upon his sword and died.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The one conversation in the chapter is a request to be killed.

Draw your sword and thrust me through with it, lest these uncircumcised come and mistreat me. Saul is not asking to escape death; he is asking to control it. What he cannot bear is not dying but being handled — the shame of what the Philistines will do with a captured king.

The armour-bearer refuses, and the reason given is for he feared greatly. He would not put a sword through the LORD's anointed. That scruple is the last flicker of something right in the chapter, and it belongs to a servant whose name nobody recorded.

Then Saul takes his own sword and falls on it, and the armour-bearer, having refused to kill the king, kills himself. He would not do the thing he was afraid of and then did something worse. Fear of the wrong action is not the same as trust in God, and on Gilboa it saved nobody.

The whole exchange is about appearances at the end. Saul's last decision as king of Israel is a decision about how his body will look to his enemies, and it is a decision he makes without reference to God, which is exactly what verse 14 will say about his life.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus Saul died; he and his three sons and all his house died together. And when all the men of Israel who were in the valley saw that the army had fled and that Saul and his sons were dead, they abandoned their cities and fled, and the Philistines came and lived in them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus Saul died; he and his three sons and all his house died together.

A reader with Samuel open will stop here, because Saul's house did not all die that day. Ish-bosheth reigned two years afterwards, Mephibosheth lived at David's table for decades, and this very book has just traced Saul's descendants through six further generations of bowmen. The Chronicler is not contradicting any of that. He is saying that the dynasty died on Gilboa — that whatever survived, nothing of the house of Saul ever sat on a throne again.

And verse 7 measures the defeat in geography. The men in the valley saw the army gone and the king dead, and they walked out of their own towns, and the Philistines moved in. Israel lost the middle of the country in an afternoon.

That is what the failure of one man cost a nation. The Chronicler is writing for people who had lost far more than a valley, and he begins their history by showing them that the loss of a land follows the loss of a king who would not seek God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–12 — The Head in the Temple of Dagon
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Philistines strip the dead the next day, take Saul's head and his armour, and send messengers to carry the good news to their idols and to the people (v. 9). The armour goes into the temple of their gods and the head is fastened in the temple of Dagon (v. 10). Then the one act of loyalty in the chapter: the valiant men of Jabesh-gilead walk through the night, take the bodies down, bury the bones under the oak, and fast seven days (vv. 11-12).
verseByVerse.theology: Dagon is the god who was found face down before the ark at Ashdod, and then found again with his head and his hands broken off on the threshold. Saul's head is nailed up in that god's house. The Chronicler's readers knew both stories and he leaves them to collide.
verseByVerse.examples: Jabesh-gilead was the town Saul saved in the first week of his reign, when the Ammonites offered to spare them at the price of everyone's right eye. Forty years later they are the only people in Israel who come for his body.

verseByVerse.quote: The next day, when the Philistines came to strip the slain, they found Saul and his sons fallen on Mount Gilboa. And they stripped him and took his head and his armor, and sent messengers throughout the land of the Philistines to carry the good news to their idols and to the people. And they put his armor in the temple of their gods and fastened his head in the temple of Dagon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The next day the Philistines come back to strip the dead, and what they do with Saul's body is a religious act.

They take his head and his armour and send messengers to carry the good news to their idols and to the people. The verb is the ordinary word for announcing good news; in Greek it becomes the word for preaching a gospel. The Philistines evangelise their gods. They believe something has happened in the heavens as well as on the hill.

Then the armour into the temple of their gods, and the head fastened in the temple of Dagon.

Dagon. The reader is meant to hear it. When the Philistines captured the ark two generations earlier they set it up in Dagon's house at Ashdod, and in the morning Dagon was face down on the floor in front of it; and when they propped him up, the next morning his head and his hands were broken off on the threshold. Now the head of Israel's king is nailed up in the same god's temple.

The Chronicler does not comment. He does not need to. A god who could not stand up in the presence of the ark is given the head of a king who would not go to the ark for guidance, and the trophy is a verdict on the man rather than a victory over his God.

verseByVerse.quote: But when all Jabesh-gilead heard all that the Philistines had done to Saul, all the valiant men arose and took away the body of Saul and the bodies of his sons, and brought them to Jabesh. And they buried their bones under the oak in Jabesh and fasted seven days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One act of decency in fourteen verses, and it comes from a town nobody expects.

The valiant men of Jabesh-gilead heard what had been done, and they walked — across the Jordan, up the valley, to a Philistine-held hill — and took down the bodies of Saul and his sons and carried them home and buried the bones under an oak and fasted seven days.

Their reason is forty years old. In the first week of his reign, Saul heard that Nahash the Ammonite had besieged Jabesh-gilead and offered them terms: he would spare the town at the price of the right eye of every man in it. Saul cut a yoke of oxen in pieces, sent them through Israel, raised the country, and marched all night and broke the siege at dawn. It was the best day of his life.

So when everything else about the man had gone wrong, one town remembered the morning he came. They could do nothing for him except carry his body off a hill and give it a grave and go without food for a week, and they did all of it.

God is not the only one keeping a record. A single act of rescue, done properly at the beginning, was still being honoured at a funeral four decades later by men who had been children at the time.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Two verses of verdict, and they are the reason the chapter exists. So Saul died for his breach of faith. He broke faith with the LORD in that he did not keep the command of the LORD, and also consulted a medium, seeking guidance. He did not seek guidance from the LORD. Therefore the LORD put him to death and turned the kingdom over to David the son of Jesse.
verseByVerse.theology: Both of the book's key verbs are here in one sentence. He broke faith — the word used of Achan, of the trans-Jordan tribes, and of Judah going to Babylon. And he did not seek — which will become the measure of David, of Solomon, and of every king after them.
verseByVerse.examples: Saul died of a Philistine arrow and his own sword on a hilltop in a lost battle. The Chronicler says the LORD put him to death. Both accounts are in the same chapter and neither cancels the other.

verseByVerse.quote: So Saul died for his breach of faith. He broke faith with the LORD in that he did not keep the command of the LORD, and also consulted a medium, seeking guidance. He did not seek guidance from the LORD. Therefore the LORD put him to death and turned the kingdom over to David the son of Jesse.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now the verdict, and it is the reason the chapter is in the book.

So Saul died for his breach of faith. He broke faith with the LORD in that he did not keep the command of the LORD, and also consulted a medium, seeking guidance. He did not seek guidance from the LORD.

Both of this book's great verbs are in those two sentences. Broke faith is the word that has been running through the genealogies since Achan stole from the devoted things at Jericho, through the tribes east of the Jordan who whored after the gods of the peoples of the land, to Judah carried off to Babylon. Saul is the fourth and the last occurrence, and the smallest subject: one man.

And seek is the word the rest of the book will be built on. Saul consulted a medium at Endor the night before he died — he was seeking, urgently, at the end, and he was seeking in the one place forbidden to him. The charge is not that he never asked. It is that he asked everyone except God.

Watch what the word does from here. Three chapters on, David will say the ark must come back because we did not seek it in the days of Saul. Then he will inquire of God twice before a battle and win twice. Then the ark will go wrong and he will admit we did not seek him according to the rule. Then he will write into a psalm let the hearts of those who seek the LORD rejoice. And at the end of his life he will hand his son a kingdom with one sentence attached: If you seek him, he will be found by you.

Then the last clause, and it takes the whole weight of the chapter. Therefore the LORD put him to death and turned the kingdom over to David the son of Jesse. Saul died of an arrow and a sword, on a hill, in a battle the Philistines won. The Chronicler says the LORD put him to death. Both are true, and the second one is the reason the first one happened, and there is no seam between them anywhere in this book.

10.theology:
The chapter states the doctrine of providence that the whole book assumes. Saul died in a normal military disaster, of ordinary wounds, by his own hand. The text says the LORD put him to death. No attempt is made to reconcile these, because the writer sees no tension: secondary causes are real and God is not one of them competing among them. The same logic will explain the exile in chapter 9 and Assyria in chapter 5.

And the two verbs that govern the book are set here as opposites. To break faith is to treat what belongs to God as available. To seek is to go to God for what only he can give. Saul did the first and refused the second, and at the end he was seeking hard enough to visit a medium in the dark. Desperation is not the same as seeking God, and the difference is not intensity but direction.
10.examples:
Saul's last recorded decision is about how his body will look to his enemies. It is the instinct of a man who has spent a career managing appearances — the same man who once begged Samuel to come back and honour him before the elders after he had been rejected. A life organised around not being humiliated ends on a hill with nobody left to see.

Against that stands Jabesh-gilead. They could not undo anything, could not fix the reign or win the battle or restore the throne. They could walk a long way and bury a man properly and go hungry for a week. Where nothing can be mended, that is very often the whole of what love is able to do, and Scripture records it in the same chapter as the verdict of God.

11.title: David Crowned and His Mighty Men: The King Who Draws Loyal Hearts

And the LORD your God said to you, 'You shall be shepherd of my people Israel, and you shall be prince over my people Israel.'"<sup>3</sup>So all the elders of Israel came to the king at Hebron, and David made a covenant with them at Hebron before the LORD. And Joab the son of Zeruiah went up first, so he became chief.<sup>7</sup>And David lived in the stronghold; therefore it was called the city of David.<sup>8</sup>And he built the city all around from the Millo in complete circuit, and Joab repaired the rest of the city.<sup>9</sup>And David became greater and greater, for the LORD of hosts was with him.<sup>10</sup>Now these are the chiefs of David's mighty men, who gave him strong support in his kingdom, together with all Israel, to make him king, according to the word of the LORD concerning Israel.<sup>11</sup>This is an account of David's mighty men: Jashobeam, a Hachmonite, was chief of the three. He wielded his spear against 300 whom he killed at one time.<sup>12</sup>And next to him among the three mighty men was Eleazar the son of Dodo, the Ahohite.<sup>13</sup>He was with David at Pas-dammim when the Philistines were gathered there for battle. And the LORD saved them by a great victory.<sup>15</sup>Three of the thirty chief men went down to the rock to David at the cave of Adullam, when the army of Philistines was encamped in the Valley of Rephaim.<sup>16</sup>David was then in the stronghold, and the garrison of the Philistines was then at Bethlehem.<sup>17</sup>And David said longingly, "Oh that someone would give me water to drink from the well of Bethlehem that is by the gate!"<sup>18</sup>Then the three mighty men broke through the camp of the Philistines and drew water out of the well of Bethlehem that was by the gate and took it and brought it to David. For at the risk of their lives they brought it." Therefore he would not drink it. These things did the three mighty men.<sup>20</sup>Now Abishai, the brother of Joab, was chief of the thirty. And David set him over his bodyguard.<sup>26</sup>The mighty men were Asahel the brother of Joab, Elhanan the son of Dodo of Bethlehem,<sup>27</sup>Shammoth of Harod, Helez the Pelonite,<sup>28</sup>Ira the son of Ikkesh of Tekoa, Abiezer of Anathoth,<sup>29</sup>Sibbecai the Hushathite, Ilai the Ahohite,<sup>30</sup>Maharai of Netophah, Heled the son of Baanah of Netophah,<sup>31</sup>Ithai the son of Ribai of Gibeah of the people of Benjamin, Benaiah of Pirathon,<sup>32</sup>Hurai of the brooks of Gaash, Abiel the Arbathite,<sup>33</sup>Azmaveth of Baharum, Eliahba the Shaalbonite,<sup>34</sup>Hashem the Gizonite, Jonathan the son of Shagee the Hararite,<sup>35</sup>Ahiam the son of Sachar the Hararite, Eliphal the son of Ur,<sup>36</sup>Hepher the Mecherathite, Ahijah the Pelonite,<sup>37</sup>Hezro of Carmel, Naarai the son of Ezbai,<sup>38</sup>Joel the brother of Nathan, Mibhar the son of Hagri,<sup>39</sup>Zelek the Ammonite, Naharai of Beeroth, the armor-bearer of Joab the son of Zeruiah,<sup>40</sup>Ira the Ithrite, Gareb the Ithrite,<sup>41</sup>Uriah the Hittite, Zabad the son of Ahlai,<sup>42</sup>Adina the son of Shiza the Reubenite, a leader of the Reubenites, and thirty with him,<sup>43</sup>Hanan the son of Maacah, and Joshaphat the Mithnite,<sup>44</sup>Uzzia the Ashterathite, Shama and Jeiel the sons of Hotham the Aroerite,<sup>45</sup>Jediael the son of Shimri, and Joha his brother, the Tizite,<sup>46</sup>Eliel the Mahavite, and Jeribai, and Joshaviah, the sons of Elnaam, and Ithmah the Moabite,<sup>47</sup>Eliel, and Obed, and Jaasiel the Mezobaite.
11.overview:
Israel comes to Hebron, makes a covenant with David and anoints him (vv. 1-3); Jerusalem is taken from the Jebusites and Joab wins the command by going up first (vv. 4-9); and the rest of the chapter is the roll of the mighty men — the three, the water of Bethlehem, Abishai and Benaiah, and then thirty-odd names with their towns (vv. 10-47).

The Chronicler passes over seven and a half years of civil war in the gap between chapters. He is not writing a life of David; he is writing how Israel came to have this king, this city and these men, and the answer he keeps giving is in verse 9.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — A Covenant at Hebron, a Stronghold at Jerusalem
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: All Israel comes to Hebron and says we are your bone and flesh, recalling that even under Saul it was David who led them out and brought them in, and that the LORD had said You shall be shepherd of my people Israel (vv. 1-2). David makes a covenant with them before the LORD and is anointed (v. 3). Then Jerusalem: the Jebusites tell him You will not come in here, and he takes the stronghold of Zion anyway, promising the command to whoever strikes first — which Joab does (vv. 4-6). The section ends on the sentence that explains the reign: David became greater and greater, for the LORD of hosts was with him (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: The kingship here is threefold: the people choose him, the LORD had already appointed him, and a covenant is cut between king and nation before God. Israel's monarchy was never a bare conquest and never a bare election. It was a covenant with a witness.
verseByVerse.examples: Joab gets the command because he went up the shaft first. That single act of nerve bought him a position David spent the next forty years unable to remove, and it is the only explanation the Bible offers for why the king could never be rid of the man.

verseByVerse.quote: Then all Israel gathered together to David at Hebron and said, "Behold, we are your bone and flesh. In times past, even when Saul was king, it was you who led out and brought in Israel. And the LORD your God said to you, 'You shall be shepherd of my people Israel, and you shall be prince over my people Israel.'" So all the elders of Israel came to the king at Hebron, and David made a covenant with them at Hebron before the LORD. And they anointed David king over Israel, according to the word of the LORD by Samuel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Between the last verse of chapter 10 and the first of chapter 11 there is a gap of seven and a half years, and the Chronicler does not mention it. There is no civil war here, no Ish-bosheth, no Abner, no long struggle between the house of Saul and the house of David. Saul dies, and then all Israel gathered together to David at Hebron.

What they say is a claim of kinship — Behold, we are your bone and flesh — followed by two reasons. The first is experience: even under Saul, it was you who led out and brought in Israel. The second is the word of God: You shall be shepherd of my people Israel.

So the elders give a practical reason and a theological one, in that order, and the Chronicler lets both stand. They wanted a competent soldier and they knew God had said so, and there is no suggestion that the second motive was contaminated by the first.

The word they use for the office is not king but shepherd. It is what David had been doing when Samuel sent for him, and it is the word God will use of himself when the kings have all failed and he says he will search for his sheep himself. A crown described as a flock is a crown with a duty of care built into the job title.

Then something easy to skip: David made a covenant with them at Hebron before the LORD. The king does not simply receive the throne; he binds himself, in God's presence, to the people who are giving it to him. Israel's monarchy begins with an obligation running in both directions.

verseByVerse.quote: And David and all Israel went to Jerusalem, that is, Jebus, where the Jebusites were, the inhabitants of the land. The inhabitants of Jebus said to David, "You will not come in here." Nevertheless, David took the stronghold of Zion, that is, the city of David. David said, "Whoever strikes the Jebusites first shall be chief and commander." And Joab the son of Zeruiah went up first, so he became chief. And David lived in the stronghold; therefore it was called the city of David.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem was not Israelite. Four hundred years after Joshua, a Canaanite city sat on the ridge between Judah and Benjamin, unconquered, and the men in it were confident enough to shout down from the wall: You will not come in here.

They had reason. The place is built on a spur with valleys on three sides, and the only approach is from the north. It had held out against Israel since Joshua and against the judges after him, and its garrison had watched Saul reign for forty years without troubling them.

The Chronicler gives the assault in eleven words. Nevertheless, David took the stronghold of Zion, that is, the city of David. No siege works, no casualty figures, no speech.

What he does record is the incentive and who claimed it. Whoever strikes the Jebusites first shall be chief and commander, and Joab went up first. That is the whole explanation, anywhere in Scripture, of how Joab came to hold the army. He bought the command with one act of nerve, and David spent the next forty years with a general he could neither control nor sack — a man who would murder Abner in a gateway, and Amasa on a road, and Absalom in a tree against a direct order.

Then the city is renamed. And David lived in the stronghold; therefore it was called the city of David. A Canaanite fortress with no history in Israel becomes, in one sentence, the address of the covenant. Every prophecy about Zion for the next thousand years is about this hill, and until this verse it belonged to somebody else.

verseByVerse.quote: And he built the city all around from the Millo in complete circuit, and Joab repaired the rest of the city. And David became greater and greater, for the LORD of hosts was with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two verses on construction, and they are the first thing David does after taking the place. And he built the city all around from the Millo in complete circuit, and Joab repaired the rest of the city.

The Millo is a terrace or a filled platform on the slope — the engineering that made a steep spur usable. David walls the circuit and Joab repairs what is inside it. The king and his general spend their first months as builders, and the Chronicler, whose whole book is heading towards a building, notices.

And then verse 9, which is the sentence the entire reign hangs on. And David became greater and greater, for the LORD of hosts was with him.

The greatness is reported and the reason is given, and the reason is not the man. Not his generalship, not the loyalty of the thirty, not the strength of the ridge. The Chronicler will say this in one form or another over and over, and he says it here at the top of the reign so that everything that follows is read underneath it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–25 — The Three, and the Water
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The roll opens with the chiefs who gave him strong support in his kingdom ... to make him king, according to the word of the LORD (v. 10): Jashobeam, who killed three hundred at one time (v. 11), and Eleazar, who stood alone in a barley field when the army had run and the LORD saved them by a great victory (vv. 13-14). Then the story the chapter is remembered for — three men breaking through a Philistine garrison for a drink of water from the well at Bethlehem, and David refusing to drink it (vv. 15-19). Abishai and Benaiah follow, each winning a name beside the three but not attaining to them (vv. 20-25).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 14 puts the credit where the chapter keeps putting it. A man stood in a barley field and would not run, and the sentence that follows is not that he saved them but that the LORD did. Courage is real and it is not the cause.
verseByVerse.examples: David poured out the water. He would not take the benefit of a risk he had not asked anyone to run, and the only thing he could do with a gift that cost that much was to give it to God.

verseByVerse.quote: Now these are the chiefs of David's mighty men, who gave him strong support in his kingdom, together with all Israel, to make him king, according to the word of the LORD concerning Israel. This is an account of David's mighty men: Jashobeam, a Hachmonite, was chief of the three. He wielded his spear against 300 whom he killed at one time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The roll of the mighty men opens with a statement of what they were for: they gave him strong support in his kingdom, together with all Israel, to make him king, according to the word of the LORD concerning Israel.

Every clause is doing something. These men made him king — a human act, deliberate and costly. All Israel did it with them. And it happened according to the word of the LORD. The Chronicler stacks the human agency and the divine word into a single verse without the slightest embarrassment, and never once suggests that the more God did, the less they did.

Then the first of the three. Jashobeam wielded his spear against 300 whom he killed at one time. The number is not the interesting part. What the roll is establishing is that the throne was not handed to David by acclamation alone; men bled for it, and their names were written down.

verseByVerse.quote: And next to him among the three mighty men was Eleazar the son of Dodo, the Ahohite. He was with David at Pas-dammim when the Philistines were gathered there for battle. There was a plot of ground full of barley, and the men fled from the Philistines. But he took his stand in the midst of the plot and defended it and killed the Philistines. And the LORD saved them by a great victory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eleazar's story is one verse long and it is a picture of something.

There is a plot of ground full of barley at Pas-dammim. The Philistines come, and the men fled from the Philistines — the whole line breaks and runs. And one man took his stand in the midst of the plot and defended it.

A barley field. Not a pass, not a citadel, not a bridge — somebody's crop. He stood in the middle of a field of grain because it belonged to Israel and the Philistines wanted it, and he stayed there while everyone he knew was running away behind him.

And then the verse that keeps the chapter honest. And the LORD saved them by a great victory. Not Eleazar saved them. A man had just done something extraordinary and the credit is handed straight past him, and the Chronicler will do this every single time.

verseByVerse.quote: Three of the thirty chief men went down to the rock to David at the cave of Adullam, when the army of Philistines was encamped in the Valley of Rephaim. David was then in the stronghold, and the garrison of the Philistines was then at Bethlehem. And David said longingly, "Oh that someone would give me water to drink from the well of Bethlehem that is by the gate!" Then the three mighty men broke through the camp of the Philistines and drew water out of the well of Bethlehem that was by the gate and took it and brought it to David. But David would not drink it. He poured it out to the LORD and said, "Far be it from me before my God that I should do this. Shall I drink the lifeblood of these men? For at the risk of their lives they brought it." Therefore he would not drink it. These things did the three mighty men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The finest story in the chapter, and nothing turns on it militarily.

David is in the stronghold; the Philistine garrison is in Bethlehem, five miles south, sitting on the town he grew up in. Three of the thirty come down to him at the cave of Adullam, and he says out loud what he is thinking. Oh that someone would give me water to drink from the well of Bethlehem that is by the gate!

He is homesick. He is not giving an order; he is a man in a cave remembering the taste of water from a particular well, and there is an enemy garrison standing on it.

Three men hear him and go. They break through a Philistine camp, draw the water, break back out, and bring it to their king.

And he will not drink it. Far be it from me before my God that I should do this. Shall I drink the lifeblood of these men? For at the risk of their lives they brought it. He calls the water their blood, because that is what it cost, and pours it on the ground as an offering to the LORD.

Consider what he is refusing. He wanted it. They fetched it. It was freely given and he had every right to it, and he would not put his own comfort on the far side of another man's life. Some things are too expensive to be enjoyed by the person they were bought for, and the only fit thing to do with them is to give them back to God.

A thousand years later, in that same town, blood was poured out at a cost nobody asked for and could not have repaid. That gift is not too expensive to receive. It was bought precisely so that it could be drunk, and the Son who paid for it puts the cup into his people's hands and tells them to take it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Abishai, the brother of Joab, was chief of the thirty. And he wielded his spear against 300 men and killed them and won a name beside the three. He was the most renowned of the thirty and became their commander, but he did not attain to the three.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abishai, Joab's brother, killed three hundred men and won a name beside the three. He was the most renowned of the thirty and their commander. And then: but he did not attain to the three.

The official chronicle of Israel records, in writing, that one of its bravest men was not quite in the first rank. Nobody softens it and nobody explains it away.

Abishai spent his life a step behind — behind Joab, who was his older brother and held the command; behind the three, whom he never joined. He was the man who offered twice to kill Saul and twice to kill Shimei and was refused every time. And he stayed.

verseByVerse.quote: And Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was a valiant man of Kabzeel, a doer of great deeds. He struck down two heroes of Moab. He also went down and struck down a lion in a pit on a day when snow had fallen. And he struck down an Egyptian, a man of great stature, five cubits tall. The Egyptian had in his hand a spear like a weaver's beam, but Benaiah went down to him with a staff and snatched the spear out of the Egyptian's hand and killed him with his own spear. These things did Benaiah the son of Jehoiada and won a name beside the three mighty men. He was renowned among the thirty, but he did not attain to the three. And David set him over his bodyguard.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Benaiah gets four verses and three feats, and the third of them is written to be recognised.

He struck down two heroes of Moab. He went down and struck down a lion in a pit on a day when snow had fallen — a detail nobody needed, kept because somebody who was there remembered the snow. And then he met an Egyptian of great stature, and the text says The Egyptian had in his hand a spear like a weaver's beam, but Benaiah went down to him with a staff.

A giant with a spear like a weaver's beam is Goliath. That is the phrase 1 Samuel uses of the shaft of his spear, and it will be used once more in this book, of Goliath's brother (20:5). And a man who goes down to him with a staff in his hand is David, who took his staff and five stones out of a brook.

Benaiah wrenched the spear out of the Egyptian's hand and killed him with it, which is what David did with Goliath's sword. The king's man repeats the king's victory, in the king's manner, with the king's kind of weapon — and the writer sets it down without a word of comment.

That is what a good king does to the men around him. They start doing what he does. And the sentence still ends but he did not attain to the three, and Benaiah went on to command David's bodyguard, then Solomon's army, and never seems to have raised it once.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–47 — The Roll of the Mighty Men
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Thirty-odd names with their towns — Asahel of Bethlehem's neighbourhood, Ira of Tekoa, Abiezer of Anathoth, men from Harod and Netophah and Gibeah, and at the end a run of outsiders: Zelek the Ammonite (v. 39), Ithmah the Moabite (v. 46), and in verse 41, without a syllable of comment, Uriah the Hittite.
verseByVerse.theology: The Chronicler never tells the story of Bathsheba. It is the largest deliberate omission in his book. And then he writes Uriah's name into the roll of honour and moves on to Zabad the son of Ahlai. The silence is not a cover-up; a cover-up would have left the name out.
verseByVerse.examples: Asahel is in verse 26 and he was dead long before this list was needed — Abner killed him in the retreat from Gibeon. The roll of the mighty men is partly a roll of the dead, which is what an honour roll usually is.

verseByVerse.quote: The mighty men were Asahel the brother of Joab, Elhanan the son of Dodo of Bethlehem, Shammoth of Harod, Helez the Pelonite, Ira the son of Ikkesh of Tekoa, Abiezer of Anathoth, Sibbecai the Hushathite, Ilai the Ahohite, Maharai of Netophah, Heled the son of Baanah of Netophah, Ithai the son of Ribai of Gibeah of the people of Benjamin, Benaiah of Pirathon, Hurai of the brooks of Gaash, Abiel the Arbathite,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the roll proper, and it is mostly geography. Asahel. Elhanan of Bethlehem. Shammoth of Harod, Helez the Pelonite, Ira of Tekoa, Abiezer of Anathoth, Sibbecai the Hushathite, men from Netophah and Anathoth and the brooks of Gaash.

Asahel is first, and Asahel had been dead for years by the time this roll mattered. Abner killed him in the retreat from Gibeon with the butt end of a spear, running backwards, after telling him three times to turn aside. He is in the honour roll all the same, which is what an honour roll is for.

Anathoth is here, the priestly town from chapter 6, sending fighting men to David. And Tekoa, which will send a wise woman to trick this king into bringing Absalom home, and three centuries later a shepherd called Amos.

verseByVerse.quote: Azmaveth of Baharum, Eliahba the Shaalbonite, Hashem the Gizonite, Jonathan the son of Shagee the Hararite, Ahiam the son of Sachar the Hararite, Eliphal the son of Ur, Hepher the Mecherathite, Ahijah the Pelonite, Hezro of Carmel, Naarai the son of Ezbai, Joel the brother of Nathan, Mibhar the son of Hagri, Zelek the Ammonite, Naharai of Beeroth, the armor-bearer of Joab the son of Zeruiah, Ira the Ithrite, Gareb the Ithrite,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eight more verses of names and towns, and the towns are the point. Baharum, Shaalbon, Gizon, Harar, Carmel, Zobah, Beeroth, Gilo, Carmel again, Ammon.

Read the map and something appears. These men are not from one clan or one tribe. They come from the hill country and the coastal edge, from Judah and Benjamin and the far north and beyond the Jordan, and one of them is from Zobah in Syria and one is an Ammonite. The army that took Jerusalem was assembled out of everywhere.

The Chronicler is writing for a community of a few thousand people who had come home from one city in one empire. Handing them a list like this says something a sermon could not: the people of God has never been a single village, and the men who put the first king of Jerusalem on his throne walked in from thirty different places.

verseByVerse.quote: Uriah the Hittite, Zabad the son of Ahlai, Adina the son of Shiza the Reubenite, a leader of the Reubenites, and thirty with him, Hanan the son of Maacah, and Joshaphat the Mithnite, Uzzia the Ashterathite, Shama and Jeiel the sons of Hotham the Aroerite, Jediael the son of Shimri, and Joha his brother, the Tizite, Eliel the Mahavite, and Jeribai, and Joshaviah, the sons of Elnaam, and Ithmah the Moabite, Eliel, and Obed, and Jaasiel the Mezobaite.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And then, in a list of names, this one: Uriah the Hittite.

Nothing else. No note, no asterisk, no explanation. The name sits between Ahijah the Pelonite and Zabad the son of Ahlai, and the Chronicler goes straight on to Adina the son of Shiza the Reubenite.

He has told none of the story. The whole affair — the roof, the message, the letter carried by the man it condemned, Nathan and the lamb, the child that died — is absent from this book. It is the largest deliberate omission in Chronicles, and readers have argued for centuries about whether it was reverence or politics.

Whatever the reason, it was not concealment, because here is the name. A writer hiding what David did to Uriah would not have put Uriah in the roll of David's mighty men. He is listed among the men who made David king: a foreigner who fought for Israel and was faithful to a king who was not faithful to him. The silence around his name is louder than any comment would have been.

Two other outsiders close the roll — Zelek the Ammonite and Ithmah the Moabite. The army that took Jerusalem had Ammonites and Moabites and a Hittite in it, and the man who led it was the great-grandson of a Moabite woman who had come home to Bethlehem behind her mother-in-law.

11.theology:
Twice in nine verses the credit is moved off the men and onto God: David became greater and greater, for the LORD of hosts was with him (v. 9), and after Eleazar's stand in the barley field, the LORD saved them by a great victory (v. 14). Neither statement diminishes what the men did — the Chronicler records the three hundred and the lion and the Egyptian in detail. He simply refuses to let the achievement be the explanation.

And the kingship is founded on a covenant made before the LORD, not on the conquest of a city. David takes Zion in verse 5, but he is king in verse 3, and the order is the argument.
11.examples:
David would not drink water that had cost three men their safety. It is the instinct of a man who understands what other people spend on him, and it is rarer than courage. The hardest gifts to receive are the ones we would never have asked anybody to pay for.

And two of the bravest men in the book are recorded as not having made the first rank, twice, in writing. Benaiah went on to command the army. There is a kind of servant who can be told exactly where he stands and go on working, and Scripture puts his name in the chronicle.

12.title: Those Who Came to David: Voluntary Allegiance and the Spirit's Work
12.text: <sup>1</sup>Now these are the men who came to David at Ziklag, while he could not move about freely because of Saul the son of Kish. And they were among the mighty men who helped him in war.<sup>2</sup>They were bowmen and could shoot arrows and sling stones with either the right or the left hand; they were Benjaminites, Saul's kinsmen.<sup>3</sup>The chief was Ahiezer, then Joash, both sons of Shemaah of Gibeah; also Jeziel and Pelet, the sons of Azmaveth; Beracah, Jehu of Anathoth,<sup>4</sup>Ishmaiah of Gibeon, a mighty man among the thirty and a leader over the thirty; Jeremiah, Jahaziel, Johanan, Jozabad of Gederah,<sup>5</sup>Eluzai, Jerimoth, Bealiah, Shemariah, Shephatiah the Haruphite;<sup>6</sup>Elkanah, Isshiah, Azarel, Joezer, and Jashobeam, the Korahites;<sup>7</sup>And Joelah and Zebadiah, the sons of Jeroham of Gedor.<sup>8</sup>From the Gadites there went over to David at the stronghold in the wilderness mighty and experienced warriors, expert with shield and spear, whose faces were like the faces of lions and who were swift as gazelles upon the mountains:<sup>9</sup>Ezer the chief, Obadiah second, Eliab third,<sup>10</sup>Mishmannah fourth, Jeremiah fifth,<sup>11</sup>Attai sixth, Eliel seventh,<sup>12</sup>Johanan eighth, Elzabad ninth,<sup>13</sup>Jeremiah tenth, Machbannai eleventh.<sup>14</sup>These Gadites were officers of the army; the least was a match for a hundred men and the greatest for a thousand.<sup>15</sup>These are the men who crossed the Jordan in the first month, when it was overflowing all its banks, and put to flight all those in the valleys, to the east and to the west.<sup>16</sup>And some of the men of Benjamin and Judah came to the stronghold to David.<sup>17</sup>David went out to meet them and said to them, "If you have come to me in friendship to help me, my heart will be joined to you; but if to betray me to my adversaries, although there is no wrong in my hands, then may the God of our fathers see and rebuke you."<sup>18</sup>Then the Spirit clothed Amasai, chief of the thirty, and he said, "We are yours, O David, and with you, O son of Jesse! Peace, peace to you, and peace to your helpers! For your God helps you." Then David received them and made them officers of his troops.<sup>19</sup>Some of the men of Manasseh deserted to David when he came with the Philistines for the battle against Saul. (Yet he did not help them, for the rulers of the Philistines took counsel and sent him away, saying, "At peril to our heads he will desert to his master Saul.")<sup>20</sup>As he went to Ziklag, these men of Manasseh deserted to him: Adnah, Jozabad, Jediael, Michael, Jozabad, Elihu, and Zillethai, chiefs of thousands in Manasseh.<sup>21</sup>They helped David against the band of raiders, for they were all mighty men of valor and were commanders in the army.<sup>22</sup>For from day to day men came to David to help him, until there was a great army, like an army of God.<sup>23</sup>These are the numbers of the divisions of the armed troops who came to David in Hebron to turn the kingdom of Saul over to him, according to the word of the LORD.<sup>24</sup>The men of Judah bearing shield and spear were 6,800 armed troops.<sup>25</sup>Of the Simeonites, mighty men of valor for war, 7,100.<sup>26</sup>Of the Levites 4,600.<sup>27</sup>The prince Jehoiada, of the house of Aaron, and with him 3,700.<sup>28</sup>Zadok, a young man mighty in valor, and twenty-two commanders from his own fathers' house.<sup>29</sup>Of the Benjaminites, the kinsmen of Saul, 3,000, of whom the majority had to that point kept their allegiance to the house of Saul.<sup>30</sup>Of the Ephraimites 20,800, mighty men of valor, famous men in their fathers' houses.<sup>31</sup>Of the half-tribe of Manasseh 18,000, who were expressly named to come and make David king.<sup>32</sup>Of Issachar, men who had understanding of the times, to know what Israel ought to do, 200 chiefs, and all their kinsmen under their command.<sup>33</sup>Of Zebulun 50,000 seasoned troops, equipped for battle with all the weapons of war, to help David with singleness of purpose.<sup>34</sup>Of Naphtali 1,000 commanders with whom were 37,000 men armed with shield and spear.<sup>35</sup>Of the Danites 28,600 men equipped for battle.<sup>36</sup>Of Asher 40,000 seasoned troops ready for battle.<sup>37</sup>Of the Reubenites and Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh from beyond the Jordan, 120,000 men armed with all the weapons of war.<sup>38</sup>All these, men of war, arrayed in battle order, came to Hebron with a whole heart to make David king over all Israel. Likewise, all the rest of Israel were of a single mind to make David king.<sup>39</sup>And they were there with David for three days, eating and drinking, for their brothers had made preparation for them.<sup>40</sup>And also their relatives, from as far as Issachar and Zebulun and Naphtali, came bringing food on donkeys and on camels and on mules and on oxen, abundant provisions of flour, cakes of figs, clusters of raisins, and wine and oil, oxen and sheep, for there was joy in Israel.
12.overview:
The chapter runs backwards before it runs forwards. It opens years before the coronation, at Ziklag, where men were slipping out of Israel to join a fugitive: Benjaminites from Saul's own clan (vv. 1-7), Gadites who swam a flooded Jordan (vv. 8-15), a mixed party met at the gate by a suspicious David and vouched for by the Spirit (vv. 16-18), and deserters from Manasseh who arrived days before Ziklag burned (vv. 19-22). Then Hebron, and the muster of all twelve tribes to make him king (vv. 23-37), ending in a three-day feast (vv. 38-40).

It has no parallel in Samuel. The Chronicler wrote it to answer a question his own readers were living inside: how does the kingdom God promised actually arrive? His answer is that it arrives the way it arrived here — one person at a time, over years, while nothing looks like working.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — Men Who Came While It Cost Something
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter turns back the clock. David is at Ziklag, a Philistine border town, unable to move about freely because of Saul the son of Kish (v. 1), and men are walking out of Israel to join him. First Benjaminites — Saul's own tribe, Saul's own relatives — ambidextrous with bow and sling, named clan by clan (vv. 2-7). Then Gadites who cross to the desert stronghold, whose faces were like the faces of lions and who were swift as gazelles upon the mountains, ranked first to eleventh (vv. 8-13). The section closes on two measurements: the least was a match for a hundred men and the greatest for a thousand (v. 14), and they crossed the Jordan in the first month, when it was overflowing all its banks (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: Every man in this list backed David before there was anything to gain by it. The kingdom God had promised was, at this point, one hunted man in a foreign town, and these are the people who read the promise rather than the odds.
verseByVerse.examples: The Gadites came at the one season of the year when the Jordan cannot be crossed. They did not wait for the water to drop. Some decisions have a window, and the window is open when the crossing is hardest.

verseByVerse.quote: Now these are the men who came to David at Ziklag, while he could not move about freely because of Saul the son of Kish. And they were among the mighty men who helped him in war. They were bowmen and could shoot arrows and sling stones with either the right or the left hand; they were Benjaminites, Saul's kinsmen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Chapter 11 crowned David at Hebron in front of all Israel. Chapter 12 goes back several years to a Philistine border town where he had a price on his head, and starts naming the men who came to him there.

The Chronicler has never told that story and does not tell it now. Nothing about Saul hunting him through the wilderness of Ziph, nothing about the cave at Adullam, nothing about the sixteen months he spent living under a Philistine warlord's protection because there was nowhere in Israel he could sleep. All of it is compressed into one clause — while he could not move about freely because of Saul the son of Kish — and the reader is expected to supply the rest.

What the clause does fix is the cost. Coming to David at Ziklag was not joining a winning side; it was leaving the country to attach yourself to a wanted man in enemy territory. There was no throne to be near, no spoil to share, and a very good chance of ending up on a list of traitors. Every name in the first twenty-two verses of this chapter belongs to somebody who moved before there was anything in it.

Then the detail that ought to stop a reader flat. They were bowmen and could shoot arrows and sling stones with either the right or the left hand; they were Benjaminites, Saul's kinsmen.

Saul's own tribe. Saul's own relations. And ambidextrous slinging is precisely what Benjamin was famous for — Ehud was a left-handed Benjaminite, and the tribe once put seven hundred left-handed men in the field who could sling at a hair and not miss. These are the best soldiers Benjamin produced, and they walked away from the head of their own clan to stand behind a man from Judah.

Saul had stood in front of men like these and asked whether the son of Jesse would give them fields and vineyards and make them commanders. He was betting that blood would hold them. It did not hold all of them. Some of his cousins had worked out what God had already said about the throne, and they went where the word had gone.

verseByVerse.quote: The chief was Ahiezer, then Joash, both sons of Shemaah of Gibeah; also Jeziel and Pelet, the sons of Azmaveth; Beracah, Jehu of Anathoth, Ishmaiah of Gibeon, a mighty man among the thirty and a leader over the thirty; Jeremiah, Jahaziel, Johanan, Jozabad of Gederah, Eluzai, Jerimoth, Bealiah, Shemariah, Shephatiah the Haruphite; Elkanah, Isshiah, Azarel, Joezer, and Jashobeam, the Korahites; And Joelah and Zebadiah, the sons of Jeroham of Gedor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Five verses of names, and the Chronicler is doing with them what he has done all through this book: putting individuals on record.

Ahiezer and Joash of Gibeah — Saul's own town. Jeziel and Pelet of Azmaveth. Jehu of Anathoth, which is the priestly village that Jeremiah will come from. Ishmaiah of Gibeon, who is marked out as a mighty man among the thirty and a leader over the thirty. Jozabad of Gederah, Shephatiah the Haruphite, the Korahites, the sons of Jeroham of Gedor.

Roughly two dozen men, and about half of them are pinned to a village. That is the point of a list like this to the people first reading it. These are not legends; they are somebody's great-grandfather from a place you can walk to in an afternoon.

The community the Chronicler wrote for was a few thousand returned exiles rebuilding a provincial town, and their besetting fear was that they were too small to matter. He hands them a list of men from Gibeah and Gibeon and Gederah who changed the history of Israel by getting up and walking to Ziklag, and he does not tell them what to make of it.
