He has been given a view down the centuries, and the sight of it stops him: And what more can David say to you for honoring your servant?

He has run out of words and says so, which is a strange thing for the man who wrote half the Psalter to admit. And then he gives the reason he can stop talking: For you know your servant. There is no need to explain himself to someone who already knows what he is. It is the relief that comes at the end of every honest prayer.

Verse 19 gives the cause of the whole thing, and it is not David. For your servant's sake, O LORD, and according to your own heart, you have done all this greatness. According to your own heart. Not according to my record, not because the kingdom needed a dynasty, not as wages for the ark. God did it because of what he is like, and a covenant founded there cannot be undone by anything the other party turns out to be.

verseByVerse.quote: There is none like you, O LORD, and there is no God besides you, according to all that we have heard with our ears. And who is like your people Israel, the one nation on earth whom God went to redeem to be his people, making for yourself a name for great and awesome things, in driving out nations before your people whom you redeemed from Egypt? And you made your people Israel to be your people forever, and you, O LORD, became their God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prayer now lifts away from David's house altogether and says two things that cannot be said about anybody else.

The first: There is none like you, O LORD, and there is no God besides you, according to all that we have heard with our ears. Not merely the best of the gods. None like him and none besides him, and the ground given is testimony — what has been heard, handed down, told from one generation to the next. David believes it because Israel remembered it, and the psalm he wrote that afternoon had told them to keep remembering.

The second is the surprising one. And who is like your people Israel, the one nation on earth whom God went to redeem to be his people?

He has just said there is none like God, and he immediately says there is no people like Israel — and the second claim rests entirely on the first. Israel is not incomparable because of anything in Israel. It is incomparable because of who came after it. The nation was a company of slaves in a brickyard, and the distinguishing fact about them is that God himself went down to fetch them.

Note the verb: God went to redeem. He did not send. And the purpose given is not the slaves' comfort but God's reputation — making for yourself a name for great and awesome things. God rescued a nation and got a name by it, and then turned round and made a name for David. The whole economy of the chapter runs on a God who gives away what he could have kept.

And verse 22 fixes it in place: you made your people Israel to be your people forever, and you, O LORD, became their God. Both halves of that were his doing. He made them his, and he became theirs.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–27 — Do As You Have Spoken
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The prayer turns into petition, and the petition is that God will keep his own promise: let the word that you have spoken ... be established forever, and do as you have spoken (v. 23) — so that God's name is magnified and men say The LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, is Israel's God (v. 24). Then David explains his own boldness: because God revealed the promise, therefore your servant has found courage to pray before you (v. 25). It ends where it must: you are God, and you have promised this good thing (v. 26), and it is you, O LORD, who have blessed, and it is blessed forever (v. 27).
verseByVerse.theology: David asks God for exactly what God has just offered him, which is what most real praying consists of. And the goal he names is not the security of his family but the magnifying of the name — his house is the means and God's reputation is the end.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 25 gives the reason a man dares to pray at all, and it is not his mood or his record. God had spoken first. Courage in prayer is a response to a promise, and David says so in as many words.

verseByVerse.quote: And now, O LORD, let the word that you have spoken concerning your servant and concerning his house be established forever, and do as you have spoken, and your name will be established and magnified forever, saying, 'The LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, is Israel's God,' and the house of your servant David will be established before you. For you, my God, have revealed to your servant that you will build a house for him. Therefore your servant has found courage to pray before you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the prayer turns into a request, and the request is remarkable for what it asks. And now, O LORD, let the word that you have spoken concerning your servant and concerning his house be established forever, and do as you have spoken.

Do as you have spoken. He asks God for precisely what God has just offered, and adds nothing of his own. There is not a single petition in this prayer that was not first a promise in the message, which is what praying largely is once a person has learned how: taking what God has said and handing it back to him as a request.

And the goal he names is not his family's security. Your name will be established and magnified forever, saying, The LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, is Israel's God. The dynasty is the means; the sentence people will say about God is the end. David wants his house to last so that a certain thing will be said about the LORD, and he puts it in that order himself.

Then verse 25, which explains how a man dares to talk like this at all.

For you, my God, have revealed to your servant that you will build a house for him. Therefore your servant has found courage to pray before you.

Therefore. The boldness has a cause and the cause is outside him. The Hebrew says he found his heart to pray — he located the nerve for it — and what located it was not a surge of feeling or a run of obedient days. It was a promise, spoken first, by God. Take the promise away and there is nothing to be confident about; leave it there and a shepherd can sit down in front of the ark and ask the Almighty to keep his word.

That is still the only door in. The letter to the Hebrews tells frightened people to come to the throne of grace with confidence, and the confidence is never in the one approaching. It is in the one who went before, and in what he has said he will do.

verseByVerse.quote: And now, O LORD, you are God, and you have promised this good thing to your servant. Now you have been pleased to bless the house of your servant, that it may continue forever before you, for it is you, O LORD, who have blessed, and it is blessed forever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prayer ends in two short sentences that do not ask for anything more.

And now, O LORD, you are God, and you have promised this good thing to your servant. Those are the two facts he lies down on. You are God — so you are able. You have promised — so you are willing. Everything a man needs to be sure of is contained in that pair, and David has stopped trying to add to it.

Then the last verse, and the tense changes. Now you have been pleased to bless the house of your servant, that it may continue forever before you, for it is you, O LORD, who have blessed, and it is blessed forever.

It is blessed. Not it will be blessed if the sons behave, or it may be blessed should the kingdom hold. The blessing is spoken of as a thing already done, and the reason given is that the one who did it was God. What God has blessed stays blessed, because the blessing was never a comment on the recipient.

Eight times in this chapter the word forever appears, and David uses the last two of them. He is sitting in a tent city, in a kingdom thirty years old, with a son not yet grown and a throne no descendant of his has ever inherited, and he says forever twice in one breath.

He was right, though not in the way he could have measured. His line held Jerusalem for four centuries and then lost it, and the last of his sons to wear the crown was blinded and taken to Babylon in chains. Five hundred years after that, an angel stood in a village in Galilee and told a girl that her son would be given the throne of his father David and would reign over the house of Jacob with no end to his kingdom. The house is still standing. It is you, O LORD, who have blessed, and it is blessed forever.

17.theology:
The covenant rests on God's character and nothing else. David asks why and is told: according to your own heart (v. 19). Not for services rendered, not because the ark had been fetched, not as wages. God is not answering a need of his own either — he had gone from tent to tent for four centuries and never mentioned it (vv. 5-6). A covenant founded on what God is like cannot be undone by what the other party turns out to be.

Chronicles prints the promise without the discipline clause that stands in 2 Samuel 7:14 and calls the throne God's own (v. 14). Both changes point the same way, at readers who had no king left: the kingdom was never David's property, so its loss was not the loss of the promise. I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son is applied in the New Testament not to Solomon but to Christ, and the word forever, used eight times here, finally means what it says.
17.examples:
Nathan told David to do what was in his heart, and God overturned it that night. Godly instinct, warm approval and a true observation that God was with him added up to advice that was simply wrong, and the prophet went back the next morning and said so. Being sincerely encouraging is not the same as having heard from God.

David wanted to build and was told his son would. He spent the rest of his life buying the site, stockpiling the materials, drawing the plans and organising the priesthood for a building he would never walk into. A refused ambition can be worked at for forty years by somebody who has accepted the refusal.

Verse 25 names the source of boldness in prayer: God had spoken first, therefore the servant found the courage to ask. Confidence before God is not a temperament and not a reward for a good week. It is a response to something that has been said.

18.title: David's Victories: The King Who Subdues the Nations
18.text: <sup>1</sup>After this David defeated the Philistines and subdued them, and he took Gath and its villages out of the hand of the Philistines.<sup>2</sup>And he defeated Moab, and the Moabites became servants to David and brought tribute.<sup>3</sup>David also defeated Hadadezer king of Zobah-Hamath, as he went to set up his monument at the river Euphrates.<sup>4</sup>And David took from him 1,000 chariots, 7,000 horsemen, and 20,000 foot soldiers. And David hamstrung all the chariot horses, but left enough for 100 chariots.<sup>5</sup>And when the Syrians of Damascus came to help Hadadezer king of Zobah, David struck down 22,000 men of the Syrians.<sup>6</sup>Then David put garrisons in Syria of Damascus, and the Syrians became servants to David and brought tribute. And the LORD gave victory to David wherever he went.<sup>7</sup>And David took the shields of gold that were carried by the servants of Hadadezer and brought them to Jerusalem.<sup>8</sup>And from Tibhath and from Cun, cities of Hadadezer, David took a large amount of bronze. With it Solomon made the bronze sea and the pillars and the vessels of bronze.<sup>9</sup>When Tou king of Hamath heard that David had defeated the whole army of Hadadezer, king of Zobah,<sup>10</sup>he sent his son Hadoram to King David, to ask about his health and to bless him because he had fought against Hadadezer and defeated him; for Hadadezer had often been at war with Tou. And he sent all sorts of articles of gold, of silver, and of bronze.<sup>11</sup>These also King David dedicated to the LORD, together with the silver and gold that he had carried off from all the nations, from Edom, Moab, the Ammonites, the Philistines, and Amalek.<sup>12</sup>And Abishai, the son of Zeruiah, killed 18,000 Edomites in the Valley of Salt.<sup>13</sup>Then he put garrisons in Edom, and all the Edomites became David's servants. And the LORD gave victory to David wherever he went.<sup>14</sup>So David reigned over all Israel, and he administered justice and equity to all his people.<sup>15</sup>And Joab the son of Zeruiah was over the army; and Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud was recorder;<sup>16</sup>and Zadok the son of Ahitub and Ahimelech the son of Abiathar were priests; and Shavsha was secretary;<sup>17</sup>and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and the Pelethites; and David's sons were the chief officials in the service of the king.
18.overview:
The wars are told at speed: Philistia and Gath, Moab, Hadadezer of Zobah at the Euphrates with his chariot horses hamstrung, and Damascus (vv. 1-6). The gold shields come to Jerusalem and the bronze is set aside for a temple that does not exist yet (vv. 7-8). Tou of Hamath sends gifts, and every scrap of plunder from five nations is dedicated to the LORD (vv. 9-11). Abishai beats the Edomites, garrisons are set (vv. 12-13) — and then the verse the chapter exists for: David administered justice and equity to all his people (v. 14), followed by his list of officials (vv. 15-17).

Twice, in identical words, the campaigns are bracketed by the LORD gave victory to David wherever he went. The verb is the word for saving.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Victories, and Bronze for a Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The wars are reported at speed. Philistia is subdued and Gath taken (v. 1); Moab pays tribute (v. 2); Hadadezer of Zobah is beaten at the Euphrates and his chariotry crippled — David hamstrung all the chariot horses, but left enough for 100 chariots (vv. 3-4); Damascus comes to help and loses 22,000 men (v. 5). Then the refrain: the LORD gave victory to David wherever he went (v. 6). The gold shields go to Jerusalem (v. 7), and the bronze goes somewhere the parallel account never mentions: with it Solomon made the bronze sea and the pillars and the vessels of bronze (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 6 says it plainly, and verse 13 will say it again at the other end of the campaigns. The word underneath the phrase is the word for saving. David won every war he fought, and the record calls it rescue rather than conquest.
verseByVerse.examples: David crippled the captured chariot horses instead of building a chariot corps with them. The law had told the king not to accumulate horses, and Joshua had done exactly this at the waters of Merom by direct command. His son kept fourteen hundred chariots.

verseByVerse.quote: After this David defeated the Philistines and subdued them, and he took Gath and its villages out of the hand of the Philistines. And he defeated Moab, and the Moabites became servants to David and brought tribute.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter opens with a list of wars won and a first entry that carries thirty years of history in one place name. He took Gath and its villages out of the hand of the Philistines.

Gath was Goliath's town. It was also where a young fugitive had once run for asylum with the giant's own sword strapped to his back, realised the servants of Achish had recognised him, and got out alive only by scrabbling at the gateposts and letting spittle run into his beard until they threw him out as a madman. He went back later and lived there for sixteen months as a Philistine vassal with nowhere else to go.

Now he owns it. The Chronicler does not say any of that; he writes the name of the town and moves on.

Then Moab, which has its own weight. David's great-grandmother had walked out of Moab behind Naomi, and when Saul was hunting him David had taken his father and mother across the Jordan and asked the king of Moab to shelter them. The line in this verse is that the Moabites became servants and brought tribute. The account in Samuel adds a detail about prisoners measured with a line, and the Chronicler leaves it out.

verseByVerse.quote: David also defeated Hadadezer king of Zobah-Hamath, as he went to set up his monument at the river Euphrates. And David took from him 1,000 chariots, 7,000 horsemen, and 20,000 foot soldiers. And David hamstrung all the chariot horses, but left enough for 100 chariots. And when the Syrians of Damascus came to help Hadadezer king of Zobah, David struck down 22,000 men of the Syrians. Then David put garrisons in Syria of Damascus, and the Syrians became servants to David and brought tribute. And the LORD gave victory to David wherever he went.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hadadezer of Zobah is the largest enemy in the chapter — an Aramean king whose reach ran north-east towards the Euphrates, and who was setting up a monument on that river when David caught him. The Hebrew leaves it slightly open whose monument it was, and most readers take it as Hadadezer's. Either way the fighting has reached the river God named to Abraham when he first described the land.

The spoil is counted: a thousand chariots, seven thousand horsemen, twenty thousand foot. And then a detail that would look like vandalism to any other king in the region. And David hamstrung all the chariot horses, but left enough for 100 chariots.

Chariots were the tanks of the age. He has just captured the single most valuable military asset in the ancient Near East and he cripples nine tenths of it on the spot.

The law of the king had said he must not multiply horses to himself, and Joshua had done precisely this at the waters of Merom because God told him to. David is not being sentimental about horses or careless about defence; he is refusing to build the kind of army that makes a nation trust its own hardware. His son will keep fourteen hundred chariots and twelve thousand horsemen, and the difference between father and son is already visible in this verse.

Then the line that explains the whole run of victories. And the LORD gave victory to David wherever he went. The verb underneath is the word for saving. It was not a campaign season; it was a rescue, repeated.

verseByVerse.quote: And David took the shields of gold that were carried by the servants of Hadadezer and brought them to Jerusalem. And from Tibhath and from Cun, cities of Hadadezer, David took a large amount of bronze. With it Solomon made the bronze sea and the pillars and the vessels of bronze.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two verses about metal, and the second one is why this chapter is in the book at all.

First the gold. David took the shields of gold that were carried by the servants of Hadadezer and brought them to Jerusalem. Ceremonial shields, made to be seen rather than used, the sort of thing a king's guard carried to display what he could afford. They go to the capital.

Then the bronze, from two of Hadadezer's cities, and the Chronicler adds a sentence that the parallel account does not have. With it Solomon made the bronze sea and the pillars and the vessels of bronze.

Follow that through. The bronze sea was the great basin standing in the temple court on twelve oxen, holding thousands of gallons, where the priests washed before they went in to God. The pillars were Jachin and Boaz, standing at the entrance. And the metal in all of it came out of a Syrian war fought a generation before the building existed, carried home by a king who was told he would never build the house.

He knew what he was doing with it. That is the point of the sentence. David could not lay a stone, so he spent his wars stockpiling the material and left it for a son who was not yet born to melt down into the furniture of God's house.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Tou of Hamath, who had been fighting Hadadezer for years, sends his son with congratulations and a load of gold, silver and bronze (vv. 9-10). And every bit of it goes the same way: These also King David dedicated to the LORD, along with the plunder of Edom, Moab, Ammon, Philistia and Amalek (v. 11). Abishai kills 18,000 Edomites in the Valley of Salt, garrisons are set, and the refrain closes the section — the LORD gave victory to David wherever he went (vv. 12-13).
verseByVerse.theology: Five nations are named in verse 11 and the whole take from all of them is dedicated. A generation later Solomon will build a temple out of a treasury his father never spent, and this verse is where it started.
verseByVerse.examples: Tou sent gifts because David had beaten his enemy for him. It was self-interested diplomacy and the Chronicler records it without comment, and the gold went into the same pile as everything else.

verseByVerse.quote: When Tou king of Hamath heard that David had defeated the whole army of Hadadezer, king of Zobah, he sent his son Hadoram to King David, to ask about his health and to bless him because he had fought against Hadadezer and defeated him; for Hadadezer had often been at war with Tou. And he sent all sorts of articles of gold, of silver, and of bronze. These also King David dedicated to the LORD, together with the silver and gold that he had carried off from all the nations, from Edom, Moab, the Ammonites, the Philistines, and Amalek.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An embassy arrives from Hamath, further north still. Tou has been at war with Hadadezer for years and someone else has just beaten him, so he sends his son Hadoram with congratulations, good wishes and articles of gold and silver and bronze.

It is diplomacy and it is self-interested, and the Chronicler reports it without a word of comment on the motive. A northern king has decided that the man in Jerusalem is now the power in the region and would rather be his friend than find out.

Then verse 11, which is what David did with all of it. These also King David dedicated to the LORD, together with the silver and gold that he had carried off from all the nations, from Edom, Moab, the Ammonites, the Philistines, and Amalek.

Five nations named, and everything taken from every one of them handed over. Not tithed, not shared out among the commanders, not put in a royal treasury. Dedicated — set apart, made unavailable for any other use.

A man who has been told his life's ambition belongs to someone else could have spent the rest of it comfortably. Instead he ran a thirty-year campaign of acquisition on behalf of a building he would never see, and by chapter 29 the pile is so large that the numbers stop sounding real.

verseByVerse.quote: And Abishai, the son of Zeruiah, killed 18,000 Edomites in the Valley of Salt. Then he put garrisons in Edom, and all the Edomites became David's servants. And the LORD gave victory to David wherever he went.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Abishai, the son of Zeruiah, killed 18,000 Edomites in the Valley of Salt.

Three places in Scripture describe this battle and each credits a different man. Samuel puts it down to David, who was the king. The title of one of the psalms puts it down to Joab, who commanded the army. This verse names Abishai, who led the action in the field. None of them is wrong; they are answering different questions about the same day.

And it is a good name to find here. Abishai is the man chapter 11 recorded as the most renowned of the thirty, who did not attain to the three. He is still fighting, still winning, still second. The public record of his life includes the sentence that he never quite made the first rank, and eighteen thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt.

Then the refrain again, closing the campaigns as it opened them: And the LORD gave victory to David wherever he went. Twice in eight verses, in identical words, with everything the king achieved set between the two of them like a statement inside brackets.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Then the sentence the wars existed for: So David reigned over all Israel, and he administered justice and equity to all his people (v. 14). A list of officials follows — Joab over the army, Jehoshaphat as recorder, Zadok and Ahimelech as priests, Shavsha as secretary, Benaiah over the foreign bodyguard, and David's sons as the chief officials in the service of the king (vv. 15-17).
verseByVerse.theology: Justice and equity is the pair the prophets use ever afterwards to test a king. Verse 14 is not a change of subject after thirteen verses of fighting; it is what all the fighting was supposed to produce, and the phrase to all his people is doing as much work as the nouns.
verseByVerse.examples: The account in Samuel says David's sons were priests. The Chronicler will not write that sentence. He has spent three chapters on who may carry, who may sing and who may sacrifice, and the king's sons are given a civil title instead.

verseByVerse.quote: So David reigned over all Israel, and he administered justice and equity to all his people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So David reigned over all Israel, and he administered justice and equity to all his people.

Thirteen verses of armies and tribute and hamstrung horses, and then this. It is not a change of subject. It is the point of everything before it, stated in one line, and if the line were missing the chapter would only be a record of a successful warlord.

The two words are the pair Israel used ever afterwards to test a king. Justice is the verdict being right; equity is the whole arrangement being right, so that the verdicts do not have to keep rescuing people from a system built to crush them. Jeremiah would one day ask a descendant of David whether he thought being a king consisted of cedar panelling, and answer his own question by saying that David's son Josiah judged the cause of the poor and needy — Is not this to know me?

And the last three words are the hardest part of the verse: to all his people. Not to the tribes that turned out at Hebron, not to the men who came to Ziklag while it cost something. Justice that stops at the people who deserve it from you is not justice; it is gratitude with a gavel.

The prophet who saw furthest put the two words in the mouth of a child not yet born, whose government would have no end, and said he would uphold his kingdom with justice and with righteousness from this time forth and forevermore. Israel got a taste of it under David, and has been waiting for the rest ever since.

verseByVerse.quote: And Joab the son of Zeruiah was over the army; and Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud was recorder; and Zadok the son of Ahitub and Ahimelech the son of Abiathar were priests; and Shavsha was secretary; and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and the Pelethites; and David's sons were the chief officials in the service of the king.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the cabinet, and a cabinet is what a settled kingdom has. Joab over the army. Jehoshaphat the recorder, who kept the chronicle. Zadok and Ahimelech as priests. Shavsha the secretary, running the correspondence of a state that now has correspondence.

Benaiah is over the Cherethites and the Pelethites, and those are not Israelite names. The king's personal bodyguard was made up of professional soldiers from the Philistine coast — men from the nation David spent his life fighting, trusted with his life at close quarters. He had lived among them for sixteen months as a fugitive and evidently learned who could be relied on.

And then the last clause, where the Chronicler quietly declines to repeat something. The account in Samuel says that David's sons were priests. This book says they were the chief officials in the service of the king.

He has spent three chapters on who may do what. Only Levites may carry the ark; only the sons of Aaron may offer on the altar; a man died on a cart track for putting out his hand. Whatever David's sons did in his court, this writer will not call them priests, and the care he takes over one word at the end of a list of officials is the same care that runs through the whole book.

18.theology:
The Chronicler is not interested in the battles for their own sake. He is interested in where the metal went. Verse 8 adds a sentence the parallel account does not have — the bronze from Hadadezer's cities became the sea and the pillars of Solomon's temple — and verse 11 says the whole take from five nations was dedicated. A king who had been told he would never build the house spent his wars supplying it.

And verse 14 is where the fighting was aimed. Justice and equity to all his people is the standard by which every later king of Judah is measured, and the prophet who saw the true son of David coming used the same two words of a government that would have no end.
18.examples:
David hamstrung the captured chariot horses because the law had told the king not to accumulate them. It is the least intuitive decision in the chapter: a commander destroying the best equipment he has just won, because of a sentence in a book. His son kept fourteen hundred chariots.

Everything taken from five nations was dedicated and none of it was spent. A man who cannot do the thing he most wants to do can still spend thirty years making it possible for somebody else, and Solomon washed the priests in a basin his father had captured.

Abishai wins eighteen thousand and is still the man who did not attain to the three. Second place, on the permanent record, with no complaint attached and another victory beside it.

19.title: The Ammonite Humiliation and the Wars That Follow
19.text: <sup>1</sup>Now after this Nahash the king of the Ammonites died, and his son reigned in his place.<sup>2</sup>And David said, "I will deal kindly with Hanun the son of Nahash, for his father dealt kindly with me." So David sent messengers to console him concerning his father. And David's servants came to the land of the Ammonites to Hanun to console him.<sup>3</sup>But the princes of the Ammonites said to Hanun, "Do you think, because David has sent comforters to you, that he is honoring your father? Have not his servants come to you to search and to overthrow and to spy out the land?"<sup>4</sup>So Hanun took David's servants and shaved them and cut off their garments in the middle, at their hips, and sent them away;<sup>5</sup>and they departed. When David was told concerning the men, he sent messengers to meet them, for the men were greatly ashamed. And the king said, "Remain at Jericho until your beards have grown and then return."<sup>6</sup>When the Ammonites saw that they had become a stench to David, Hanun and the Ammonites sent 1,000 talents of silver to hire chariots and horsemen from Mesopotamia, from Aram-maacah, and from Zobah.<sup>7</sup>They hired 32,000 chariots and the king of Maacah with his army, who came and encamped before Medeba. And the Ammonites were mustered from their cities and came to battle.<sup>8</sup>When David heard of it, he sent Joab and all the army of the mighty men.<sup>9</sup>And the Ammonites came out and drew up in battle array at the entrance of the city, and the kings who had come were by themselves in the open country.<sup>10</sup>When Joab saw that the battle was set against him both in front and in the rear, he chose some of the best men of Israel and arrayed them against the Syrians.<sup>11</sup>The rest of his men he put in the charge of Abishai his brother, and they were arrayed against the Ammonites.<sup>12</sup>And he said, "If the Syrians are too strong for me, then you shall help me, but if the Ammonites are too strong for you, then I will help you.<sup>13</sup>Be strong, and let us use our strength for our people and for the cities of our God, and may the LORD do what seems good to him."<sup>14</sup>So Joab and the people who were with him drew near before the Syrians for battle, and they fled before him.<sup>15</sup>And when the Ammonites saw that the Syrians fled, they likewise fled before Abishai, Joab's brother, and entered the city. Then Joab came to Jerusalem.<sup>16</sup>But when the Syrians saw that they had been defeated by Israel, they sent messengers and brought out the Syrians who were beyond the Euphrates, with Shophach the commander of the army of Hadadezer at their head.<sup>17</sup>And when it was told to David, he gathered all Israel together and crossed the Jordan and came to them and drew up his forces against them. And when David set the battle in array against the Syrians, they fought with him.<sup>18</sup>And the Syrians fled before Israel, and David killed of the Syrians the men of 7,000 chariots and 40,000 foot soldiers, and put to death also Shophach the commander of their army.<sup>19</sup>And when the servants of Hadadezer saw that they had been defeated by Israel, they made peace with David and became subject to him. So the Syrians were not willing to save the Ammonites anymore.
19.overview:
David sends condolences to Hanun of Ammon because Hanun's father had been good to him (vv. 1-2). Hanun's counsellors persuade him the envoys are spies, and he has them shaved and stripped to the waist and sent home; David meets them on the road and settles them at Jericho until their beards grow (vv. 3-5). Ammon then hires four Syrian armies (vv. 6-7). Joab, caught between two forces, splits his army with Abishai and charges them to be strong and leave the outcome to God (vv. 8-13); both enemy lines break (vv. 14-15). Syria escalates with troops from beyond the Euphrates, David crosses the Jordan himself, and the coalition is destroyed and sues for peace (vv. 16-19).

Nothing in the chapter was necessary. A kindness was offered and a council of advisers could not believe it was meant.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — A Kindness Repaid with an Outrage
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Nahash of Ammon dies and David sends condolences, for his father dealt kindly with me (vv. 1-2). Hanun's advisers tell him the comforters are spies (v. 3), so he has them shaved and their robes cut off at the hips and sends them home (v. 4). David hears, sends messengers to meet them on the road, and says: Remain at Jericho until your beards have grown and then return (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: David is repaying a kindness he received when he was nobody, from a pagan king, years before. The word for it is the covenant word — the same steadfast love the psalm at the ark said endures forever. Having been dealt with that way, he deals that way.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 5 is the measure of the man. He does not summon the humiliated men to court and he does not tell them their shame is unimportant. He intercepts them before the city, gives them somewhere to stay, and lets them take as long as it takes.

verseByVerse.quote: Now after this Nahash the king of the Ammonites died, and his son reigned in his place. And David said, "I will deal kindly with Hanun the son of Nahash, for his father dealt kindly with me." So David sent messengers to console him concerning his father. And David's servants came to the land of the Ammonites to Hanun to console him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nahash king of the Ammonites is not a stranger to this story. He is the man who besieged Jabesh-gilead a lifetime ago and offered the town surrender terms of one gouged-out right eye per man, as a disgrace on all Israel. Saul's first act as king was to cut him to pieces for it.

Which is very likely why he was good to David. Saul spent seven years hunting a fugitive, and the Ammonite king across the river had a use for anyone Saul wanted dead. The Chronicler does not say what the kindness was — food, shelter, safe passage, a place his family could sit out a war.

What he does record is that David remembered it. I will deal kindly with Hanun the son of Nahash, for his father dealt kindly with me. Years have passed, Nahash is dead, the debt is unenforceable and the creditor is in his grave, and the king of Israel sends an embassy across the Jordan to sit with a bereaved son.

The word for dealing kindly is the covenant word — the steadfast love the choir at the ark had just sung endures forever. David uses it of a pagan king's favour to an outlaw, and then does the same back. That is the ordinary logic of a man who has understood what he has received: he had been treated better than he deserved, so he goes looking for someone to treat better than they deserve.

verseByVerse.quote: But the princes of the Ammonites said to Hanun, "Do you think, because David has sent comforters to you, that he is honoring your father? Have not his servants come to you to search and to overthrow and to spy out the land?" So Hanun took David's servants and shaved them and cut off their garments in the middle, at their hips, and sent them away; and they departed. When David was told concerning the men, he sent messengers to meet them, for the men were greatly ashamed. And the king said, "Remain at Jericho until your beards have grown and then return."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The advisers get to Hanun first. Do you think, because David has sent comforters to you, that he is honoring your father? Have not his servants come to you to search and to overthrow and to spy out the land?

It is plausible. David has been swallowing kingdoms for a decade; Moab pays him tribute and Edom has garrisons in it. A hard-headed man in an Ammonite council chamber has every reason to wonder what a delegation of Israelites is really doing measuring the approaches to his capital.

But look at what the suspicion does. It takes the one thing in the world that cannot be faked without cost — a group of men sent to sit with a young king whose father has just died — and reads it as reconnaissance. Cynicism is cheap and it is almost never embarrassed, because it explains everything and can be checked by nothing. Once Hanun accepted it, kindness itself became evidence against David.

Then the outrage. So Hanun took David's servants and shaved them and cut off their garments in the middle, at their hips, and sent them away.

Both halves are calculated. A beard was a man's standing in that world, and shaving one off by force was a punishment for criminals. Cutting the robes at the hip left them exposed from the waist down. Men who had gone on an errand of sympathy were pushed back onto the road to walk sixty miles home, hairless and half-naked, past every village on the way.

And now the verse most readers skim. When David was told concerning the men, he sent messengers to meet them, for the men were greatly ashamed. And the king said, Remain at Jericho until your beards have grown and then return.

He does not summon them to the palace to be thanked in public. He sends riders down the road to catch them before they reach the city, so that they never have to be seen. He gives them a town to stay in, at his expense. And he sets no date. Until your beards have grown — which is months, and which is however long it takes.

The king took their humiliation seriously. He did not tell them it was only hair, or that the honour of the mission covered it, or that a soldier should be above such things. He assumed that what had been done to them would take time to get over, and arranged the time. Men who have been shamed are usually told to be reasonable about it by people who were not there.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Realising what they have done, the Ammonites spend a thousand talents of silver hiring chariots from three Syrian states (vv. 6-7). Joab arrives to find the Ammonites drawn up at the city gate and the hired kings behind him in the open country — the battle was set against him both in front and in the rear (vv. 8-10). He splits the army, takes the Syrians himself and gives the Ammonites to Abishai, with each brother pledged to reinforce the other (vv. 10-12). Then his charge: Be strong ... and may the LORD do what seems good to him (v. 13). The Syrians break, the Ammonites break behind them, and Joab goes home (vv. 14-15).
verseByVerse.theology: Joab's sentence holds both halves without strain. Use your strength, for your people and for the cities of our God; and the LORD will do what seems good to him. Neither clause is an excuse for dropping the other, and the man who said it was surrounded at the time.
verseByVerse.examples: He made a plan for being beaten. If the Syrians are too strong for me, you come; if the Ammonites are too strong for you, I will come. Two commanders agreed in advance what would happen if either of them started to lose.

verseByVerse.quote: When the Ammonites saw that they had become a stench to David, Hanun and the Ammonites sent 1,000 talents of silver to hire chariots and horsemen from Mesopotamia, from Aram-maacah, and from Zobah. They hired 32,000 chariots and the king of Maacah with his army, who came and encamped before Medeba. And the Ammonites were mustered from their cities and came to battle. When David heard of it, he sent Joab and all the army of the mighty men. And the Ammonites came out and drew up in battle array at the entrance of the city, and the kings who had come were by themselves in the open country.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Ammonites now understand what they have done. When the Ammonites saw that they had become a stench to David — the word is the one used of something rotting — they start buying an army.

A thousand talents of silver. Chariots and horsemen from Mesopotamia, from Aram-maacah and from Zobah; thirty-two thousand chariots and the king of Maacah with his whole force, camped at Medeba. It is one of the largest mobilisations in the Old Testament, and it is the direct result of a young man being unable to say that he had made a mistake.

Consider what an apology would have cost. A message across the river: my counsellors misjudged you and I acted on it; the men will be compensated. It might have been humiliating. Instead Hanun spent his treasury, hired four foreign armies, and put his capital under siege for two campaigning seasons.

Joab arrives with the mighty men and finds the trap already set: Ammonites drawn up at the city gate in front of him, and the hired kings out in the open country behind.

verseByVerse.quote: When Joab saw that the battle was set against him both in front and in the rear, he chose some of the best men of Israel and arrayed them against the Syrians. The rest of his men he put in the charge of Abishai his brother, and they were arrayed against the Ammonites. And he said, "If the Syrians are too strong for me, then you shall help me, but if the Ammonites are too strong for you, then I will help you. Be strong, and let us use our strength for our people and for the cities of our God, and may the LORD do what seems good to him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Surrounded, Joab does two things, and they are the two things that have to be done in that order.

First he makes a plan. He picks the best troops in Israel and turns them to face the Syrians, who are the professionals; he gives the rest to his brother Abishai to hold the Ammonites at the gate. Then he arranges what happens if it goes wrong: If the Syrians are too strong for me, then you shall help me, but if the Ammonites are too strong for you, then I will help you.

Two commanders, back to back, each promising to break off his own battle to save the other. Neither of them pretends the plan will certainly work. They have agreed in advance what to do when one of them starts losing, which is a kind of foresight that only comes from men who have lost before.

Then he speaks to the army. Be strong, and let us use our strength for our people and for the cities of our God, and may the LORD do what seems good to him.

Every clause carries weight. Be strong, and use the strength — no passivity, no waiting for a sign, no suggestion that trusting God means doing less. For our people and for the cities of our God — he tells them what they are fighting for, and he calls Israel's towns God's own property. And then the last clause hands the result away entirely: may the LORD do what seems good to him.

Not may the LORD give us victory. Joab does not tell his men that God is obliged to win this, and he does not tell them the outcome does not matter. He tells them to fight with everything they have for a cause that belongs to God, and to leave the verdict with the one whose cause it is.

And it comes from Joab. The man who knifed Abner in a gateway, and Amasa on a road, and put three spears through Absalom against a direct order from the king. He bought his command by going up a water shaft first and David never dared remove him. That man says the truest sentence about courage and providence in the whole book, and Scripture records it under his name without a word of comment.

verseByVerse.quote: So Joab and the people who were with him drew near before the Syrians for battle, and they fled before him. And when the Ammonites saw that the Syrians fled, they likewise fled before Abishai, Joab's brother, and entered the city. Then Joab came to Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Syrians break first. Professional troops, hired for silver, with no stake in the quarrel and no reason to die at Medeba for an Ammonite king's wounded pride — they take one charge from Israel's best and run.

And the Ammonites, watching their expensive allies disappear over the horizon, run too, back through the gate into the city they had come out of. Not one of them has been beaten in a fight. The whole line collapses because the men beside them left.

Then Joab came to Jerusalem. No siege, no sack, no pursuit. He has scattered the field army and he goes home, and the Chronicler offers no explanation. Rabbah is still standing, and it will take another spring and another campaign to bring it down — which is where the next chapter opens, and what David was doing while it happened.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–19 — The Syrians Sue for Peace
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Syrians will not leave it there. They send for troops beyond the Euphrates under Shophach, Hadadezer's commander (v. 16). This time David comes out himself, crosses the Jordan and meets them (v. 17). Seven thousand chariot crews and forty thousand foot soldiers fall, Shophach among them (v. 18), and Hadadezer's vassals make peace: So the Syrians were not willing to save the Ammonites anymore (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: The chapter began with one young king taking bad advice about an embassy of sympathy. It ends with a coalition broken, a commander dead, and a whole region changing sides. Nothing in between was necessary.
verseByVerse.examples: Hanun's allies were bought with silver, and the last verse records what bought loyalty is worth: they were not willing to come again. He still had the Ammonite army and no friends left in the world.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the Syrians saw that they had been defeated by Israel, they sent messengers and brought out the Syrians who were beyond the Euphrates, with Shophach the commander of the army of Hadadezer at their head. And when it was told to David, he gathered all Israel together and crossed the Jordan and came to them and drew up his forces against them. And when David set the battle in array against the Syrians, they fought with him. And the Syrians fled before Israel, and David killed of the Syrians the men of 7,000 chariots and 40,000 foot soldiers, and put to death also Shophach the commander of their army. And when the servants of Hadadezer saw that they had been defeated by Israel, they made peace with David and became subject to him. So the Syrians were not willing to save the Ammonites anymore.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Syrians will not accept it. They send beyond the Euphrates for reinforcements and put Shophach, Hadadezer's own commander, at the head of them. This is no longer about Ammon; it is Aram deciding whether it can live with an Israelite kingdom on its southern border.

And this time David comes out himself. He gathered all Israel together and crossed the Jordan and came to them. He had sent Joab to the first battle and stayed home; for the second he calls up the nation and goes over the river in person, because the scale has changed.

The result is stated in figures. Seven thousand chariot crews. Forty thousand foot soldiers. Shophach dead on the field. And then the sentence that ends the war: And when the servants of Hadadezer saw that they had been defeated by Israel, they made peace with David and became subject to him.

The last line is the epitaph on Hanun's decision. So the Syrians were not willing to save the Ammonites anymore. He had bought an alliance with a thousand talents of silver, and when the silver was spent the allies discovered they had other commitments. Loyalty that was purchased behaves exactly like a purchase.

All of it began with a delegation sent to sit with a grieving young man, and a room full of clever advisers who could not believe that anybody meant it.

19.theology:
Verse 13 is the chapter's centre and it holds two things most people hold one at a time. Be strong, and let us use our strength for our people and for the cities of our God, and may the LORD do what seems good to him. Fight with everything you have; the verdict is not yours. Joab does not promise his men victory and does not excuse them from the battle.

And it is Joab who says it — a man who murdered two commanders and disobeyed his king over Absalom. The Chronicler prints his words as they stand. God's truth is not confined to the mouths of people whose lives commend it, and a sentence is not less true for the man who happens to be saying it.
19.examples:
David remembered a favour done to him years earlier by a foreign king who was now dead, and went out of his way to repay it to a son who owed him nothing. The debt was unenforceable. He paid it because of the kind of man being kindly treated had made him.

He met his humiliated envoys on the road so they need not be seen, gave them a town to stay in, and set no date for their return. He did not minimise what had been done to them or hurry them through it. Shame takes as long as it takes, and the king budgeted for it.

Hanun could have sent one message admitting he had listened to bad advice. Instead he spent a thousand talents of silver, lost two armies and a commander, and ended with no allies willing to come back. The cost of an apology is always quoted before it is paid, and never afterwards.

20.title: The Siege of Rabbah and the Giants: Completing the Conquest
20.text: <sup>1</sup>In the spring of the year, the time when kings go out to battle, Joab led out the army and ravaged the country of the Ammonites and came and besieged Rabbah. But David remained at Jerusalem. And Joab struck down Rabbah and overthrew it.<sup>2</sup>And David took the crown of their king from his head. He found that it weighed a talent of gold, and in it was a precious stone. And it was placed on David's head. And he brought out the spoil of the city, a very great amount.<sup>3</sup>And he brought out the people who were in it and set them to labor with saws and iron picks and axes. And thus David did to all the cities of the Ammonites. Then David and all the people returned to Jerusalem.<sup>4</sup>And after this there arose war with the Philistines at Gezer. Then Sibbecai the Hushathite struck down Sippai, who was one of the descendants of the giants, and the Philistines were subdued.<sup>5</sup>And there was again war with the Philistines, and Elhanan the son of Jair struck down Lahmi the brother of Goliath the Gittite, the shaft of whose spear was like a weaver's beam.<sup>6</sup>And there was again war at Gath, where there was a man of great stature, who had six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot, twenty-four in number, and he also was descended from the giants.<sup>7</sup>And when he taunted Israel, Jonathan the son of Shimea, David's brother, struck him down.<sup>8</sup>These were descended from the giants in Gath, and they fell by the hand of David and by the hand of his servants.
20.overview:
Joab takes the army back in the spring, ravages Ammon and destroys Rabbah while David stays in Jerusalem; the enemy king's crown is lifted onto David's head and the population is put to forced labour (vv. 1-3). Then three notices of Philistine war, each ending with a dead giant: Sippai at Gezer, Lahmi the brother of Goliath, and a six-fingered taunter at Gath — and all of them fell by the hand of David and by the hand of his servants (vv. 4-8).

Verse 1 is the setting of 2 Samuel 11, word for word, and this book does not tell what happened next. Bathsheba, Uriah, Nathan, Absalom — none of it is here. The Chronicler is writing the story of the throne rather than the story of the man, and he leaves the door open and walks past it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — Rabbah, and What Is Not Here
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the spring of the year, the time when kings go out to battle, Joab takes the army back across the Jordan, ravages Ammon and besieges Rabbah — but David remained at Jerusalem (v. 1). The city falls, and its king's crown, a talent of gold with a jewel in it, is lifted onto David's head; the spoil is enormous (v. 2). The population is put to forced labour with saws and picks and axes, and the same is done to every Ammonite town before the army goes home (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: The opening sentence is, word for word, the setting of the worst episode in David's life, and this book does not tell it. What it does is keep the sentence. The reader who knows 2 Samuel finds the scene set, the king at home, the army away — and then the fall of a city, with the whole spring in between left blank.
verseByVerse.examples: The crown weighed about seventy-five pounds. Nobody wore it; it was lifted onto David's head and taken off again. In the other account this moment comes after a prophet has told the king a story about a lamb. Here it comes after nothing at all.

verseByVerse.quote: In the spring of the year, the time when kings go out to battle, Joab led out the army and ravaged the country of the Ammonites and came and besieged Rabbah. But David remained at Jerusalem. And Joab struck down Rabbah and overthrew it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the spring of the year, the time when kings go out to battle, Joab led out the army and ravaged the country of the Ammonites and came and besieged Rabbah. But David remained at Jerusalem.

Anyone who has read the book of Samuel will stop at the last five words, because that is where the other account stops too. The same season, the same siege, the same general, the same clause about the king staying home — and then, there, a sentence about a man who could not sleep, who got up from his couch and walked on his roof in the evening and saw something.

The Chronicler writes the setting and does not write the scene. He moves in the same verse from David at home in the spring to Joab knocking Rabbah down, and everything that happened in Jerusalem while the army was away is simply not there. Bathsheba is not in this book. Neither is Uriah's death, nor the letter he carried, nor Nathan and the lamb, nor the child who died, nor Amnon, nor Absalom in the oak.

It is the largest deliberate omission in Chronicles and readers have argued about it for a very long time. Some have called it whitewash. It cannot be, and the reason is nine chapters back: in the roll of David's mighty men this same writer prints the name Uriah the Hittite and passes on without a word. A man concealing what David did to Uriah does not put Uriah in the honour roll.

What he is doing is something else. He is writing for people who have no king, no army and no independence, and who need to know what God promised to David's house and what that house was for. So he tells the story of the throne rather than the story of the man: how Israel got a king, a city, an ark, a covenant, a site and a temple. The private ruin of David is not his subject, and he assumes his readers know it, because he leaves the door of verse 1 standing open and walks past it.

The effect on a reader who knows both books is stronger than telling it would have been. The sentence sits there — the kings went out, and David stayed — and the silence after it is the loudest thing in the chapter.

verseByVerse.quote: And David took the crown of their king from his head. He found that it weighed a talent of gold, and in it was a precious stone. And it was placed on David's head. And he brought out the spoil of the city, a very great amount. And he brought out the people who were in it and set them to labor with saws and iron picks and axes. And thus David did to all the cities of the Ammonites. Then David and all the people returned to Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rabbah falls, and David comes for the crown.

He found that it weighed a talent of gold, and in it was a precious stone. And it was placed on David's head. A talent is about seventy-five pounds. No neck could carry that for more than a moment, which is why the verse says it was placed on his head rather than that he wore it. It was the crown of a god or of a statue, brought out and held over the king of Israel for as long as the ceremony took.

Then the spoil, a very great amount, and the population set to work with saws and iron picks and axes, and the same treatment given to every town in Ammon. It is the harsh end of an ancient war and the Chronicler reports it without softening and without relish. A nation that hired four armies rather than admit a mistake has been broken, and its people are quarrying stone.

Set the two verses side by side and the shape of the chapter appears. A king who stayed at home has a foreign crown lifted onto his head and carts of gold brought to his capital, and the men who took the city are still standing in the breach. In the other account this is the moment David has just come through the worst year of his life. Here it is a coronation with a hole in the middle of it, and the writer trusts his reader to feel the draught.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–8 — The Sons of the Giants
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Three short notices of war with the Philistines, and each one ends with a giant dead. Sibbecai the Hushathite kills Sippai at Gezer (v. 4). Elhanan kills Lahmi the brother of Goliath, the shaft of whose spear was like a weaver's beam (v. 5). At Gath a man of great stature with six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot taunts Israel and is struck down by Jonathan, David's nephew (vv. 6-7). And the summary: These were descended from the giants in Gath, and they fell by the hand of David and by the hand of his servants (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 8 credits David with four killings he did not carry out. The champion in the valley was his; the champion's family were finished off over years by other men, in his name and in his manner, and the record puts it all down to the king.
verseByVerse.examples: Every one of these men had a name and a home town — Sibbecai of Hushah, Elhanan son of Jair, Jonathan son of Shimea. Nobody remembers them. They spent their lives killing the relatives of a giant somebody else had already beaten.

verseByVerse.quote: And after this there arose war with the Philistines at Gezer. Then Sibbecai the Hushathite struck down Sippai, who was one of the descendants of the giants, and the Philistines were subdued. And there was again war with the Philistines, and Elhanan the son of Jair struck down Lahmi the brother of Goliath the Gittite, the shaft of whose spear was like a weaver's beam.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three brief notices follow, and they are all the same shape: there was war, and a giant died.

The first is at Gezer, where Sibbecai the Hushathite strikes down Sippai, one of the descendants of the giants. Sibbecai was in the roll of the mighty men in chapter 11, one line among thirty. Here he kills a giant, in one sentence, and disappears.

The second verse raises a real difficulty and it should be stated plainly. This text says that Elhanan the son of Jair struck down Lahmi the brother of Goliath the Gittite. The corresponding verse in 2 Samuel says that Elhanan struck down Goliath the Gittite himself — which would put the death of Goliath in someone else's hands.

Nobody can settle it from here. The oldest explanation, and still the most likely, is that a copyist's eye slipped somewhere in the Samuel verse, whose Hebrew has a recognised awkwardness at exactly that point, and that Chronicles preserves what was originally written. Others have supposed two men or two names. What is not honest is to pretend the question does not exist, and what is not necessary is to be troubled by it: the killing of Goliath is told at length in 1 Samuel 17 and referred back to all through Scripture, and one damaged line in a list of Philistine wars does not touch it.

And notice the phrase attached to Lahmi: the shaft of whose spear was like a weaver's beam. That is the description of Goliath's spear in the valley of Elah, and it is the description of the Egyptian that Benaiah went down to with a staff in his hand. It runs in the family, and so does what happens to them.

verseByVerse.quote: And there was again war at Gath, where there was a man of great stature, who had six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot, twenty-four in number, and he also was descended from the giants. And when he taunted Israel, Jonathan the son of Shimea, David's brother, struck him down. These were descended from the giants in Gath, and they fell by the hand of David and by the hand of his servants.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The third notice is at Gath, and the Chronicler counts. A man of great stature, who had six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot, twenty-four in number. He totals them up, as though he wants the reader to have the figure and not just the impression.

And when he taunted Israel, Jonathan the son of Shimea, David's brother, struck him down.

Taunted. It is the same posture as the first giant: a man of enormous size standing in front of the army of the living God and jeering, waiting for somebody to come out. And somebody does — David's nephew, the son of one of the older brothers who had been standing in that valley years before, doing nothing.

Then the last verse, and it is the one to carry away. These were descended from the giants in Gath, and they fell by the hand of David and by the hand of his servants.

David did not kill any of these four. He was in Jerusalem, and by now too old to be let near a battlefield at all. The text credits him with the deaths anyway, because they were won in his name, by his men, in the manner he had taught them, against the family of the champion he had already beaten.

That is the shape of the whole thing. One decisive fight in a valley, settled by one man with a sling while everyone else watched; and then a long, unglamorous mopping-up carried out over years by men whose names nobody remembers, against opponents who were already beaten in principle and still had to be faced one at a time. The victory was the king's. The clearing of the field was given to his servants to do, and it went down on his record. There is a giant somewhere still taunting, and the church is at Gath and at Gezer with a sword in its hand, and every one of them falls by the hand of David.

20.theology:
Chronicles omits David's great sin and does not conceal it. The same writer put Uriah the Hittite in the roll of the mighty men at 11:41 with no comment attached, which is not what a man covering his tracks would do. He is answering a different question from the one Samuel answers — not what was David like, but what did God promise to this house and what was it for — and his readers, who had no king at all, needed the second.

Verse 8 states the principle the honour roll has been working towards since chapter 11. Four giants fall, and not one of them by David's hand, and the record says they fell by his hand and by his servants'. A victory won in the king's name, in the king's manner, by men the king trained, is counted as the king's.
20.examples:
Sibbecai, Elhanan and Jonathan each get one sentence and one giant. None of them fought the famous one; they fought his relatives, at Gezer and Gath, years after the story everyone tells was over. Most faithful work is the clearing up after somebody else's decisive victory, and it still has to be done a giant at a time.

Rabbah fell in the spring the king stayed home. The chapter records the crown coming to him anyway. Success arriving on schedule is no evidence at all about how a man has spent the season.

21.title: The Census, the Plague, and the Altar: Where the Temple Will Stand
21.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Satan stood against Israel and incited David to number Israel.<sup>2</sup>So David said to Joab and the commanders of the army, "Go, number Israel, from Beersheba to Dan, and bring me a report, that I may know their number."<sup>3</sup>But Joab said, "May the LORD add to his people a hundred times as many as they are! Are they not, my lord the king, all of them my lord's servants? Why then should my lord require this? Why should it be a cause of guilt for Israel?"<sup>4</sup>But the king's word prevailed against Joab. So Joab departed and went throughout all Israel and came back to Jerusalem.<sup>5</sup>And Joab gave the sum of the numbering of the people to David. In all Israel there were 1,100,000 men who drew the sword, and in Judah 470,000 who drew the sword.<sup>6</sup>But he did not include Levi and Benjamin in the numbering, for the king's command was abhorrent to Joab.<sup>7</sup>But God was displeased with this thing, and he struck Israel.<sup>8</sup>And David said to God, "I have sinned greatly in that I have done this thing. But now, please take away the iniquity of your servant, for I have acted very foolishly."<sup>9</sup>And the LORD spoke to Gad, David's seer, saying,<sup>10</sup>"Go and say to David, 'Thus says the LORD, Three things I offer you; choose one of them, that I may do it to you.'"<sup>11</sup>So Gad came to David and said to him, "Thus says the LORD, 'Choose what you will:<sup>12</sup>either three years of famine, or three months of devastation by your foes while the sword of your enemies overtakes you, or else three days of the sword of the LORD, pestilence on the land, with the angel of the LORD destroying throughout all the territory of Israel.' Now decide what answer I shall return to him who sent me."<sup>13</sup>Then David said to Gad, "I am in great distress. Let me fall into the hand of the LORD, for his mercy is very great, but do not let me fall into the hand of man."<sup>14</sup>So the LORD sent a pestilence on Israel, and 70,000 men of Israel fell.<sup>15</sup>And God sent the angel to Jerusalem to destroy it, but as he was about to destroy it, the LORD saw, and he relented from the calamity. And he said to the angel who was working destruction, "It is enough; now stay your hand." And the angel of the LORD was standing by the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite.<sup>16</sup>And David lifted his eyes and saw the angel of the LORD standing between earth and heaven, and in his hand a drawn sword stretched out over Jerusalem. Then David and the elders, clothed in sackcloth, fell upon their faces.<sup>17</sup>And David said to God, "Was it not I who gave command to number the people? It is I who have sinned and done great evil. But these sheep, what have they done? Please let your hand, O LORD my God, be against me and against my father's house. But do not let the plague be on your people."<sup>18</sup>Now the angel of the LORD had commanded Gad to say to David that David should go up and raise an altar to the LORD on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite.<sup>19</sup>So David went up at Gad's word, which he had spoken in the name of the LORD.<sup>20</sup>Now Ornan was threshing wheat. He turned and saw the angel, and his four sons who were with him hid themselves.<sup>21</sup>As David came to Ornan, Ornan looked and saw David and went out from the threshing floor and paid homage to David with his face to the ground.<sup>22</sup>And David said to Ornan, "Give me the site of the threshing floor that I may build on it an altar to the LORD—give it to me at its full price—that the plague may be averted from the people."<sup>23</sup>Then Ornan said to David, "Take it, and let my lord the king do what seems good to him. See, I give the oxen for burnt offerings and the threshing sledges for the wood and the wheat for a grain offering; I give it all."<sup>24</sup>But King David said to Ornan, "No, but I will buy them for the full price. I will not take for the LORD what is yours, nor offer burnt offerings that cost me nothing."<sup>25</sup>So David paid Ornan 600 shekels of gold by weight for the site.<sup>26</sup>And David built there an altar to the LORD and presented burnt offerings and peace offerings and called on the LORD, and the LORD answered him with fire from heaven upon the altar of burnt offering.<sup>27</sup>Then the LORD commanded the angel, and he put his sword back into its sheath.<sup>28</sup>At that time, when David saw that the LORD had answered him at the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite, he sacrificed there.<sup>29</sup>For the tabernacle of the LORD, which Moses had made in the wilderness, and the altar of burnt offering were at that time in the high place at Gibeon,<sup>30</sup>but David could not go before it to inquire of God, for he was afraid of the sword of the angel of the LORD.
21.overview:
David orders a census of the fighting men against Joab's protest (vv. 1-6). God is displeased and strikes Israel; David confesses immediately, and Gad the seer brings three punishments to choose from (vv. 7-12). David chooses to fall into God's hand rather than man's, and seventy thousand die before the LORD stops the angel at the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite (vv. 13-15). Seeing the drawn sword, David asks to be struck instead of the people (vv. 16-17). Told to build an altar there, he refuses Ornan's offer of the site for nothing, pays the full price, and God answers with fire from heaven; the angel sheathes his sword (vv. 18-27). The chapter ends by explaining why the sacrifice was not made at Gibeon (vv. 28-30).

This is the hinge of the book. The temple site is located here, at the place where a plague stopped, on ground bought at full price out of the worst thing David ever did.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — A King Who Wanted a Number
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Then Satan stood against Israel and incited David to number Israel (v. 1), and David orders a count of every man who draws a sword, that I may know their number (v. 2). Joab objects on the spot — may the LORD multiply his people a hundredfold; they are all my lord's servants already; why should it be a cause of guilt for Israel? (v. 3). The king overrules him (v. 4). The total comes back at 1,100,000 in Israel and 470,000 in Judah (v. 5), with two tribes quietly missing, for the king's command was abhorrent to Joab (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: The account in 2 Samuel says the LORD incited David; this one says Satan did. Scripture holds both causes elsewhere without embarrassment, and neither version reduces the man's guilt by a syllable — David will say twice, in his own words, that the sin was his.
verseByVerse.examples: Joab told the king he was wrong, was overruled, obeyed, and then left two tribes out of the return. It is not a clean act. He is on record twice in two chapters saying the right thing, and once again unable to stop what he could see coming.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Satan stood against Israel and incited David to number Israel. So David said to Joab and the commanders of the army, "Go, number Israel, from Beersheba to Dan, and bring me a report, that I may know their number."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Satan stood against Israel and incited David to number Israel.

The same episode is told in 2 Samuel 24, and it opens: the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and he incited David against them. One book names God as the mover; this one names Satan. It is the plainest example in Scripture of two writers assigning the same action to different agents, and it should not be smoothed over.

Two things need saying, and neither of them is a trick. The first is a matter of language. The Hebrew word here has no article on it, and elsewhere the same word plainly means an adversary — the LORD raised up an adversary against Solomon, and the adversary was a man called Hadad. Some readers therefore take this verse to mean that a hostile power, or a human enemy, stood against Israel. Most English versions read it as the accuser of Job and the tempter of the Gospels, and that may well be right. The verse alone will not settle it.

The second thing is larger and does not depend on the first. Scripture repeatedly puts two causes behind one event and refuses to choose. Satan strips Job of everything, and Job says the LORD gave and the LORD has taken away, and the book says he did not sin in saying it. A lying spirit volunteers to deceive Ahab's prophets, and it is God who sends him. Men with lawless hands crucify Jesus, and Peter says they did it by the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, and then charges them with murder in the same sentence.

So the older account looks at the census from above and says God was behind it; this one looks from below and names the adversary who pushed. Neither writer thought he was correcting the other, and the Chronicler had 2 Samuel in front of him.

What neither of them does is excuse David. That is the point to hold onto, because it is where this kind of question usually goes wrong. Twice in this chapter the king says the sin was his — I have sinned greatly, and later it is I who have sinned and done great evil — and nobody in the story so much as mentions the tempter again. A man who has been incited is not a man who has been excused.

And the order he gives is revealing in itself. Go, number Israel, from Beersheba to Dan, and bring me a report, that I may know their number. Not so that I may raise a levy, or plan a campaign, or share out the land. So that I may know. He wants the figure for its own sake, and this is the king who has been told twice in three chapters that the LORD saved him wherever he went.

verseByVerse.quote: But Joab said, "May the LORD add to his people a hundred times as many as they are! Are they not, my lord the king, all of them my lord's servants? Why then should my lord require this? Why should it be a cause of guilt for Israel?" But the king's word prevailed against Joab. So Joab departed and went throughout all Israel and came back to Jerusalem. And Joab gave the sum of the numbering of the people to David. In all Israel there were 1,100,000 men who drew the sword, and in Judah 470,000 who drew the sword. But he did not include Levi and Benjamin in the numbering, for the king's command was abhorrent to Joab.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joab objects, and the objection is better than anything the king says in this chapter.

May the LORD add to his people a hundred times as many as they are! Are they not, my lord the king, all of them my lord's servants? Why then should my lord require this? Why should it be a cause of guilt for Israel?

Three arguments in four lines. The first is that numbers are God's business to give, not the king's to audit. The second is that they already belong to him, so the count adds nothing. And the third is the one Joab alone seems to see: this will not stop with David. It will be a cause of guilt for Israel, and seventy thousand men are going to find out how right he was.

The law had already said why. When a census was taken in Israel, every man counted had to pay a ransom for his life, and the reason given was that there be no plague among them when they are numbered. A head that is counted is a life that must be redeemed. Nothing in this chapter mentions the ransom money, and the plague comes exactly as promised, which is as close to an explanation as the text offers.

But the king's word prevailed against Joab. He was told he was wrong by the most experienced man in his kingdom, and he used his authority to end the conversation. It is the one power a king has that no adviser can answer.

The figures come back: 1,100,000 men in Israel who drew the sword, 470,000 in Judah. They do not match the totals in the parallel account, and no one has reconciled the two with certainty. What this book adds is the footnote: he did not include Levi and Benjamin in the numbering, for the king's command was abhorrent to Joab. Levi was exempt from any military census by law. Benjamin was not, and Joab simply left it out.

It is not obedience and it is not refusal. He carried out an order he believed was a sin, under protest, and then quietly falsified the return. Men who cannot stop a thing very often do something like this, and Scripture reports it without telling us what to make of it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–17 — Three Days, and a Drawn Sword
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God strikes Israel (v. 7) and David confesses at once (v. 8). Gad the seer brings three options — three years of famine, three months of defeat, or three days of pestilence (vv. 9-12) — and David chooses by agent rather than by length: Let me fall into the hand of the LORD, for his mercy is very great, but do not let me fall into the hand of man (v. 13). Seventy thousand die (v. 14). At Jerusalem the LORD stops it — It is enough; now stay your hand — and the angel halts at the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite (v. 15). David sees him standing between earth and heaven, and in his hand a drawn sword, and prays to be struck instead: these sheep, what have they done? (vv. 16-17).
verseByVerse.theology: He asked to be told how many men he had. The number he was finally given was seventy thousand fewer than the one Joab brought him, and the Chronicler sets the two figures in the same chapter without a word joining them.
verseByVerse.examples: David chose the option that put him directly in God's hand, and gave his reason: his mercy is very great. He would rather be struck by God than spared by men, which is a judgement about the character of God made at the worst moment of his life.

verseByVerse.quote: But God was displeased with this thing, and he struck Israel. And David said to God, "I have sinned greatly in that I have done this thing. But now, please take away the iniquity of your servant, for I have acted very foolishly."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But God was displeased with this thing, and he struck Israel.

Displeased is a mild word in English for what follows. The Hebrew says the thing was evil in God's eyes, and the response is immediate.

And so is David's. I have sinned greatly in that I have done this thing. But now, please take away the iniquity of your servant, for I have acted very foolishly.

No prophet has spoken yet. Gad does not appear until the next verse. Nobody has confronted him, nobody has told a story about a lamb, and the king is not defending himself, explaining the strategic value of accurate returns, or asking what exactly was wrong with it. He says he sinned greatly, asks for the guilt to be taken away, and calls himself a fool.

Three sentences, and every one of them concedes something. That capacity was in him from the beginning and it is the reason God calls this man a man after his own heart — not because he sinned less than Saul, but because when he was caught he did not manage the situation. Saul, confronted about the Amalekite cattle, explained that the people had kept the best animals to sacrifice.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Gad, David's seer, saying, "Go and say to David, 'Thus says the LORD, Three things I offer you; choose one of them, that I may do it to you.'"
