These also, the head of each father's house and his younger brother alike, cast lots, just as their brothers the sons of Aaron, in the presence of King David, Zadok, Ahimelech, and the heads of fathers' houses of the priests and of the Levites.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Merari's line is set out, and then verse 28 repeats something the last chapter already said. Of Mahli: Eleazar, who had no sons.

He is on the roll twice, with the same note both times. A man whose family stopped with him is written into the permanent record of the tribe of Levi in two consecutive chapters, and nothing else is said about him. The register keeps him anyway, twice over.

Then the last verse, and it is where the chapter has been going.

These also, the head of each father's house and his younger brother alike, cast lots, just as their brothers the sons of Aaron, in the presence of King David, Zadok, Ahimelech, and the heads of fathers' houses of the priests and of the Levites.

Two things are being said and both matter. The Levites drew on exactly the same terms as the priests — the man who would never touch the altar put his hand in the bag beside the man who would. And within each family, the head of the house and his younger brother drew alike, which means being the eldest bought nothing at all.

The work was divided and the standing was not. Every man in that court had a different job and precisely the same claim on it, which was none, because the assignments were coming from somewhere outside the room.

25.title: The Temple Musicians: Prophecy Through Song
25.text: <sup>1</sup>David and the chiefs of the service also set apart for the service the sons of Asaph, and of Heman, and of Jeduthun, who prophesied with lyres, with harps, and with cymbals. The list of those who did the work and of their duties was:<sup>2</sup>Of the sons of Asaph: Zaccur, Joseph, Nethaniah, and Asharelah, sons of Asaph, under the direction of Asaph, who prophesied under the direction of the king.<sup>3</sup>Of Jeduthun, the sons of Jeduthun: Gedaliah, Zeri, Jeshaiah, Shimei, Hashabiah, and Mattithiah, six, under the direction of their father Jeduthun, who prophesied with the lyre in thanksgiving and praise to the LORD.<sup>4</sup>Of Heman, the sons of Heman: Bukkiah, Mattaniah, Uzziel, Shebuel and Jerimoth, Hananiah, Hanani, Eliathah, Giddalti, and Romamti-ezer, Joshbekashah, Mallothi, Hothir, Mahazioth.<sup>5</sup>All these were the sons of Heman the king's seer, according to the promise of God to exalt him, for God had given Heman fourteen sons and three daughters.<sup>6</sup>They were all under the direction of their father in the music in the house of the LORD with cymbals, harps, and lyres for the service of the house of God. Asaph, Jeduthun, and Heman were under the order of the king.<sup>7</sup>The number of them along with their brothers, who were trained in singing to the LORD, all who were skillful, was 288.<sup>8</sup>And they cast lots for their duties, small and great, teacher and pupil alike.<sup>9</sup>The first lot fell for Asaph to Joseph; the second to Gedaliah, to him and his brothers and his sons, twelve;<sup>10</sup>the third to Zaccur, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>11</sup>the fourth to Izri, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>12</sup>the fifth to Nethaniah, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>13</sup>the sixth to Bukkiah, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>14</sup>the seventh to Jesharelah, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>15</sup>the eighth to Jeshaiah, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>16</sup>the ninth to Mattaniah, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>17</sup>the tenth to Shimei, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>18</sup>the eleventh to Azarel, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>19</sup>the twelfth to Hashabiah, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>20</sup>to the thirteenth, Shubael, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>21</sup>to the fourteenth, Mattithiah, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>22</sup>to the fifteenth, to Jeremoth, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>23</sup>to the sixteenth, to Hananiah, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>24</sup>to the seventeenth, to Joshbekashah, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>25</sup>to the eighteenth, to Hanani, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>26</sup>to the nineteenth, to Mallothi, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>27</sup>to the twentieth, to Eliathah, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>28</sup>to the twenty-first, to Hothir, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>29</sup>to the twenty-second, to Giddalti, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>30</sup>to the twenty-third, to Mahazioth, his sons and his brothers, twelve;<sup>31</sup>to the twenty-fourth, to Romamti-ezer, his sons and his brothers, twelve.
25.overview:
The temple musicians are set apart, and the word used of their work is prophesied — three times in three verses, of men with lyres and harps and cymbals in their hands (vv. 1-3). Heman the king's seer is given fourteen sons and three daughters as God's way of exalting him (vv. 4-6). Two hundred and eighty-eight trained and skilful singers are then divided into twenty-four courses of twelve by lot, small and great, teacher and pupil alike (vv. 7-8), and the draw is recorded in full (vv. 9-31).

Twenty-four courses of twelve is exactly the 288 of verse 7. The list balances, and it is written out at length rather than summarised, because the working document is part of what the Chronicler wants his readers to hold.
25.theology:
Singing is called prophecy, and the usage is not loose. A company of prophets comes down a hill in 1 Samuel with harp and tambourine and flute before them, and Elisha cannot get a word until somebody plays. The largest book in the Bible is a hymn book, and Israel learned most of what it knew about God by singing it. The men in this chapter took what God had said and set it where a nation could carry it.

And the same chapter insists the singers were trained and skillful (v. 7). Nothing here treats craft as a rival to inspiration. This is the book that gave Chenaniah the conductor's post because he understood music, and it hands the prophetic office to men who had been apprenticed and could play.
25.examples:
The lots were cast small and great, teacher and pupil alike. A master of thirty years could draw an empty week while the boy he had taught drew the feast. The system was built to make seniority irrelevant to the assignment, and both men had to live with the result.

God's promise to exalt Heman arrived as seventeen children. Not office or land or a mention in the royal annals — a full house, and nine of the twenty-four musical courses carrying his sons' names.

Twelve men, one week, then twelve more. Most of them are named once in Scripture and never again, and the singing went on in that house for four hundred years because a rota is duller and more durable than enthusiasm.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David and the officers set apart the sons of Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun for a service described in an unexpected word — they prophesied with lyres, with harps, and with cymbals (v. 1), and the verb comes twice more in the next two verses (vv. 2-3). Heman is called the king's seer, and God had given him fourteen sons and three daughters (vv. 4-5); the three families served under their own fathers and all of them under the king (v. 6). The trained and skilful singers numbered 288 (v. 7). And then the draw: they cast lots for their duties, small and great, teacher and pupil alike (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: Music is called prophecy here three times over. It is not a loose way of speaking: the same Scripture has a company of prophets coming down a hill with a harp and a lyre in front of them, and a prophet who cannot get a word until somebody plays.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 8 puts the teacher and his pupil in the same draw. A man who had spent thirty years learning his instrument could be handed a worse week than the boy he had taught it to, and the rota was made that way deliberately.

verseByVerse.quote: David and the chiefs of the service also set apart for the service the sons of Asaph, and of Heman, and of Jeduthun, who prophesied with lyres, with harps, and with cymbals. The list of those who did the work and of their duties was: Of the sons of Asaph: Zaccur, Joseph, Nethaniah, and Asharelah, sons of Asaph, under the direction of Asaph, who prophesied under the direction of the king. Of Jeduthun, the sons of Jeduthun: Gedaliah, Zeri, Jeshaiah, Shimei, Hashabiah, and Mattithiah, six, under the direction of their father Jeduthun, who prophesied with the lyre in thanksgiving and praise to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter opens by describing the temple musicians in a word nobody would predict. The sons of Asaph and Heman and Jeduthun are set apart for a service in which they prophesied with lyres, with harps, and with cymbals.

And the verb comes again in verse 2, of Asaph's sons, and again in verse 3, of Jeduthun, who prophesied with the lyre in thanksgiving and praise to the LORD. Three times in three verses, of men with instruments in their hands.

It is not a loose way of speaking. When Samuel sent Saul away he told him he would meet a company of prophets coming down from the high place with a harp, a tambourine, a flute and a lyre in front of them, prophesying. When two kings came to Elisha wanting a word from God, he told them to bring him a musician, and while the man played, the hand of the LORD came upon him. Music and the word of God have been standing next to each other in Israel from the beginning.

What the singers did was take what God had said and give it back to the people set to music, so that a truth could get into a nation's memory in a way a sermon cannot. The largest book in the Bible is a hymn book, and Israel learned most of its theology by singing it.

Verse 2 adds that Asaph prophesied under the direction of the king, which sounds alarming until you notice what it can and cannot mean. David set the rota, appointed the men and made the instruments. Nobody in this chapter is telling a prophet what God says.

verseByVerse.quote: Of Heman, the sons of Heman: Bukkiah, Mattaniah, Uzziel, Shebuel and Jerimoth, Hananiah, Hanani, Eliathah, Giddalti, and Romamti-ezer, Joshbekashah, Mallothi, Hothir, Mahazioth. All these were the sons of Heman the king's seer, according to the promise of God to exalt him, for God had given Heman fourteen sons and three daughters. They were all under the direction of their father in the music in the house of the LORD with cymbals, harps, and lyres for the service of the house of God. Asaph, Jeduthun, and Heman were under the order of the king.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Heman's household comes next, and it is a large one: fourteen sons, listed by name, and then a note about why. All these were the sons of Heman the king's seer, according to the promise of God to exalt him, for God had given Heman fourteen sons and three daughters.

The exalting God promised him arrived as children. Not office, not land, not a name in the chronicle of the kings — a full house, and a family so large that nine of its twenty-four musical courses were his own boys.

The three daughters are named in the same breath as God's gift. The text does not say what became of them, and verse 6's they were all under the direction of their father most naturally reaches back to the sons just listed. It should not be pressed further than it goes. What can be said plainly is that women did sing in Israel's worship: the lists of those who came back from Babylon count two hundred singers, men and women, and a psalm about a procession into the sanctuary puts the young women with tambourines in the middle of it.

One more thing about Heman's sons, and it is a curiosity worth knowing. The last nine names in verse 4 — Hananiah, Hanani, Eliathah, Giddalti, Romamti-ezer, Joshbekashah, Mallothi, Hothir, Mahazioth — are odd as names and ordinary as Hebrew words, and read in order they make a continuous petition: be gracious to me, LORD, be gracious to me; you are my God; I have magnified and exalted help; sitting in trouble, I said, give visions abundantly. Many readers have noticed it and it cannot be proved. If it is right, a prayer has been standing inside a staff list for three thousand years, and a father named his sons one line at a time.

verseByVerse.quote: The number of them along with their brothers, who were trained in singing to the LORD, all who were skillful, was 288. And they cast lots for their duties, small and great, teacher and pupil alike.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The number of them along with their brothers, who were trained in singing to the LORD, all who were skillful, was 288.

Two hundred and eighty-eight, which is twenty-four courses of twelve, and the figure balances against the list that follows. Two words in the verse do the work. They were trained — the word means taught, apprenticed, put through something — and they were skillful. Somebody spent years on these men, and at the end of it they were good.

Neither word is an accident in a book this concerned with doing things God's way. The same chapter that calls the singing prophecy insists that the singers were taught their trade, and there is no suggestion anywhere that the two are in tension. Chenaniah got the conductor's post because he understood music. These men got their places because they had been trained and could play.

And then verse 8, which is the sentence to carry out of the chapter. And they cast lots for their duties, small and great, teacher and pupil alike.

The master and the student put their hands in the same bag. A man who had given thirty years to his instrument might draw a bad week while the boy he taught last spring drew the Passover. Nothing in the system rewarded seniority, and nothing protected reputation, because the appointments were not being made by anyone in the room.

Small and great. The phrase is used elsewhere of God taking no account of a man's standing, and here it has been built into a duty roster. Israel's worship was arranged so that the most experienced musician in the country could be handed an ordinary Tuesday.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The lots are then recorded one at a time, from the first to the twenty-fourth, and the same phrase closes almost every line: his sons and his brothers, twelve. Joseph, Gedaliah, Zaccur, Izri, Nethaniah, Bukkiah, Jesharelah, Jeshaiah, Mattaniah, Shimei, Azarel, Hashabiah, Shubael, Mattithiah, Jeremoth, Hananiah, Joshbekashah, Hanani, Mallothi, Eliathah, Hothir, Giddalti, Mahazioth, and last the twenty-fourth, to Romamti-ezer, his sons and his brothers, twelve (v. 31).
verseByVerse.theology: Twenty-four courses of twelve is two hundred and eighty-eight, which is exactly the figure verse 7 gave. The Chronicler has set out a rota that balances, and then written it out in full rather than summarising it.
verseByVerse.examples: The repetition is the design and not a fault in the writing. A rota reads like this because a rota works like this, and the singing in that house went on for four centuries because somebody was willing to be dull on paper.

verseByVerse.quote: The first lot fell for Asaph to Joseph; the second to Gedaliah, to him and his brothers and his sons, twelve; the third to Zaccur, his sons and his brothers, twelve; the fourth to Izri, his sons and his brothers, twelve; the fifth to Nethaniah, his sons and his brothers, twelve; the sixth to Bukkiah, his sons and his brothers, twelve; the seventh to Jesharelah, his sons and his brothers, twelve; the eighth to Jeshaiah, his sons and his brothers, twelve; the ninth to Mattaniah, his sons and his brothers, twelve; the tenth to Shimei, his sons and his brothers, twelve; the eleventh to Azarel, his sons and his brothers, twelve; the twelfth to Hashabiah, his sons and his brothers, twelve;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the draw, and it reads exactly as a draw reads. The first lot to Joseph; the second to Gedaliah, to him and his brothers and his sons, twelve; the third to Zaccur, his sons and his brothers, twelve; the fourth to Izri, twelve; the fifth to Nethaniah, twelve.

And on it goes — Bukkiah, Jesharelah, Jeshaiah, Mattaniah, Shimei, Azarel, Hashabiah — the same clause every time, the same number every time.

The three families are shuffled together by the lot rather than kept in blocks. Asaph's sons, Jeduthun's and Heman's come up in no particular order, which means no family held a run of the best weeks and no family was pushed to the end of the year.

verseByVerse.quote: to the thirteenth, Shubael, his sons and his brothers, twelve; to the fourteenth, Mattithiah, his sons and his brothers, twelve; to the fifteenth, to Jeremoth, his sons and his brothers, twelve; to the sixteenth, to Hananiah, his sons and his brothers, twelve; to the seventeenth, to Joshbekashah, his sons and his brothers, twelve; to the eighteenth, to Hanani, his sons and his brothers, twelve; to the nineteenth, to Mallothi, his sons and his brothers, twelve; to the twentieth, to Eliathah, his sons and his brothers, twelve; to the twenty-first, to Hothir, his sons and his brothers, twelve; to the twenty-second, to Giddalti, his sons and his brothers, twelve; to the twenty-third, to Mahazioth, his sons and his brothers, twelve; to the twenty-fourth, to Romamti-ezer, his sons and his brothers, twelve.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second half of the list is the first half again: Shubael thirteenth, Mattithiah fourteenth, Jeremoth, Hananiah, Joshbekashah, Hanani, Mallothi, Eliathah, Hothir, Giddalti, Mahazioth, and at the end the twenty-fourth, to Romamti-ezer, his sons and his brothers, twelve.

Twenty-three times the same phrase — once for every lot but the very first. It is not careless writing; it is what a rota looks like, and the Chronicler has copied it out in full instead of summarising it, because the document itself is part of what he wants his readers to have.

Consider what the list actually provided for. Every week of the year, in that house, twelve trained men turned up and sang, and were replaced the following week by twelve more, and the year came round and it began again. The men in the ninth course never had the feast-day crowds. Nobody in the country could have named more than a handful of them.

The house they sang in was burned to the ground four hundred years later and the rota was carried into exile and brought back and started again. Two hundred and eighty-eight names on a page, drawn by lot, small and great alike, teacher and pupil, twelve at a time — and God has never once needed his praise to be interesting to be worth having.

26.title: Gatekeepers and Administrators: Guarding the Holy and Serving the Community
26.text: <sup>1</sup>As for the divisions of the gatekeepers: of the Korahites, Meshelemiah the son of Kore, of the sons of Asaph.<sup>2</sup>And Meshelemiah had sons: Zechariah the firstborn, Jediael the second, Zebadiah the third, Jathniel the fourth,<sup>3</sup>Elam the fifth, Jehohanan the sixth, Eliehoenai the seventh.<sup>4</sup>And Obed-edom had sons: Shemaiah the firstborn, Jehozabad the second, Joah the third, Sachar the fourth, Nethanel the fifth,<sup>5</sup>Ammiel the sixth, Issachar the seventh, Peullethai the eighth, for God blessed him.<sup>6</sup>Also to his son Shemaiah were sons born who were rulers in their fathers' houses, for they were men of great ability.<sup>7</sup>The sons of Shemaiah: Othni, Rephael, Obed and Elzabad, whose brothers were able men, Elihu and Semachiah.<sup>8</sup>All these were of the sons of Obed-edom with their sons and brothers, able men qualified for the service; sixty-two of Obed-edom.<sup>9</sup>And Meshelemiah had sons and brothers, able men, eighteen.<sup>10</sup>And Hosah, of the sons of Merari, had sons: Shimri the chief (for though he was not the firstborn, his father made him chief),<sup>11</sup>Hilkiah the second, Tebaliah the third, Zechariah the fourth: all the sons and brothers of Hosah were thirteen.<sup>12</sup>These divisions of the gatekeepers, corresponding to their chief men, had duties, just as their brothers did, ministering in the house of the LORD.<sup>13</sup>And they cast lots by fathers' houses, small and great alike, for their gates.<sup>14</sup>The lot for the east fell to Shelemiah. They cast lots also for his son Zechariah, a shrewd counselor, and his lot came out for the north.<sup>15</sup>Obed-edom's came out for the south, and to his sons was allotted the gatehouse.<sup>16</sup>For Shuppim and Hosah it came out for the west, at the gate of Shallecheth on the road that goes up. Watch corresponded to watch.<sup>17</sup>On the east there were six each day, on the north four each day, on the south four each day, as well as two and two at the gatehouse.<sup>18</sup>And for the colonnade on the west there were four at the road and two at the colonnade.<sup>19</sup>These were the divisions of the gatekeepers among the Korahites and the sons of Merari.<sup>20</sup>And of the Levites, Ahijah had charge of the treasuries of the house of God and the treasuries of the dedicated gifts.<sup>21</sup>The sons of Ladan, the sons of the Gershonites belonging to Ladan, the heads of the fathers' houses belonging to Ladan the Gershonite: Jehieli.<sup>22</sup>The sons of Jehieli, Zetham, and Joel his brother, were in charge of the treasuries of the house of the LORD.<sup>23</sup>Of the Amramites, the Izharites, the Hebronites, and the Uzzielites—<sup>24</sup>and Shebuel the son of Gershom, son of Moses, was chief officer in charge of the treasuries.<sup>25</sup>His brothers: from Eliezer were his son Rehabiah, and his son Jeshaiah, and his son Joram, and his son Zichri, and his son Shelomoth.<sup>26</sup>This Shelomoth and his brothers were in charge of all the treasuries of the dedicated gifts that David the king and the heads of the fathers' houses and the officers of the thousands and the hundreds and the commanders of the army had dedicated.<sup>27</sup>From spoil won in battles they dedicated gifts for the maintenance of the house of the LORD.<sup>28</sup>Also all that Samuel the seer and Saul the son of Kish and Abner the son of Ner and Joab the son of Zeruiah had dedicated—all dedicated gifts were in the care of Shelomoth and his brothers.<sup>29</sup>Of the Izharites, Chenaniah and his sons were appointed to external duties for Israel, as officers and judges.<sup>30</sup>Of the Hebronites, Hashabiah and his brothers, 1,700 men of ability, had the oversight of Israel westward of the Jordan for all the work of the LORD and for the service of the king.<sup>31</sup>Of the Hebronites, Jerijah was chief of the Hebronites of whatever genealogy or fathers' houses. (In the fortieth year of David's reign search was made and men of great ability among them were found at Jazer in Gilead.)<sup>32</sup>King David appointed him and his brothers, 2,700 men of ability, heads of fathers' houses, to have the oversight of the Reubenites, the Gadites and the half-tribe of the Manassites for everything pertaining to God and for the affairs of the king.
26.overview:
The gatekeepers are organised by family — Korahites under Meshelemiah, the sixty-two of Obed-edom's household, Hosah's thirteen — and described throughout as able men (vv. 1-12). The gates are drawn by lot, small and great alike, and the daily watch is set: six on the east, four on the north, four on the south, and the rest at the storehouse and the western colonnade (vv. 13-19). Then the treasuries, kept by Moses' own grandson (vv. 20-24), holding gifts dedicated from the spoil of war by David, and by Samuel, Saul, Abner and Joab (vv. 25-28). And finally Levites posted outside the sanctuary as officers and judges over Israel on both sides of the Jordan (vv. 29-32).

The figures for the watch add to twenty-four men on duty every day, with the most of them on the east, which is the front.
26.theology:
The doorkeepers are Korah's descendants. Their ancestor wanted the priesthood and the ground opened under him — and a single line in Numbers records that his sons did not die. Eleven psalms carry the family name, and one of them says that a day in God's courts beats a thousand elsewhere and that its writer would rather keep a door in the house of his God than live in the tents of the wicked. That is the family whose duty roster this chapter is.

And verse 28 keeps Saul's dedicated gifts in the treasury, catalogued beside Samuel's. This book has already given Saul's obituary and it is unsparing: he broke faith and did not seek the LORD. Both things stand. What he gave was not thrown out with him.
26.examples:
Twenty-four men stood at those gates every day, six of them on the east from first light. They were chosen by lot, described as able men, and not one of them is remembered for anything. The house was guarded for four hundred years by people nobody can name.

Moses' grandson kept the accounts of the storerooms. The priesthood had gone to another branch of the family altogether, and the work he was given was real, necessary and entirely unglamorous, and Scripture puts his name and his grandfather's in the same verse.

In the fortieth and last year of his reign, David sent men over the Jordan to find capable administrators for a temple that had not been begun. He knew he would not see it. He was still hiring.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The doorkeepers are organised by family: the Korahites under Meshelemiah with seven sons (vv. 1-3); Obed-edom with eight, the eighth entered with a reason — for God blessed him (vv. 4-5) — and his household coming to sixty-two of Obed-edom, all able men qualified for the service (vv. 6-8); Meshelemiah's eighteen (v. 9); and Hosah's thirteen, headed by a son who was not the firstborn (vv. 10-11). Then the gates are drawn by lot, small and great alike (vv. 12-13): east, north, south, the storehouse and the western colonnade (vv. 14-16), with the daily watch numbered gate by gate (vv. 17-19).
verseByVerse.theology: These men are Korah's descendants. Their ancestor grasped at the priesthood and the ground opened under him, and the line did not die out; eleven psalms carry the family name, and one of them says a day at the doorway of God's house beats a thousand anywhere else.
verseByVerse.examples: Obed-edom is here for the fourth time. He took the ark into his yard when the king was frightened of it, walked to Jerusalem beside it as a doorkeeper, stood on the permanent staff with sixty-eight brothers, and now heads a family of sixty-two on the gates.

verseByVerse.quote: As for the divisions of the gatekeepers: of the Korahites, Meshelemiah the son of Kore, of the sons of Asaph. And Meshelemiah had sons: Zechariah the firstborn, Jediael the second, Zebadiah the third, Jathniel the fourth, Elam the fifth, Jehohanan the sixth, Eliehoenai the seventh. And Obed-edom had sons: Shemaiah the firstborn, Jehozabad the second, Joah the third, Sachar the fourth, Nethanel the fifth, Ammiel the sixth, Issachar the seventh, Peullethai the eighth, for God blessed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first word of the gatekeeper list is a name with a history in it. Of the Korahites, Meshelemiah the son of Kore.

Korah was the Levite who stood up in the wilderness with two hundred and fifty men and told Moses and Aaron they had taken too much on themselves, and that the whole congregation was holy. He wanted the priesthood. The ground opened and swallowed him and his household and everything that belonged to them, and fire took the two hundred and fifty who had brought censers.

And then, buried in a census ten chapters later, one sentence: the sons of Korah did not die. The line survived, and here they are, four hundred years on, appointed to the doors of the house of God.

There are eleven psalms in the Psalter with their name on them, and one of them says this: a day in your courts is better than a thousand elsewhere; I would rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God than dwell in the tents of wickedness. The family that grasped at the altar and lost everything wrote the song about being content at the threshold, and this chapter is their duty roster.

Then Obed-edom, with eight sons listed by number, and against the eighth a clause that explains all of them: Peullethai the eighth, for God blessed him. That is the sentence from chapter 13, when the ark stood in his house for three months and the LORD blessed his household and all that he had. Two generations later the clerk keeping the staff register still knows why that family is large.

verseByVerse.quote: Also to his son Shemaiah were sons born who were rulers in their fathers' houses, for they were men of great ability. The sons of Shemaiah: Othni, Rephael, Obed and Elzabad, whose brothers were able men, Elihu and Semachiah. All these were of the sons of Obed-edom with their sons and brothers, able men qualified for the service; sixty-two of Obed-edom. And Meshelemiah had sons and brothers, able men, eighteen. And Hosah, of the sons of Merari, had sons: Shimri the chief (for though he was not the firstborn, his father made him chief), Hilkiah the second, Tebaliah the third, Zechariah the fourth: all the sons and brothers of Hosah were thirteen. These divisions of the gatekeepers, corresponding to their chief men, had duties, just as their brothers did, ministering in the house of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The description of these men is not what a modern reader expects of church doorkeepers.

Men of great ability. Able men qualified for the service. The word behind it is the one used of soldiers and of fighting strength, and it is used seven times in this chapter. Guarding the gates of the temple was a physical job. Somebody had to stop the wrong people going in, hold the doors at festival crowds, and be awake all night on the north side.

Obed-edom's household comes to sixty-two. Meshelemiah's to eighteen. Hosah's to thirteen. And of Hosah's sons there is a note dropped in without explanation: Shimri the chief (for though he was not the firstborn, his father made him chief).

Someone looked at his own sons, passed over the eldest, and put a younger one in charge. The Chronicler records it and does not say whether it was wisdom or favouritism. He has already noted that the sons of Moses were ordinary Levites and that a younger brother drew lots on the same terms as the head of the house, and this is one more place where the expected order simply does not hold.

verseByVerse.quote: And they cast lots by fathers' houses, small and great alike, for their gates. The lot for the east fell to Shelemiah. They cast lots also for his son Zechariah, a shrewd counselor, and his lot came out for the north. Obed-edom's came out for the south, and to his sons was allotted the gatehouse. For Shuppim and Hosah it came out for the west, at the gate of Shallecheth on the road that goes up. Watch corresponded to watch. On the east there were six each day, on the north four each day, on the south four each day, as well as two and two at the gatehouse. And for the colonnade on the west there were four at the road and two at the colonnade. These were the divisions of the gatekeepers among the Korahites and the sons of Merari.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they cast lots by fathers' houses, small and great alike, for their gates.

That is the third time in three chapters. The priests drew lots, head of house and younger brother alike. The singers drew lots, teacher and pupil alike. The doorkeepers draw lots, small and great alike. The Chronicler has used the phrase deliberately at each of the three rosters, and the effect is cumulative: nobody in the service of that house got a posting because of who he was.

The gates come out one by one. East to Shelemiah. North to his son Zechariah, who is described as a shrewd counselor — a man with judgement was put on a door. South to Obed-edom, with the storehouse to his sons. West to Shuppim and Hosah, at the gate of Shallecheth on the road that goes up. And then a small clause about how it all fitted together: Watch corresponded to watch.

Then the numbers, and they add up. Six on the east each day, four on the north, four on the south, two and two at the storehouse, and on the west four at the road and two at the colonnade. Twenty-four men on duty every day of the year.

The east has the most, and the east is the front. It is the side the sun comes up on, the direction the sanctuary faced, and the way a king would come. Six men stood there every morning, and nobody has ever heard of any of them.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Then the treasuries — the stores of the house of God and the stores of dedicated gifts — with Ahijah in charge (v. 20) and, as chief officer, Shebuel the son of Gershom, son of Moses (vv. 21-24). Shelomoth and his brothers keep the gifts dedicated by David and the commanders from spoil won in battles (vv. 25-27), including everything dedicated by Samuel the seer and Saul the son of Kish and Abner the son of Ner and Joab the son of Zeruiah (v. 28). Others are posted outside — Chenaniah as an officer and judge (v. 29), Hashabiah with 1,700 men west of the Jordan (v. 30), and Jerijah with 2,700 east of it (vv. 31-32).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 28 keeps Saul's offerings on the shelf. This is the book that said he died for breaking faith and not seeking the LORD, and it also records that what he had once given to God was still in the treasury, cared for and written down.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 30 sends Levites out to oversee Israel for all the work of the LORD and for the service of the king, in a single clause. Nobody in the chapter seems to think the two phrases are pulling against each other.

verseByVerse.quote: And of the Levites, Ahijah had charge of the treasuries of the house of God and the treasuries of the dedicated gifts. The sons of Ladan, the sons of the Gershonites belonging to Ladan, the heads of the fathers' houses belonging to Ladan the Gershonite: Jehieli. The sons of Jehieli, Zetham, and Joel his brother, were in charge of the treasuries of the house of the LORD. Of the Amramites, the Izharites, the Hebronites, and the Uzzielites— and Shebuel the son of Gershom, son of Moses, was chief officer in charge of the treasuries. His brothers: from Eliezer were his son Rehabiah, and his son Jeshaiah, and his son Joram, and his son Zichri, and his son Shelomoth. This Shelomoth and his brothers were in charge of all the treasuries of the dedicated gifts that David the king and the heads of the fathers' houses and the officers of the thousands and the hundreds and the commanders of the army had dedicated. From spoil won in battles they dedicated gifts for the maintenance of the house of the LORD. Also all that Samuel the seer and Saul the son of Kish and Abner the son of Ner and Joab the son of Zeruiah had dedicated—all dedicated gifts were in the care of Shelomoth and his brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the treasuries, and there are two kinds: the stores of the house itself, and the stores of dedicated gifts. Both need keeping and both need accounts.

Then verse 24. And Shebuel the son of Gershom, son of Moses, was chief officer in charge of the treasuries.

Moses' grandson is the treasurer. Three chapters ago the sons of Moses were entered on the roll among the ordinary Levites, with the priesthood going to Aaron's line instead, and here is what that meant in practice: the descendant of the man who spoke with God face to face spent his life keeping the accounts of the storerooms. It is real work and it is not the altar, and Scripture names him doing it.

What is in those stores comes next. Gifts dedicated by David, by the heads of the fathers' houses, by the officers of thousands and hundreds and the commanders — from spoil won in battles they dedicated gifts for the maintenance of the house of the LORD. Everything David brought back from Edom and Moab and Ammon and Philistia is in there, and the interest on it maintains the building.

And then verse 28, which is the surprise of the chapter. Also all that Samuel the seer and Saul the son of Kish and Abner the son of Ner and Joab the son of Zeruiah had dedicated — all dedicated gifts were in the care of Shelomoth and his brothers.

Saul is on that list. The king whose obituary in chapter 10 says he died for breaking faith with the LORD and for not seeking him had, at some point in his forty years, brought things to God and set them apart. They were still there. Nobody had melted them down or quietly removed his name from the ledger. Beside them sit gifts from Abner and from Joab, two generals who spent years killing each other's men and who both died by violence, filed on the same shelf as Samuel's.

God kept what Saul gave him. That does not undo chapter 10 and the Chronicler does not pretend it does. It simply stands there in an inventory, and anyone who has ever wondered whether the good they did before they went wrong was wasted may sit with it for a while.

verseByVerse.quote: Of the Izharites, Chenaniah and his sons were appointed to external duties for Israel, as officers and judges. Of the Hebronites, Hashabiah and his brothers, 1,700 men of ability, had the oversight of Israel westward of the Jordan for all the work of the LORD and for the service of the king. Of the Hebronites, Jerijah was chief of the Hebronites of whatever genealogy or fathers' houses. (In the fortieth year of David's reign search was made and men of great ability among them were found at Jazer in Gilead.) King David appointed him and his brothers, 2,700 men of ability, heads of fathers' houses, to have the oversight of the Reubenites, the Gadites and the half-tribe of the Manassites for everything pertaining to God and for the affairs of the king.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The last four verses send Levites out of the sanctuary altogether.

Chenaniah and his sons are appointed to external duties for Israel, as officers and judges. Hashabiah and his brothers, seventeen hundred able men, have the oversight of Israel west of the Jordan. Jerijah and his brothers, twenty-seven hundred, have the trans-Jordan tribes.

And the terms of the appointment are given in one clause that refuses to split: they had the oversight of Israel for all the work of the LORD and for the service of the king. Both, together, in one commission, with no seam between them. A Levite riding out to settle a boundary dispute in Gilead was doing the work of the LORD, and nobody in this chapter thought that needed defending.

There is a note in brackets in verse 31 that is easy to miss. In the fortieth year of David's reign search was made and men of great ability among them were found at Jazer in Gilead.

The fortieth year is the last one. He is an old man who has already handed the throne to his son, and he is still sending people out to comb the far side of the Jordan for capable men to staff a building that has not been started. He had been told he would not see it finished, and he went on recruiting until the year he died.

27.title: The Civic Order of David's Kingdom: Twelve Months, Twelve Tribes, One King
27.text: <sup>1</sup>This is the number of the people of Israel, the heads of fathers' houses, the commanders of thousands and hundreds, and their officers who served the king in all matters concerning the divisions that came and went, month after month throughout the year, each division numbering 24,000:<sup>2</sup>Jashobeam the son of Zabdiel was in charge of the first division in the first month; in his division were 24,000.<sup>3</sup>He was a descendant of Perez and was chief of all the commanders. He served for the first month.<sup>4</sup>Dodai the Ahohite was in charge of the division of the second month; in his division were 24,000.<sup>5</sup>The third commander, for the third month, was Benaiah, the son of Jehoiada the chief priest; in his division were 24,000.<sup>6</sup>This is the Benaiah who was a mighty man of the thirty and in command of the thirty; Ammizabad his son was in charge of his division.<sup>7</sup>Asahel the brother of Joab was fourth, for the fourth month, and his son Zebadiah after him; in his division were 24,000.<sup>8</sup>The fifth commander, for the fifth month, was Shamhuth the Izrahite; in his division were 24,000.<sup>9</sup>Sixth, for the sixth month, was Ira, the son of Ikkesh the Tekoite; in his division were 24,000.<sup>10</sup>Seventh, for the seventh month, was Helez the Pelonite, of the sons of Ephraim; in his division were 24,000.<sup>11</sup>Eighth, for the eighth month, was Sibbecai the Hushathite, of the Zerahites; in his division were 24,000.<sup>12</sup>Ninth, for the ninth month, was Abiezer of Anathoth, a Benjaminite; in his division were 24,000.<sup>13</sup>Tenth, for the tenth month, was Maharai of Netophah, of the Zerahites; in his division were 24,000.<sup>14</sup>Eleventh, for the eleventh month, was Benaiah of Pirathon, of the sons of Ephraim; in his division were 24,000.<sup>15</sup>Twelfth, for the twelfth month, was Heldai the Netophathite, of Othniel; in his division were 24,000.<sup>16</sup>Over the tribes of Israel, for the Reubenites, Eliezer the son of Zichri was chief officer; for the Simeonites, Shephatiah the son of Maacah;<sup>17</sup>for Levi, Hashabiah the son of Kemuel; for Aaron, Zadok;<sup>18</sup>for Judah, Elihu, one of David's brothers; for Issachar, Omri the son of Michael;<sup>19</sup>for Zebulun, Ishmaiah the son of Obadiah; for Naphtali, Jeremoth the son of Azriel;<sup>20</sup>for the Ephraimites, Hoshea the son of Azaziah; Joab was commander of the king's army.
27.overview:
Israel's fighting strength is set out as a rota: twelve divisions of 24,000, one on duty each month, commanded almost entirely by men from the roll of the mighty men in chapter 11 (vv. 1-15). Then a chief officer for each tribe, with Gad and Asher unaccountably absent and Abner's own son over Benjamin (vv. 16-22). Two verses go back to the census, giving a reason chapter 21 never gave and reporting that the total was not entered in the chronicles of King David (vv. 23-24). Twelve stewards then run the crown estates — fields, vines, wine, olives, oil, cattle, camels, donkeys, flocks — and the household staff closes the list (vv. 25-34).

Twelve divisions of twenty-four thousand come to 288,000, and the temple singers numbered 288. The kingdom and the sanctuary were organised on the same shape.
27.theology:
Verse 23 supplies what chapter 21 left out. The young were not counted for the LORD had promised to make Israel as many as the stars of heaven. God had taken Abraham outside and told him to try counting them; a census of the next generation is that promise contradicted with a ledger.

And verse 24 says what happened to the figure: it was never entered in the annals. The wrath is on the record and the sin is on the record, told twice and confessed in the king's own words — and the total he had sinned to obtain was struck out. Scripture keeps what has to be remembered and loses what was wanted.
27.examples:
Obil the Ishmaelite ran the camels and Jaziz the Hagrite ran the flocks, because desert peoples know desert stock. The king appointed the men who understood the animals, and where they came from does not appear to have been raised.

Asahel had been dead for years and his name still heads the fourth division, with his son entered after him. An organisation can honour the man who began a thing while getting on with the work he left.

Abner's son administers Benjamin. His father was Saul's general, was killed by David's, and is buried at Hebron; his son holds royal office over Saul's own tribe. Whatever it took to reach that, it is recorded in six words in a staff list.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — Twelve Divisions, One a Month
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The standing army is a rota. Twelve divisions of 24,000 men serve month after month throughout the year, so that every man gives one month in twelve and the rest of the time is at home (v. 1). The commanders are named month by month — Jashobeam of the line of Perez, chief of all the commanders (vv. 2-3); Dodai; Benaiah the son of Jehoiada the chief priest, a mighty man of the thirty and in command of the thirty (vv. 4-6); Asahel, with his son Zebadiah after him (v. 7); and on through Shamhuth, Ira, Helez, Sibbecai, Abiezer, Maharai, Benaiah of Pirathon and Heldai (vv. 8-15).
verseByVerse.theology: Twelve divisions of twenty-four thousand is two hundred and eighty-eight thousand, and the temple singers of the last chapter but one numbered two hundred and eighty-eight. The kingdom and the sanctuary were organised on the same shape.
verseByVerse.examples: Almost every commander on this list is a name from the roll of the mighty men in chapter 11 — men who walked out to a fugitive at Ziklag or held a barley field when the army ran. They ended up running the timetable.

verseByVerse.quote: This is the number of the people of Israel, the heads of fathers' houses, the commanders of thousands and hundreds, and their officers who served the king in all matters concerning the divisions that came and went, month after month throughout the year, each division numbering 24,000: Jashobeam the son of Zabdiel was in charge of the first division in the first month; in his division were 24,000. He was a descendant of Perez and was chief of all the commanders. He served for the first month. Dodai the Ahohite was in charge of the division of the second month; in his division were 24,000. The third commander, for the third month, was Benaiah, the son of Jehoiada the chief priest; in his division were 24,000. This is the Benaiah who was a mighty man of the thirty and in command of the thirty; Ammizabad his son was in charge of his division.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The army is a rota, and the arithmetic is the point. Twelve divisions of twenty-four thousand men, one on duty each month, month after month throughout the year. Every soldier in Israel served one month in twelve and spent the other eleven on his own land.

It is a militia rather than a standing army, and it keeps the kingdom out of two traps at once. A nation with no force is at everybody's mercy; a nation with a permanent professional army under a king tends to find out what that costs. David built neither. He built a timetable.

Twelve times twenty-four thousand is two hundred and eighty-eight thousand. The singers in chapter 25 came to two hundred and eighty-eight — twenty-four courses of twelve. The priests were twenty-four courses, the doorkeepers twenty-four a day. Whoever organised the worship organised the army, and used the same shape for both.

The first commander is Jashobeam, described as a descendant of Perez and chief of all the commanders. Perez was Judah's son by Tamar, and the line runs through Boaz and Obed and Jesse to David, and a long way past him.

And the third month belongs to Benaiah, the son of Jehoiada the chief priest. The man who killed a lion in a pit on a snowy day and took an Egyptian's spear out of his hand was a priest's son. He would command Solomon's army in the end.

verseByVerse.quote: Asahel the brother of Joab was fourth, for the fourth month, and his son Zebadiah after him; in his division were 24,000. The fifth commander, for the fifth month, was Shamhuth the Izrahite; in his division were 24,000. Sixth, for the sixth month, was Ira, the son of Ikkesh the Tekoite; in his division were 24,000. Seventh, for the seventh month, was Helez the Pelonite, of the sons of Ephraim; in his division were 24,000. Eighth, for the eighth month, was Sibbecai the Hushathite, of the Zerahites; in his division were 24,000. Ninth, for the ninth month, was Abiezer of Anathoth, a Benjaminite; in his division were 24,000. Tenth, for the tenth month, was Maharai of Netophah, of the Zerahites; in his division were 24,000. Eleventh, for the eleventh month, was Benaiah of Pirathon, of the sons of Ephraim; in his division were 24,000. Twelfth, for the twelfth month, was Heldai the Netophathite, of Othniel; in his division were 24,000.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the fourth month, and a name that stops a careful reader. Asahel the brother of Joab was fourth, for the fourth month, and his son Zebadiah after him.

Asahel was dead. He had been killed years before this list was drawn up, run through with the butt of a spear by Abner in the retreat from Gibeon after being told three times to turn aside. His name still heads the division, with his son entered after him.

The rest of the twelve read like a page from chapter 11, because that is what they are. Shamhuth, Ira the son of Ikkesh the Tekoite, Helez the Pelonite, Sibbecai the Hushathite who killed a giant at Gezer, Abiezer of Anathoth, Maharai of Netophah, Benaiah of Pirathon, Heldai the Netophathite. Almost every one of them is in the roll of the mighty men.

These are the men who walked into a Philistine border town to join a wanted man, or stood in a barley field when everyone else ran. They are now running a duty roster. That is what usually becomes of the people who were there at the beginning, and it is not a comedown.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–24 — The Tribal Officers, and the Number That Was Not Entered
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Each tribe has a chief officer named: Eliezer for Reuben, Zadok for Aaron, Elihu, one of David's brothers for Judah, and for Benjamin Jaasiel the son of Abner (vv. 16-22). Then two verses return to the census. David did not count those under twenty, for the LORD had promised to make Israel as many as the stars of heaven (v. 23). And of the count that was taken: Joab the son of Zeruiah began to count, but did not finish. Yet wrath came upon Israel for this, and the number was not entered in the chronicles of King David (v. 24).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 23 explains what chapter 21 never said. God had promised Abraham a people beyond counting, and a census of the coming generation would have been a contradiction of the promise in the form of a spreadsheet.
verseByVerse.examples: The figure was struck from the annals. The sin stayed on the record in full, and the total it produced was never written down — which is a strange and merciful way to keep a chronicle.

verseByVerse.quote: Over the tribes of Israel, for the Reubenites, Eliezer the son of Zichri was chief officer; for the Simeonites, Shephatiah the son of Maacah; for Levi, Hashabiah the son of Kemuel; for Aaron, Zadok; for Judah, Elihu, one of David's brothers; for Issachar, Omri the son of Michael; for Zebulun, Ishmaiah the son of Obadiah; for Naphtali, Jeremoth the son of Azriel; for the Ephraimites, Hoshea the son of Azaziah; for the half-tribe of Manasseh, Joel the son of Pedaiah; for the half-tribe of Manasseh in Gilead, Iddo the son of Zechariah; for Benjamin, Jaasiel the son of Abner; for Dan, Azarel the son of Jeroham. These were the leaders of the tribes of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Each tribe gets a chief officer, named. Eliezer for Reuben, Shephatiah for Simeon, Hashabiah for Levi and Zadok for Aaron, Omri for Issachar, Hoshea for Ephraim, Iddo for the half-tribe in Gilead, Azarel for Dan.

Two are missing. Gad and Asher have no officer in this list, and nobody knows why. It may be damage to the text, or an administrative arrangement lost to us. The gap is there and it should not be papered over.

Two entries carry a story. For Judah, Elihu, one of David's brothers — one of the men who stood in the valley of Elah while a shepherd boy went out to the giant, given the largest tribe in the kingdom to administer.

And then: for Benjamin, Jaasiel the son of Abner.

Abner was Saul's cousin and Saul's general, the man who put Ish-bosheth on a throne against David, killed Asahel in a retreat, and was murdered by Joab in the gateway at Hebron. His son is a royal officer, and the tribe he administers is Saul's own. Whatever settlement was reached between the house of David and the house of Saul, it is recorded in one line of a staff list.

verseByVerse.quote: David did not count those below twenty years of age, for the LORD had promised to make Israel as many as the stars of heaven. Joab the son of Zeruiah began to count, but did not finish. Yet wrath came upon Israel for this, and the number was not entered in the chronicles of King David.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The list breaks off for two verses and goes back to the worst day of the reign.

David did not count those below twenty years of age, for the LORD had promised to make Israel as many as the stars of heaven.

That is a reason chapter 21 never gave, and it goes to the heart of what was wrong. God had taken Abraham outside and told him to look up and count the stars if he could, and said that his offspring would be like that. A man who sits down to total a people God has promised to make uncountable has already contradicted the promise, whatever his motive. The boys were left out of the count because they belonged to a number nobody was ever meant to have.

Then verse 24, and it adds two more things. Joab the son of Zeruiah began to count, but did not finish. He walked the country for the better part of a year, left Levi and Benjamin out, and stopped. And: Yet wrath came upon Israel for this, and the number was not entered in the chronicles of King David.

The figure was suppressed. Somebody had it — chapter 21 prints it — and it was kept out of the official annals of the reign, so that the one thing David had wanted out of the whole exercise was the one thing the record would not preserve.

And notice which half survived. The wrath is in the chronicle. The sin is in the chronicle, told at length, twice, with the king's own confession in his own words. What was struck out was the total he had sinned to obtain. Scripture keeps what a man needs to remember and loses what he wanted, and that is not an accident of filing.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–34 — Stewards, Counsellors, and a Friend
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Twelve stewards run the crown estates: the treasuries, the country stores, the ploughland, the vineyards and the wine cellars, the olive and sycamore trees in the Shephelah and the oil, the herds in Sharon and in the valleys, and then the camels under Obil the Ishmaelite, the donkeys, and the flocks under Jaziz the Hagrite (vv. 25-31). Finally the household: David's uncle Jonathan as counsellor and tutor to the king's sons (v. 32), Ahithophel was the king's counselor, and Hushai the Archite was the king's friend (v. 33), and the replacements — with Joab still commanding the army (v. 34).
verseByVerse.theology: The wealth of the kingdom in this list is soil and livestock. Twelve men are needed for olives, oil, vines, wine, cattle, camels, donkeys and sheep, and one for the treasury.
verseByVerse.examples: Two names sit side by side in verse 33 as though nothing ever happened between them. Anyone who has read 2 Samuel knows how that pair ends, and the Chronicler writes the job titles and moves on.

verseByVerse.quote: Over the king's treasuries was Azmaveth the son of Adiel; and over the treasuries in the country, in the cities, in the villages, and in the towers, was Jonathan the son of Uzziah; and over those who did the work of the field for tilling the soil was Ezri the son of Chelub; and over the vineyards was Shimei the Ramathite; and over the produce of the vineyards for the wine cellars was Zabdi the Shiphmite. Over the olive and sycamore trees in the Shephelah was Baal-hanan the Gederite; and over the stores of oil was Joash. Over the herds that pastured in Sharon was Shitrai the Sharonite; over the herds in the valleys was Shaphat the son of Adlai. Over the camels was Obil the Ishmaelite; and over the donkeys was Jehdeiah the Meronothite. Over the flocks was Jaziz the Hagrite. All these were stewards of King David's property.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the crown estates, and the list is a picture of what a kingdom actually was.

Azmaveth over the treasuries and Jonathan over the stores out in the country, in the villages and the towers. Ezri over the ploughmen. Shimei over the vineyards and Zabdi over the wine in the cellars. Baal-hanan over the olive and sycamore trees in the Shephelah, and Joash over the stores of oil. Shitrai over the cattle grazing on the Sharon plain and Shaphat over the cattle in the valleys.

Twelve men, and only one of them is looking after money. The wealth of Israel was soil, trees and animals, and the administration reflects it exactly: two separate officials for grapes because growing them and storing the wine are different trades, two for cattle because upland and lowland herding are different trades.

And two of the appointments are foreign. Over the camels was Obil the Ishmaelite, and over the flocks was Jaziz the Hagrite.

Ishmaelites and Hagrites were desert peoples, and camels and flocks are what desert peoples know. David put the men who understood the animals in charge of the animals, and the fact that they came from outside Israel does not appear to have entered into it. He had Philistines guarding his own body and an Ishmaelite running his camels, and the Chronicler lists them without a flicker.

verseByVerse.quote: Jonathan, David's uncle, was a counselor, being a man of understanding and a scribe. He and Jehiel the son of Hachmoni attended the king's sons. Ahithophel was the king's counselor, and Hushai the Archite was the king's friend. Ahithophel was succeeded by Jehoiada the son of Benaiah, and Abiathar. Joab was commander of the king's army.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The household comes last. Jonathan, David's uncle, was a counselor, being a man of understanding and a scribe. He and Jehiel attended the king's sons — tutors for the princes, and the man appointed to it is described first as understanding and second as literate.

Then verse 33, and it is two names in one sentence. Ahithophel was the king's counselor, and Hushai the Archite was the king's friend.

Job titles, side by side, with nothing said. But anyone who has read the other account knows these two men in a different relation entirely. Ahithophel went over to Absalom and his advice was reckoned in Israel as though a man had inquired of the word of God; David, walking up the Mount of Olives barefoot and weeping, prayed that the LORD would turn it into foolishness, and sent Hushai the Archite back into the city to do it. It worked. Ahithophel saw that his counsel had not been followed, went home to his own city, set his house in order and hanged himself.

Verse 34 records that Ahithophel was succeeded, and gives the successors' names, and does not say why the post fell vacant.

And then the last four words of this whole run of registers. Joab was commander of the king's army.

Still there. He had gone up the water shaft first and bought the command with one act of nerve, and he had murdered Abner in a gateway and Amasa on a road and killed Absalom against a direct order. He had told David the census was wrong and been overruled, and he had said the finest sentence about courage and providence in the book. Nobody could remove him, and the register of David's kingdom closes with his name and his rank.

28.title: David's Final Charge: The Blueprint from the Spirit and the Call to Seek
28.text: <sup>1</sup>David assembled at Jerusalem all the officials of Israel, the officials of the tribes, the officers of the divisions that served the king, the commanders of thousands, the commanders of hundreds, the stewards of all the property and livestock of the king and his sons, together with the palace officials, the mighty men and all the seasoned warriors.<sup>2</sup>Then King David rose to his feet and said: "Hear me, my brothers and my people. I had it in my heart to build a house of rest for the ark of the covenant of the LORD and for the footstool of our God, and I made preparations for building.<sup>3</sup>But God said to me, 'You may not build a house for my name, for you are a man of war and have shed blood.'<sup>4</sup>Yet the LORD God of Israel chose me from all my father's house to be king over Israel forever. For he chose Judah as leader, and in the house of Judah my father's house, and among my father's sons he took pleasure in me to make me king over all Israel.<sup>5</sup>And of all my sons (for the LORD has given me many sons) he has chosen Solomon my son to sit on the throne of the kingdom of the LORD over Israel.<sup>6</sup>He said to me, 'It is Solomon your son who shall build my house and my courts, for I have chosen him to be my son, and I will be his father.<sup>7</sup>I will establish his kingdom forever if he continues strong in keeping my commandments and my rules, as he is today.'<sup>8</sup>Now therefore in the sight of all Israel, the assembly of the LORD, and in the hearing of our God, observe and seek out all the commandments of the LORD your God, that you may possess this good land and leave it for an inheritance to your children after you forever.<sup>9</sup>"And you, Solomon my son, know the God of your father and serve him with a whole heart and with a willing mind, for the LORD searches all hearts and understands every plan and thought. If you seek him, he will be found by you, but if you forsake him, he will cast you off forever.<sup>10</sup>Be careful now, for the LORD has chosen you to build a house for the sanctuary; be strong and do it."<sup>11</sup>Then David gave Solomon his son the plan of the vestibule of the temple, and of its houses, its treasuries, its upper rooms, and its inner chambers, and of the room for the mercy seat;<sup>12</sup>and the plan of all that he had in mind for the courts of the house of the LORD, all the surrounding chambers, the treasuries of the house of God, and the treasuries for dedicated gifts;<sup>13</sup>for the divisions of the priests and of the Levites, and all the work of the service in the house of the LORD; for all the vessels for the service in the house of the LORD,<sup>14</sup>the weight of gold for all golden vessels for each service, the weight of silver vessels for each service,<sup>15</sup>the weight of the golden lampstands and their lamps, the weight of gold for each lampstand and its lamps, the weight of silver for a lampstand and its lamps, according to the use of each lampstand in the service,<sup>16</sup>the weight of gold for each table for the showbread, the silver for the silver tables,<sup>17</sup>and pure gold for the forks, the basins and the cups; for the golden bowls and the weight of each; for the silver bowls and the weight of each;<sup>18</sup>for the altar of incense made of refined gold, and its weight; also his plan for the golden chariot of the cherubim that spread their wings and covered the ark of the covenant of the LORD.<sup>19</sup>"All this he made clear to me in writing from the hand of the LORD, all the work to be done according to the plan."<sup>20</sup>Then David said to Solomon his son, "Be strong and courageous and do it. Do not be afraid and do not be dismayed, for the LORD God, even my God, is with you. He will not leave you or forsake you, until all the work for the service of the house of the LORD is finished.<sup>21</sup>And behold the divisions of the priests and the Levites for all the service of the house of God; and with you in all the work will be every willing man who has skill for any kind of service; also the officers and all the people will be wholly at your command."
28.overview:
David assembles every officer in the kingdom and stands up to speak (vv. 1-2). He explains the refusal — you are a man of war and have shed blood (v. 3) — and then traces the choosing that narrowed from Judah to his father's house to himself to Solomon, who will sit on the throne of the kingdom of the LORD (vv. 4-7). He charges the assembly to seek out the commandments (v. 8), and his son to know God, serve him whole, and seek him (vv. 9-10). Then he hands over the plans — rooms, courts, rotas, and the weight of gold for every vessel down to the forks — in writing from the hand of the LORD (vv. 11-19). And he ends with Joshua's words and a promise that runs to completion (vv. 20-21).

Verse 9 is the sentence the whole book has been travelling towards, and verse 19 says where the building came from: not an architect, but a pattern.
28.theology:
Verses 4-6 set out election as a funnel, in David's own mouth, about his own throne: God chose Judah, then his father's house, then him, then Solomon, and the only reason offered is he took pleasure in me. And the throne is called the throne of the kingdom of the LORD over Israel — which is why its loss centuries later did not cancel the promise attached to it.

Verse 7's if stands beside chapter 17's unconditional word, and history shows how the two worked: each generation's enjoyment of the covenant hung on that generation, and the covenant itself did not. Solomon did not continue strong. The kingdom was torn in his son's lifetime, and the promise ran on underneath the wreckage.

And verse 19 names the temple's origin with the word used of the pattern Moses was shown on the mountain. The letter to the Hebrews quotes that instruction to say the priests served a copy and shadow of heavenly things. Every weight in this chapter measures something that already existed.
28.examples:
A dying man who could not be kept warm under blankets rose to his feet to make the speech. Nothing in the chapter required him to stand, and the record says he did.

He told his son to know the God of your father — pointing at a life the boy had watched from the inside, and saying in the same breath that none of it transfers. A parent's faith is evidence for a child, never an inheritance.

The plan specified the weight of gold for the forks. There is no line in the house of God below which the care stops, and the same king who once put the ark on a cart handed his son a document with the small fittings itemised.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David assembles every officer in the kingdom (v. 1), and then King David rose to his feet and told them what had happened to his life's ambition: he had meant to build a house of rest for the ark ... and for the footstool of our God, and was refused because you are a man of war and have shed blood (vv. 2-3). He then traces the choosing that put him and his son where they are — Judah, his father's house, himself, and now Solomon to sit on the throne of the kingdom of the LORD over Israel (vv. 4-6), with a condition attached (v. 7). He charges the assembly to keep the commandments (v. 8), and then turns to his son: If you seek him, he will be found by you, but if you forsake him, he will cast you off forever (vv. 9-10).
verseByVerse.theology: Four times in three verses the verb is chose, and it narrows each time — the tribe, then the family, then the man, then the son. David is standing in front of the nation explaining his own throne, and not one clause of the explanation is about him.
verseByVerse.examples: He is a dying man who could not be kept warm under blankets, and he stands up to say it. The last public act of his reign is to get to his feet.

verseByVerse.quote: David assembled at Jerusalem all the officials of Israel, the officials of the tribes, the officers of the divisions that served the king, the commanders of thousands, the commanders of hundreds, the stewards of all the property and livestock of the king and his sons, together with the palace officials, the mighty men and all the seasoned warriors. Then King David rose to his feet and said: "Hear me, my brothers and my people. I had it in my heart to build a house of rest for the ark of the covenant of the LORD and for the footstool of our God, and I made preparations for building. But God said to me, 'You may not build a house for my name, for you are a man of war and have shed blood.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everybody is called in. Tribal officials, division commanders, captains of thousands and of hundreds, the stewards who ran the farms and the herds, the palace staff, the mighty men and all the seasoned warriors. The whole apparatus of chapters 23 to 27 is standing in one place.

Then King David rose to his feet.

He is at the end. The other account of these months describes a man so cold that no quantity of bedclothes could warm him, with his sons already circling the throne. He gets up. Whatever it cost him, the last public speech of the reign is delivered standing, and the Chronicler thought the detail belonged in the record.

He begins by naming what he wanted. I had it in my heart to build a house of rest for the ark of the covenant of the LORD and for the footstool of our God, and I made preparations for building.

The footstool. That is what he calls the ark, and the psalms call it that too — worship at his footstool, for he is holy. It is a startling way to describe the most sacred object in Israel, and it puts the scale right. The gold-covered box between the cherubim is the stool under the feet of a God whose throne is heaven and whose footstool, on his own account, is the earth. The building David wanted to raise, with its cedar and its bronze sea and its hundred thousand talents of gold, was a room for a footrest.

Then the refusal, in God's own words and blunter than anywhere else. You may not build a house for my name, for you are a man of war and have shed blood.

Not you have sinned. Not you are disqualified by guilt. You are a man of war — a description of what he was, given by the God who had made him it and given him the victories the blood came from. And he says it out loud in front of the entire kingdom, standing on his feet, without a word of complaint.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet the LORD God of Israel chose me from all my father's house to be king over Israel forever. For he chose Judah as leader, and in the house of Judah my father's house, and among my father's sons he took pleasure in me to make me king over all Israel. And of all my sons (for the LORD has given me many sons) he has chosen Solomon my son to sit on the throne of the kingdom of the LORD over Israel. He said to me, 'It is Solomon your son who shall build my house and my courts, for I have chosen him to be my son, and I will be his father. I will establish his kingdom forever if he continues strong in keeping my commandments and my rules, as he is today.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
What follows is one of the clearest things ever said about how God works, and David says it about himself.

Yet the LORD God of Israel chose me from all my father's house to be king over Israel forever. For he chose Judah as leader, and in the house of Judah my father's house, and among my father's sons he took pleasure in me to make me king over all Israel.

Follow the funnel. Out of twelve tribes, Judah. Out of all Judah, the household of a farmer in Bethlehem. Out of that household's eight sons, the youngest, who was not even called in from the sheep when the prophet came to dinner. Each stage narrows and each stage is God's doing, and the verb is the same one every time.

There is no attempt to supply a reason. He does not say God chose Judah for its faithfulness or Jesse's house for its piety or himself for his courage. The nearest thing to an explanation is the phrase he took pleasure in me, which explains nothing at all and is meant to. When Israel had asked why God set his love on them, Moses had told them flatly that it was not because they were more in number, and that he had simply loved them.

Then the funnel goes one stage further. And of all my sons (for the LORD has given me many sons) he has chosen Solomon my son to sit on the throne of the kingdom of the LORD over Israel.

Read the last phrase again. Not the throne of Israel. The throne of the kingdom of the LORD over Israel. That is what this book said in chapter 17, where God called it my house and my kingdom, and it is what the next chapter will say when Solomon sits down on the throne of the LORD as king. Israel's monarchy was a tenancy. The chair belonged to somebody else, and that is exactly why it survived the loss of every man who ever sat in it.

And then verse 7, which does not sit easily beside chapter 17. I will establish his kingdom forever if he continues strong in keeping my commandments and my rules, as he is today.

An if. The promise made to David through Nathan had no condition on it; this one does. Both are Scripture and both are true, and the way they fit is the way they worked out in history. Every generation's enjoyment of the covenant depended on that generation. The covenant itself did not. Solomon did not continue strong, and the kingdom was torn in half in his son's lifetime — and the promise ran on underneath the wreckage for four hundred years and then a thousand more, until a son of David was born who did continue strong, and in whom the word forever finally meant what it said.

verseByVerse.quote: Now therefore in the sight of all Israel, the assembly of the LORD, and in the hearing of our God, observe and seek out all the commandments of the LORD your God, that you may possess this good land and leave it for an inheritance to your children after you forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before he turns to his son, David turns to the room.

Now therefore in the sight of all Israel, the assembly of the LORD, and in the hearing of our God, observe and seek out all the commandments of the LORD your God, that you may possess this good land and leave it for an inheritance to your children after you forever.

Two sets of witnesses are named — the assembly, and God. This is being said on the record and under oath, which is how a dying man speaks when he will not get another chance.

And the verb is the book's own word again: seek out all the commandments. Not merely obey the ones you already know. Go looking for what God has said, which is exactly what David himself had failed to do the first time he went for the ark, and had done in the three months afterwards.

The promise attached is the land, held and handed on. Now think about who was reading this. The Chronicler's first readers were people whose grandparents had watched that land taken away, who lived on a fraction of it under a foreign governor, and who could remember exactly which commandments had been ignored while it happened. The sentence was not nostalgia to them. It was a diagnosis.

verseByVerse.quote: "And you, Solomon my son, know the God of your father and serve him with a whole heart and with a willing mind, for the LORD searches all hearts and understands every plan and thought. If you seek him, he will be found by you, but if you forsake him, he will cast you off forever. Be careful now, for the LORD has chosen you to build a house for the sanctuary; be strong and do it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the old man turns to his son in front of everybody, and says the sentence this whole book has been travelling towards.

And you, Solomon my son, know the God of your father and serve him with a whole heart and with a willing mind, for the LORD searches all hearts and understands every plan and thought. If you seek him, he will be found by you, but if you forsake him, he will cast you off forever.

Take it a clause at a time, because every one of them carries weight.

Know the God of your father. He does not say know about him. And he calls him the God of your father, which is doing two things at once: pointing to a life the boy has watched from the inside — the ark, the plague, the threshing floor, the years of running and the years of building — and saying that none of it transfers. Solomon has to know him for himself. A father's religion is evidence, not inheritance.

Serve him with a whole heart and with a willing mind. The whole heart is the thing this book keeps asking for; the men came to Hebron with a whole heart and Zebulun with no double heart. And the second phrase is stronger than it looks in English: it is a delighting soul, service a man actually wants to give. God is not asking to be served by somebody who would rather be elsewhere and has decided to be dutiful about it.

For the LORD searches all hearts and understands every plan and thought. There is the reason wholeness is demanded rather than suggested. A divided heart works perfectly well in front of people, and there is no one it works on here. The God who told Samuel that man looks on the outward appearance while the LORD looks on the heart is the God being served, and every intention is already open in front of him.

If you seek him, he will be found by you. The book began with a king who did not seek and died; it went on through a king who sought the wrong thing, then sought the right thing the wrong way, then learned to seek God's face and told the nation to keep seeking it after the ark was found. Here it arrives as a bare promise with nothing between the two halves. Seek, and found. Moses had said it to a people facing exile: you will seek him and you will find him if you search after him with all your heart. Jeremiah would say it to people already in Babylon. And the Son of God said it in three words on a hillside — seek, and you will find.

But if you forsake him, he will cast you off forever. David does not soften it for his own child in public. And the hardest thing about the sentence is what happened next: the boy who received this charge built the house, saw the glory fill it, heard God speak to him twice, and ended his life with altars to Chemosh and Molech on the hill east of Jerusalem. He had been warned by his father, in front of the nation, in words nobody could misunderstand.

Then the last word, and it is practical. Be careful now, for the LORD has chosen you to build a house for the sanctuary; be strong and do it. The theology has been laid out and the charge ends in a verb. Do it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Then David hands over the plans, and the detail is astonishing: the vestibule, the houses, the treasuries, the upper rooms, the inner chambers, and of the room for the mercy seat (v. 11); the courts and the surrounding chambers (v. 12); the divisions of the priests and of the Levites (v. 13); and then the weight of gold and silver for every single object — lampstands, tables, forks, basins, cups, bowls, the altar of incense, and his plan for the golden chariot of the cherubim that spread their wings and covered the ark (vv. 14-18). And the source is named: All this he made clear to me in writing from the hand of the LORD (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: The word for plan is the one used of the pattern God showed Moses on the mountain. This is not architecture that pleased a king. It is a copy of something, and the letter to the Hebrews says what the something was.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 13 puts the rota of priests and Levites inside the architectural plan, between the chambers and the vessels. Who would work there was part of the design, not an arrangement made afterwards.
