verseByVerse.quote: Then David gave Solomon his son the plan of the vestibule of the temple, and of its houses, its treasuries, its upper rooms, and its inner chambers, and of the room for the mercy seat; and the plan of all that he had in mind for the courts of the house of the LORD, all the surrounding chambers, the treasuries of the house of God, and the treasuries for dedicated gifts; for the divisions of the priests and of the Levites, and all the work of the service in the house of the LORD; for all the vessels for the service in the house of the LORD, the weight of gold for all golden vessels for each service, the weight of silver vessels for each service, the weight of the golden lampstands and their lamps, the weight of gold for each lampstand and its lamps, the weight of silver for a lampstand and its lamps, according to the use of each lampstand in the service,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then David hands over the plans, and the level of detail is the surprise of the chapter.

Not a sketch and not a brief. The plan of the vestibule of the temple, and of its houses, its treasuries, its upper rooms, and its inner chambers, and of the room for the mercy seat. Then the courts, the surrounding chambers, the treasuries of the house and the treasuries for dedicated gifts.

Then verse 13, which is not architecture at all: for the divisions of the priests and of the Levites, and all the work of the service in the house of the LORD. The rotas of the last five chapters are inside the plan, filed between the chambers and the vessels. Who would work there and when was part of the design of the building, not an arrangement bolted on once the roof was up.

Then the weights. Gold for every golden vessel, by weight, for each service. Silver for every silver vessel. The weight of each lampstand and its lamps, gold ones and silver ones, according to the use of each lampstand in the service.

Somebody had specified how much gold went into a lamp. Not roughly, and not left to the goldsmith's judgement — a figure, for each item, according to what that item was for. It is the same care that would not let the ark travel on a cart.

verseByVerse.quote: the weight of gold for each table for the showbread, the silver for the silver tables, and pure gold for the forks, the basins and the cups; for the golden bowls and the weight of each; for the silver bowls and the weight of each; for the altar of incense made of refined gold, and its weight; also his plan for the golden chariot of the cherubim that spread their wings and covered the ark of the covenant of the LORD. "All this he made clear to me in writing from the hand of the LORD, all the work to be done according to the plan."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The list of weights runs on, and it gets smaller as it goes. The gold for each table of showbread and the silver for the silver tables. Then pure gold for the forks, the basins and the cups, the golden bowls by weight and the silver bowls by weight. The altar of incense of refined gold, and its weight.

Forks. The plan given to David included the specification for the forks. Whatever else this tells us, it tells us that God is not indifferent to the small fittings of the place where he is worshipped, and that there is no line in that house below which it stops mattering.

And then the last item, and it is the greatest: his plan for the golden chariot of the cherubim that spread their wings and covered the ark of the covenant of the LORD. The two enormous figures that would stand in the Most Holy Place, wings touching wall to wall over the box, are described as a chariot — the thing a king rides. It is the same picture Ezekiel would see by a canal in Babylon and David sang in a psalm, of God riding on a cherub and flying.

Then verse 19, which changes what the whole list is. All this he made clear to me in writing from the hand of the LORD, all the work to be done according to the plan.

The word translated plan is the word used of the pattern God showed Moses on the mountain, when he told him to make the tabernacle and everything in it according to the pattern he had been shown. So the temple is not David's design and not a magnificent building commissioned by a rich king. It is a copy, and the copying is the whole point of it. Its rooms and its weights and its forks were given.

Centuries later a letter to Hebrew Christians explains what the copying was of. The priests who serve there, it says, serve a copy and shadow of the heavenly things, and quotes the very instruction to Moses about the pattern. Every measurement in this chapter is a measurement of something that already existed somewhere else.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–21 — Be Strong and Do It
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The charge ends where Joshua's began. Be strong and courageous and do it. Do not be afraid and do not be dismayed, for the LORD God, even my God, is with you. He will not leave you or forsake you, until all the work for the service of the house of the LORD is finished (v. 20). And the help is already in place: the divisions of priests and Levites, every willing man who has skill for any kind of service, and the officers and all the people wholly at your command (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: The promise has a terminus, and the terminus is not Solomon's death or his best effort. God will not leave him until all the work ... is finished — which means the finishing is part of what is being promised.
verseByVerse.examples: The men who will help are described twice over: willing, and skilled. Neither on its own was thought sufficient to build a house for God.

verseByVerse.quote: Then David said to Solomon his son, "Be strong and courageous and do it. Do not be afraid and do not be dismayed, for the LORD God, even my God, is with you. He will not leave you or forsake you, until all the work for the service of the house of the LORD is finished. And behold the divisions of the priests and the Levites for all the service of the house of God; and with you in all the work will be every willing man who has skill for any kind of service; also the officers and all the people will be wholly at your command."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The charge ends the way the last handover of this kind ended.

Be strong and courageous and do it. Do not be afraid and do not be dismayed, for the LORD God, even my God, is with you. He will not leave you or forsake you, until all the work for the service of the house of the LORD is finished.

Those are Moses' words to Joshua at the Jordan, almost syllable for syllable, and David has been using them on Solomon since chapter 22. But he puts something of his own in the middle of them: the LORD God, even my God, is with you. He cannot resist the personal pronoun. Forty years of being carried by this God are compressed into two words inserted into a promise, and they are the only credential the old man offers.

Then the terminus. He will not leave you or forsake you — until all the work for the service of the house of the LORD is finished. The promise does not run out at Solomon's best effort or at his death. It runs to completion, which means the completion is part of what is being promised, and the same sentence is picked up in the New Testament twice: once to tell frightened people to be content because God has said he will never leave them nor forsake them, and once to say that the one who began a good work will bring it to its finish.

And the last verse is the practical answer to a young man's obvious fear. You are not doing this alone. Behold the divisions of the priests and the Levites — the rotas are drawn up and the staff are in post. With you in all the work will be every willing man who has skill for any kind of service. Willing, and skilled: this book will not settle for either without the other. And the officers and all the people are wholly at your command.

So the old king sits down. He has told the nation why he was refused, traced his own throne back to a choice he had no part in, warned his son in front of everybody, handed over a pattern he received in writing, and promised a God who does not leave the work half-built.

29.title: The Offering of All Things: Generosity, Prayer, and the Passing of the Kingdom
29.text: <sup>1</sup>And David the king said to all the assembly, "Solomon my son, whom alone God has chosen, is young and inexperienced, and the work is great, for the palace will not be for man but for the LORD God.<sup>2</sup>So I have provided for the house of my God, so far as I was able, the gold for the things of gold, the silver for the things of silver, and the bronze for the things of bronze, the iron for the things of iron, and wood for the things of wood, besides great quantities of onyx and stones for setting, antimony, colored stones, all sorts of precious stones and marble.<sup>3</sup>Moreover, in addition to all that I have provided for the holy house, I have a treasure of my own of gold and silver, and because of my devotion to the house of my God I give it to the house of my God:<sup>4</sup>3,000 talents of gold, of the gold of Ophir, and 7,000 talents of refined silver, for overlaying the walls of the house,<sup>5</sup>and for all the work to be done by craftsmen, gold for the things of gold and silver for the things of silver. Who then will offer willingly, consecrating himself today to the LORD?"<sup>6</sup>Then the leaders of fathers' houses made their freewill offerings, as did also the leaders of the tribes, the commanders of thousands and of hundreds, and the officers over the king's work.<sup>7</sup>They gave for the service of the house of God 5,000 talents and 10,000 darics of gold, 10,000 talents of silver, 18,000 talents of bronze and 100,000 talents of iron.<sup>8</sup>And whoever had precious stones gave them to the treasury of the house of the LORD, in the care of Jehiel the Gershonite.<sup>9</sup>Then the people rejoiced because they had given willingly, for with a whole heart they had offered freely to the LORD. David the king also rejoiced greatly.<sup>10</sup>Therefore David blessed the LORD in the presence of all the assembly. And David said: "Blessed are you, O LORD, the God of Israel our father, forever and ever.<sup>11</sup>Yours, O LORD, is the greatness and the power and the glory and the victory and the majesty, for all that is in the heavens and in the earth is yours. Yours is the kingdom, O LORD, and you are exalted as head above all.<sup>12</sup>Both riches and honor come from you, and you rule over all. In your hand are power and might, and in your hand it is to make great and to give strength to all.<sup>13</sup>And now we thank you, our God, and praise your glorious name.<sup>14</sup>"But who am I, and what is my people, that we should be able thus to offer willingly? For all things come from you, and of your own have we given you.<sup>15</sup>For we are strangers before you and sojourners, as all our fathers were. Our days on the earth are like a shadow, and there is no abiding.<sup>16</sup>O LORD our God, all this abundance that we have provided for building you a house for your holy name comes from your hand and is all your own.<sup>17</sup>I know, my God, that you test the heart and have pleasure in uprightness. In the uprightness of my heart I have freely offered all these things, and now I have seen your people, who are present here, offering freely and joyously to you.<sup>18</sup>O LORD, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, our fathers, keep forever such purposes and thoughts in the hearts of your people, and direct their hearts toward you.<sup>19</sup>Grant to Solomon my son a whole heart that he may keep your commandments, your testimonies, and your statutes, performing all, and that he may build the palace for which I have made provision."<sup>20</sup>Then David said to all the assembly, "Bless the LORD your God." And all the assembly blessed the LORD, the God of their fathers, and bowed their heads and paid homage to the LORD and to the king.<sup>21</sup>And they offered sacrifices to the LORD, and on the next day offered burnt offerings to the LORD, 1,000 bulls, 1,000 rams, and 1,000 lambs, with their drink offerings, and sacrifices in abundance for all Israel.<sup>22</sup>And they ate and drank before the LORD on that day with great gladness. And they made Solomon the son of David king the second time, and they anointed him as prince for the LORD, and Zadok as priest.<sup>23</sup>Then Solomon sat on the throne of the LORD as king in place of David his father. And he prospered, and all Israel obeyed him.<sup>24</sup>All the leaders and the mighty men, and also all the sons of King David, pledged their allegiance to King Solomon.<sup>25</sup>And the LORD made Solomon very great in the sight of all Israel and bestowed on him such royal majesty as had not been on any king before him in Israel.<sup>26</sup>Thus David the son of Jesse reigned over all Israel.<sup>27</sup>The time that he reigned over Israel was forty years. He reigned seven years in Hebron and thirty-three years in Jerusalem.<sup>28</sup>Then he died at a good age, full of days, riches, and honor. And Solomon his son reigned in his place.<sup>29</sup>Now the acts of King David, from first to last, are written in the Chronicles of Samuel the seer, and in the Chronicles of Nathan the prophet, and in the Chronicles of Gad the seer,<sup>30</sup>with accounts of all his rule and his might and of the circumstances that came upon him and upon Israel and upon all the kingdoms of the countries.
29.overview:
David tells the assembly that Solomon is young and the work is great, lists what he has provided as king, and then gives his own private fortune on top of it — three thousand talents of the gold of Ophir, for overlaying the walls (vv. 1-4). He asks who else will offer willingly, and the leaders answer with an avalanche, and the people rejoice because they had given willingly (vv. 5-9). Then his last prayer: everything belongs to God, of your own have we given you, we are strangers and our days are a shadow — and two petitions, that God would keep his people's hearts and grant Solomon a whole one (vv. 10-19). Sacrifices, a feast, and Solomon sat on the throne of the LORD (vv. 20-25). Then David dies, full of days (vv. 26-30).

The obituary is written to be read against Saul's in chapter 10, and the whole book stands between the two.
29.theology:
Verse 14 is the theology of giving in one line: all things come from you, and of your own have we given you. Nobody has ever handed God anything he did not supply first, including the willingness to hand it over — which is why David's next petition is that God would keep that willingness in place (v. 18). Hearts do not hold themselves steady, and the only prayer worth praying about that is addressed to the one who can take hold of them.

And verse 23 finishes what 17:14 began: Solomon sat on the throne of the LORD as king. Israel's monarchy was a tenancy in God's own kingdom. That is the sentence that made this book writable for people who had no king at all — losing the tenant did not put the kingdom on the market.
29.examples:
David gave his private fortune on top of what he had provided as king, and specified that it go on the walls — spread over a surface where everyone would see it and no one would know whose it was. He had spent forty years having his victories written down, and chose at the end to disappear into the plating of a room.

Verse 9 puts the joy after the giving, not before it: they rejoiced because they had given willingly. It is an order of events most people never test.

Three times in three chapters he asked God for one thing for his son — a whole heart — and it is the last thing this book records him saying. Solomon did not keep it. The request was still the right one, and a father who prays it has asked for the only thing worth having.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Who Then Will Offer Willingly?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David tells the whole assembly what he had told Solomon privately — the boy is young and inexperienced, and the work is great, for the palace will not be for man but for the LORD God (v. 1). He lists what he has provided as king (v. 2), and then goes further: I have a treasure of my own of gold and silver, and because of my devotion to the house of my God I give it — three thousand talents of the gold of Ophir and seven thousand of refined silver, for overlaying the walls (vv. 3-4). Then the question: Who then will offer willingly, consecrating himself today to the LORD? (v. 5). The leaders answer with an avalanche of gold, silver, bronze, iron and precious stones (vv. 6-8), and the people rejoiced because they had given willingly (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: The question in verse 5 is, in Hebrew, who will fill his hand today for the LORD — which is the phrase used for ordaining a priest. Bringing a gift to this house is being described as being consecrated to serve in it.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 9 puts the joy on the far side of the giving. They did not give because they were glad; they were glad because they had given, and the old king watching them was gladder still.

verseByVerse.quote: And David the king said to all the assembly, "Solomon my son, whom alone God has chosen, is young and inexperienced, and the work is great, for the palace will not be for man but for the LORD God. So I have provided for the house of my God, so far as I was able, the gold for the things of gold, the silver for the things of silver, and the bronze for the things of bronze, the iron for the things of iron, and wood for the things of wood, besides great quantities of onyx and stones for setting, antimony, colored stones, all sorts of precious stones and marble. Moreover, in addition to all that I have provided for the holy house, I have a treasure of my own of gold and silver, and because of my devotion to the house of my God I give it to the house of my God:
verseByVerse.commentary:
David speaks to the assembly one more time, and he begins by saying in public what he had said to his son in private.

Solomon my son, whom alone God has chosen, is young and inexperienced, and the work is great, for the palace will not be for man but for the LORD God.

He tells the entire kingdom that the new king is not ready. It is not a betrayal; it is the argument he is about to build on, because if the boy is not equal to it and the work is enormous, then everyone in the room has something to do about it. And the standard is set in the last clause: the building is not for a man. That is why the young king's inexperience matters and why the cost cannot be trimmed.

Then he lists what he has already provided as king — gold for the gold work, silver for the silver, bronze, iron, timber, onyx, antimony, coloured stones, marble. Everything matched to its purpose. That is the state provision, gathered out of forty years of tribute and war.

And then verse 3, which is where the chapter turns.

Moreover, in addition to all that I have provided for the holy house, I have a treasure of my own of gold and silver, and because of my devotion to the house of my God I give it to the house of my God.

His own money. Not the treasury, not the spoil of the Ammonite wars, not what the commanders had dedicated — the private fortune of an old man, given on top of everything he had already arranged as king. And the reason he offers is not duty or example or the needs of the project. It is my devotion to the house of my God — a word that means delight, taking pleasure in a thing. He wanted to.

verseByVerse.quote: 3,000 talents of gold, of the gold of Ophir, and 7,000 talents of refined silver, for overlaying the walls of the house, and for all the work to be done by craftsmen, gold for the things of gold and silver for the things of silver. Who then will offer willingly, consecrating himself today to the LORD?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The figures are given: three thousand talents of gold, and it is the gold of Ophir, the finest known, the standard of quality a psalm uses when it wants to say purest. Seven thousand talents of refined silver.

And then he says what it is for. For overlaying the walls of the house.

Not for a vessel with his name on it, not for a memorial gate, not for the ark's own chamber. His personal fortune goes onto the walls, spread thin over a surface, where everybody would see it and nobody would know whose it was. A man who had spent his life having his victories written down chose, at the end, to disappear into the plating of a room.

Then the question to the assembly, and the way he asks it is the most striking thing in the chapter. Who then will offer willingly, consecrating himself today to the LORD?

The Hebrew behind that last phrase is a fixed expression: who will fill his hand today for the LORD. It is the language used when a priest is ordained — Moses is told to fill the hands of Aaron and his sons, and the filled hand is the sign that a man has been set apart for God's service.

So David does not ask for a subscription. He asks who will be ordained today, and the way a man answers is by putting something in his own hand and holding it out. Giving is being described as consecration, and the two are not being compared. They are the same act.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the leaders of fathers' houses made their freewill offerings, as did also the leaders of the tribes, the commanders of thousands and of hundreds, and the officers over the king's work. They gave for the service of the house of God 5,000 talents and 10,000 darics of gold, 10,000 talents of silver, 18,000 talents of bronze and 100,000 talents of iron. And whoever had precious stones gave them to the treasury of the house of the LORD, in the care of Jehiel the Gershonite. Then the people rejoiced because they had given willingly, for with a whole heart they had offered freely to the LORD. David the king also rejoiced greatly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The response is enormous. The heads of families, the tribal leaders, the commanders of thousands and hundreds, the officers over the king's work — five thousand talents of gold, ten thousand talents of silver, eighteen thousand of bronze, a hundred thousand of iron, and every man who owned precious stones handed them in to Jehiel the Gershonite for the treasury.

One item in that list is a curiosity. Alongside the talents of gold the text counts ten thousand darics, and a daric is a Persian coin that did not exist for another five hundred years. The Chronicler has quietly converted an ancient sum into money his own readers used, the way a writer today might give a medieval price in modern currency. It is not a slip. It is a man making sure the people in front of him understand what was given.

Then verse 9, and it is about none of the metals.

Then the people rejoiced because they had given willingly, for with a whole heart they had offered freely to the LORD. David the king also rejoiced greatly.

Three separate words for willingness are piled into one sentence — willingly, whole heart, freely — and then the joy is placed carefully on the far side of the act. They did not give because they were in a good mood. They rejoiced because they had given, which is an order of events most people never test and every generous person knows.

The final clause is recorded separately, as though the writer wanted it to stand on its own. The old king, who had been refused the one thing he wanted to do, watched other people fund it and was gladder than any of them.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David blesses God in front of everybody. Yours, O LORD, is the greatness and the power and the glory and the victory and the majesty ... Yours is the kingdom (v. 11); riches and honour come from him and he rules over all (vv. 12-13). Then the turn: But who am I, and what is my people, that we should be able thus to offer willingly? For all things come from you, and of your own have we given you (v. 14). We are strangers before you and sojourners ... our days on the earth are like a shadow (v. 15). He appeals to the God who tests hearts (vv. 16-17), and ends with two petitions: that God would keep forever such purposes and thoughts in the hearts of your people (v. 18), and grant Solomon a whole heart (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 14 is chapter 17's question asked again at the end of a life, and widened. There it was who am I and what is my house; here it is who am I and what is my people. Forty years of answers have not made the question smaller.
verseByVerse.examples: His last recorded prayer asks God to hold his people's willingness in place and to give his son a whole heart. He knew that a day like this one does not sustain itself, and that nobody keeps his own heart.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore David blessed the LORD in the presence of all the assembly. And David said: "Blessed are you, O LORD, the God of Israel our father, forever and ever. Yours, O LORD, is the greatness and the power and the glory and the victory and the majesty, for all that is in the heavens and in the earth is yours. Yours is the kingdom, O LORD, and you are exalted as head above all. Both riches and honor come from you, and you rule over all. In your hand are power and might, and in your hand it is to make great and to give strength to all. And now we thank you, our God, and praise your glorious name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then David blesses God in front of the whole assembly, and what follows is the last great prayer of his life.

Blessed are you, O LORD, the God of Israel our father, forever and ever. Yours, O LORD, is the greatness and the power and the glory and the victory and the majesty, for all that is in the heavens and in the earth is yours. Yours is the kingdom, O LORD, and you are exalted as head above all.

Five nouns, and every one of them is the sort of thing a king is congratulated on. Greatness, power, glory, victory, majesty. David has all five by any human measure — he took Jerusalem, beat the Philistines twice, broke the Syrian coalition, and is standing in front of a kingdom that runs from Egypt to the Euphrates. He hands the entire list over in one breath and says none of it is his.

Then yours is the kingdom, which in this book is not a figure of speech. He has just told the nation that his son will sit on the throne of the kingdom of the LORD.

Christians have been finishing the Lord's Prayer with those words for a very long time — the kingdom, and the power, and the glory. The sentence stands in the later copies of Matthew rather than the earliest, and wherever the church first put it there, it came out of this prayer. An old man at the end of his reign gave the church the words it uses to hand everything back.

Verse 12 then names two of those gifts by name. Both riches and honor come from you, and you rule over all. In your hand are power and might, and in your hand it is to make great and to give strength to all.

Riches and honour. Hold those two words, because they come back. Sixteen verses later the chronicle will close the reign by saying that David died at a good age, full of days, riches and honour — the very pair he has just said belong to God and come out of his hand. The obituary is written in the vocabulary of the prayer, which means the writer wants nobody to mistake where the old man's wealth and standing had come from.

And there is a phrase in the middle of the verse that no king says lightly: in your hand it is to make great. Greatness is something God does to people. David had been told exactly that at the start, when the word came through Nathan promising to make his name like the name of the great ones of the earth, and forty years later he repeats it back as doctrine.

And the paragraph ends in the plainest way possible: And now we thank you, our God, and praise your glorious name. After the greatness and the majesty and the dominion over all things — thank you.

verseByVerse.quote: "But who am I, and what is my people, that we should be able thus to offer willingly? For all things come from you, and of your own have we given you. For we are strangers before you and sojourners, as all our fathers were. Our days on the earth are like a shadow, and there is no abiding.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But who am I, and what is my people, that we should be able thus to offer willingly?

He has asked that before. Standing in front of the ark after Nathan brought him the covenant, he sat down and said: who am I, O LORD God, and what is my house. Decades have passed. He has taken a capital, buried a son, buried the men who died in a plague he caused, handed over a kingdom. And the question comes back unchanged except that it has got wider — not my house now, but my people.

What he cannot get over is not that God gave him a throne. It is that the assembly has just been able to give something away. He treats the capacity for generosity as the astonishing thing, and then explains why.

For all things come from you, and of your own have we given you.

Every talent in that pile had been mined, transported, taxed or captured, and every stage of it had run through God's hands before it reached theirs. So the offering was not a transfer of wealth from Israel to God. It was Israel handing back a fraction of what it was holding, and being thanked for it. Nobody has ever given God anything he did not provide first, including the willingness to hand it over.

Then verse 15, and it is said by a man with a hundred thousand talents of iron in his storehouses.

For we are strangers before you and sojourners, as all our fathers were. Our days on the earth are like a shadow, and there is no abiding.

Strangers and sojourners are resident foreigners — people with no title to the ground they stand on, living somewhere at the owner's pleasure. God had used exactly those words about Israel and the land: the land is mine, and you are strangers and sojourners with me. David is not being morbid and he is not disparaging what he has. He is stating the terms of the tenancy.

And the last clause has no comfort in it at all. Our days are a shadow, and there is nothing here to hold. The men who wrote the letter to the Hebrews said the same of Abraham and the rest: they confessed they were strangers and exiles on the earth, and people who talk like that are looking for a country. David is about to die, and he says it in a prayer, in public, on the best day of his old age.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD our God, all this abundance that we have provided for building you a house for your holy name comes from your hand and is all your own. I know, my God, that you test the heart and have pleasure in uprightness. In the uprightness of my heart I have freely offered all these things, and now I have seen your people, who are present here, offering freely and joyously to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
O LORD our God, all this abundance that we have provided for building you a house for your holy name comes from your hand and is all your own. He says it again, in case the first time was mistaken for modesty. The pile in the courtyard is God's property and always was.

Then the prayer does something unexpected and rather bold.

I know, my God, that you test the heart and have pleasure in uprightness. In the uprightness of my heart I have freely offered all these things.

He is claiming a clean motive, out loud, to the God who examines motives. That would be intolerable from most men and it is not a claim to a clean life — this is the king of the census and of the roof at evening. It is a claim about one act. He knows why he gave the gold, he knows God is testing exactly that, and he is willing to say what he found when he looked.

And then the part he plainly enjoyed most: and now I have seen your people, who are present here, offering freely and joyously to you. He has watched the whole assembly do what he did, and he stops the prayer to mention it. An old leader's last public satisfaction was not that the fund was full. It was that he had seen their faces while they gave.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, our fathers, keep forever such purposes and thoughts in the hearts of your people, and direct their hearts toward you. Grant to Solomon my son a whole heart that he may keep your commandments, your testimonies, and your statutes, performing all, and that he may build the palace for which I have made provision."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the two petitions the prayer has been travelling towards, and both of them ask God to do something inside people.

O LORD, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, our fathers, keep forever such purposes and thoughts in the hearts of your people, and direct their hearts toward you.

He is looking at a courtyard full of gold given gladly by people who meant every ounce of it, and he asks God to make it last. Because he knows it will not last by itself. He had seen a nation dance the ark up a hill and he had seen the same nation forget it was in a field for twenty years. He had felt his own heart go where it should not, and he knew there was no mechanism inside a man for holding it steady.

So he asks God to keep the purposes and to steer the hearts, and there is nothing sentimental in it. The verb he uses for direct is one for making something firm and pointing it. Left alone, hearts drift; and the only prayer worth praying about that is addressed to the one who can take hold of them.

Then the last petition of his life.

Grant to Solomon my son a whole heart that he may keep your commandments, your testimonies, and your statutes, performing all, and that he may build the palace for which I have made provision.

Not a long reign. Not wealth, not victory, not sons. A whole heart — the thing he had asked for in chapter 22 when he prayed for discretion so that his son might keep the law, and again in chapter 28 when he told him to serve God with a whole heart and a willing mind. Three times, in three chapters, the same request, and it is the last thing this book records him saying.

The son built the palace and did not keep the whole heart. He ended with shrines to Chemosh and Molech on the hill facing the house he had raised. It does not make the prayer wrong. A father asked God for the one thing worth having for his child, and asked it as his final act, and the answer to that prayer came a thousand years later out of the same family, in a son whose heart was never divided for an instant.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–25 — Solomon on the Throne of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The assembly blesses God and bows (v. 20). A thousand bulls, a thousand rams and a thousand lambs are offered, and they ate and drank before the LORD on that day with great gladness (vv. 21-22). Solomon is made king a second time and anointed as prince for the LORD, with Zadok as priest — and then the sentence the book has been building towards: Then Solomon sat on the throne of the LORD as king in place of David his father (v. 23). The leaders, the mighty men and all David's sons pledge allegiance (v. 24), and God makes Solomon greater than any king before him in Israel (v. 25).
verseByVerse.theology: The throne of the LORD. God had called it in my house and in my kingdom when the covenant was made, and David had called it the throne of the kingdom of the LORD when he handed it over, and here a man sits down on it. Israel's monarchy was a tenancy from the start.
verseByVerse.examples: The day ends with a nation eating and drinking before the LORD with great gladness — as the day at Hebron ended, and as the day the ark came home ended.

verseByVerse.quote: Then David said to all the assembly, "Bless the LORD your God." And all the assembly blessed the LORD, the God of their fathers, and bowed their heads and paid homage to the LORD and to the king. And they offered sacrifices to the LORD, and on the next day offered burnt offerings to the LORD, 1,000 bulls, 1,000 rams, and 1,000 lambs, with their drink offerings, and sacrifices in abundance for all Israel. And they ate and drank before the LORD on that day with great gladness. And they made Solomon the son of David king the second time, and they anointed him as prince for the LORD, and Zadok as priest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then David said to all the assembly, Bless the LORD your God. He has just spent ten verses doing it and now he turns and tells them to. And they do — the whole assembly blessing the God of their fathers, bowing their heads and paying homage to the LORD and to the king.

The next day the sacrifices are enormous: a thousand bulls, a thousand rams, a thousand lambs, with their drink offerings, and sacrifices in abundance for all Israel. And then a sentence this book keeps arriving at: And they ate and drank before the LORD on that day with great gladness.

It ended at a table. So did the day the tribes made him king at Hebron, when they stayed three days and the far northern tribes brought the food. So did the day the ark came home, when every man and woman in the crowd went away with bread and meat and a cake of raisins. Whenever this kingdom gets something right, the record closes with people eating.

Then Solomon is made king the second time, anointed as prince for the LORD, with Zadok anointed priest beside him. The first time had been a hurried business at a spring with a coup running in the next valley. This one is done properly, in daylight, in front of the nation, with the priest and the prince anointed together.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Solomon sat on the throne of the LORD as king in place of David his father. And he prospered, and all Israel obeyed him. All the leaders and the mighty men, and also all the sons of King David, pledged their allegiance to King Solomon. And the LORD made Solomon very great in the sight of all Israel and bestowed on him such royal majesty as had not been on any king before him in Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Solomon sat on the throne of the LORD as king in place of David his father.

The throne of the LORD. Not the throne of Israel, not the throne of David — and this is the third time the book has said it. God had called it my house and my kingdom when the covenant was made through Nathan. David had called it the throne of the kingdom of the LORD when he presented his son to the assembly. Now a man sits down on it, and the chronicle records whose chair it was.

That is the sentence that let this book be written at all. Its first readers had no king and no independence, and if the throne had ever belonged to David it was gone. It never did. The kingdom was the LORD's, held in tenancy by a family he had chosen, and losing the tenant did not put the kingdom on the market.

Then the succession is secured in the way that matters: All the leaders and the mighty men, and also all the sons of King David, pledged their allegiance to King Solomon. All the sons — including the older brothers, one of whom had tried to take the throne.

Verse 25 then answers the prayer of a few minutes earlier in a way nobody in the courtyard can have missed. And the LORD made Solomon very great in the sight of all Israel and bestowed on him such royal majesty as had not been on any king before him in Israel.

Majesty is the word David had just handed over — yours, O LORD, is the greatness and the power and the glory and the victory and the majesty. He gave it away in the prayer and God put it on his son before the day was out. That is what the whole prayer said would happen: in your hand it is to make great, and nobody has ever lost anything by giving it back first.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The obituary is four sentences. Thus David the son of Jesse reigned over all Israel (v. 26); forty years, seven in Hebron and thirty-three in Jerusalem (v. 27); then he died at a good age, full of days, riches, and honor, and Solomon reigned in his place (v. 28). And the sources are named — the chronicles of Samuel the seer, Nathan the prophet and Gad the seer, with accounts of his rule and his might and of the circumstances that came upon him (vv. 29-30).
verseByVerse.theology: Set it beside the other obituary in this book. Saul died for his breach of faith and because he did not seek the LORD. David died at a good age, full of days. The whole book stands between those two paragraphs.
verseByVerse.examples: The epitaph calls him the son of Jesse. It had been a sneer in the mouths of Saul and Nabal and a rebel, and a man once took it and swore allegiance by it, and the chronicle of the kingdom uses it as his name.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus David the son of Jesse reigned over all Israel. The time that he reigned over Israel was forty years. He reigned seven years in Hebron and thirty-three years in Jerusalem. Then he died at a good age, full of days, riches, and honor. And Solomon his son reigned in his place. Now the acts of King David, from first to last, are written in the Chronicles of Samuel the seer, and in the Chronicles of Nathan the prophet, and in the Chronicles of Gad the seer, with accounts of all his rule and his might and of the circumstances that came upon him and upon Israel and upon all the kingdoms of the countries.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the obituary, and it has been written to be read against another one.

Thus David the son of Jesse reigned over all Israel. The time that he reigned over Israel was forty years. He reigned seven years in Hebron and thirty-three years in Jerusalem. Then he died at a good age, full of days, riches, and honor. And Solomon his son reigned in his place.

Now turn back nineteen chapters. So Saul died for his breach of faith. He broke faith with the LORD in that he did not keep the command of the LORD, and also consulted a medium, seeking guidance. He did not seek guidance from the LORD. Therefore the LORD put him to death and turned the kingdom over to David the son of Jesse.

Two kings, two paragraphs, and the whole book standing between them. One died on a hill with his armour in a Philistine temple because he did not seek the LORD. The other died in his bed at a good age, full of days, having spent his last years buying a threshing floor, weighing out gold and praying for his son's heart. Everything in between is the difference between those two sentences.

And the epitaph calls him the son of Jesse. Saul used that phrase when he could not bear to say the name. Nabal used it to refuse a man food. A rebel raised the northern tribes with it. And in a stronghold in the wilderness, before any of this, the Spirit came on a man called Amasai and he took the insult and made it his oath: we are yours, O David, and with you, O son of Jesse. The official chronicle of the kingdom of Israel uses the sneer as his name.

The sources are then named: the chronicles of Samuel the seer, of Nathan the prophet, and of Gad the seer. Three prophets, and every one of them is remembered for bringing this king or the last one a word he did not want to hear. Samuel told Saul the kingdom was torn from him. Nathan told David the house would be built by somebody else, and later told him a story about a lamb. Gad brought him three punishments and made him choose. The record of the reign was kept by the men who had stood in front of it and said no.

The closing verse says what those records contained: his rule, his might, and ... the circumstances that came upon him and upon Israel and upon all the kingdoms of the countries. The word behind circumstances is simply the times — what happened to him. The chronicle of a reign is not only what a king did. It is also everything that was done to him, and the prophets who kept the record wrote down both.

So the book closes. A shepherd from Bethlehem, a fugitive at Ziklag, a king who got the ark wrong and then got it right, a man who counted his soldiers and buried seventy thousand of them, who bought a threshing floor at full price because he would not offer what cost him nothing, and who died having never laid a stone of the house he gave his life to. The house was built and filled with glory and burned to the ground four hundred years later. The throne it stood beside was the LORD's, and he had promised it to this family forever, and a thousand years after the last of David's sons was dragged in chains out of a broken city an angel stood in a village in Galilee and said that the Lord God would give a child the throne of his father David, and that of his kingdom there would be no end.
